body.t: FaaS (Function as a Service): Also called serverless computing, FaaS can automatically allocate the computing resources needed to run an application. A FaaS platform makes it easy to write the code needed for an application's backend.
CaaS (Container as a Service): CaaS provides container-based applications. CaaS platforms allow rapid, scalable deployment of applications using container technologies such as Docker.

DaaS (Desktop as a Service): DaaS provides virtual desktops in the cloud. With DaaS, users can run virtual desktops on their own terminals. This allows access to applications and data regardless of device type or operating-system differences.
NaaS (Network as a Service): NaaS provides network functions in the cloud, enabling easy network configuration and management.

AIaaS (Artificial Intelligence as a Service): AIaaS is a service running artificial intelligence and machine learning in the cloud, making it easy to train machine-learning models and perform inference.

body.t: Word2vec is a technique for natural language processing (NLP) published in 2013. The word2vec algorithm uses a neural network model to learn word associations from a large corpus of text. Once trained, such a model can detect synonymous words or suggest additional words for a partial sentence. As the name implies, word2vec represents each distinct word with a particular list of numbers called a vector. The vectors are chosen carefully such that they capture the semantic and syntactic qualities of words; as such, a simple mathematical function (cosine similarity) can indicate the level of semantic similarity between the words represented by those vectors.

body.t: Torahiko Terada was a Japanese physicist, essayist, and haiku poet. He is also known by the pen names Fuyuhiko Yoshimura, Torahiko, Newton, and Yabukoji. From Kochi Prefecture. Graduated from the University of Tokyo's physics department. During his time at the Fifth Higher School in Kumamoto, he met physicist Takuro Tamaru and Natsume Soseki, regarding these 2 as his teachers throughout his life. After entering the University of Tokyo, he published short pieces including sketch essays. Subsequently, alongside his physics research, he wrote essays under the name Fuyuhiko Yoshimura. His essay collections include Fuyuhiko Collection.

body.t: In October 2011, actress Sayuri Yoshinaga, who continues to recite atomic-bomb poems, travels to Britain at the invitation of the University of Oxford. Her first recital in Europe is accompanied by Ryuichi Sakamoto. A piano a hundred and ten years old plays a poignant melody, and a dove that wandered accidentally into the chapel flies across the ceiling at the climax of the long poem “Lamentation.” Why did her recitation move British audiences? This documentary dramatically depicts the day's events while introducing Yoshinaga's journey of over twenty years with atomic-bomb poetry. The moment atomic-bomb poems crossed national borders now comes alive here.

It receives remote-control information and sequencer data through the hardware MIDI input and transmits them with MADI data packets. Each channel's information in a MADI signal contains several bits for additional information, including various types of information (Channel Status). body.t: IGMP is a mechanism allowing multiple terminals to share 1 IP address and receive the same data, for example during video distribution. Covering multiple terminals with 1 data transmission enables efficient network use and prevents problems such as delays. However, although IGMP makes data distribution more efficient, data are sent to every terminal sharing the IP address (= every terminal connected to the switch).

IGMP snooping means snooping (peeking at) data flowing through each port of an intelligent switch so that data is not sent to terminals that do not need it. It enables more efficient transmission of large-volume data, such as video delivered using IGMP, and efficient network use.

body.t: Subtle is the Lord: The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein is a biography of Albert Einstein written by Abraham Pais. First published in 1982 by Oxford University Press, the book is one of the most acclaimed biographies of the scientist.
This was not the first popular biography of Einstein, but it was the first to focus on his scientific research as opposed to his life as a popular figure.

Pais, renowned for his work in theoretical particle physics, was a friend of Einstein's at the Institute for Advanced Study in his early career. Originally published in English in the United States and the United Kingdom, the book has translations in over a dozen languages.

Pais later released a sequel to the book in 1994 titled Einstein Lived Here and, after his death in 2000, the University Press released a posthumous reprint of the biography in 2005, with a new foreword by Roger Penrose. Considered very popular for a science book, the biography sold tens of thousands of copies of both paperback and hardcover versions in its first year.
The book has received many reviews
and, the year after its initial publication, it won both the 1983 National Book Award for Nonfiction, in Science (Hardcover), and the 1983 Science Writing Award.

body.t: The “trautonium” is an electronic instrument invented in Berlin in 1929.
Like today's synthesizers, it has knobs for adjusting filters and a part plucked with the fingers to produce sound.
Distinctively, the sound-producing part consists of a long, thin metal plate and wire stretched horizontally rather than a keyboard.
Today, it is what is called a “ribbon controller,” used in instruments such as the Otamatone.

As seen in the ondes Martenot and theremin, electrical instruments of the time had very limited polyphony, generally barely managing to produce a single note. This instrument was devised to provide rich polyphonic sounds and partials. It was released by Telefunken. Although it has no keyboard, it differs decisively from the ondes Martenot in having “control tiers” for the right and left hands, like a two-tier clavichord; its selling point was the ability to modulate generated sounds using relaxation oscillator circuits and other means to produce various timbral effects. It also has capabilities impossible on the ondes Martenot, such as performing a glissando while simultaneously sounding a triad.

Although concertos were written by Hindemith, Genzmer, and others in its home country of Germany, it declined as the later Hammond organ took its popularity. In a promotional video featuring Oskar Sala, he performs an arrangement of Paganini's Caprices.

body.t: The music of Ars Nova (new art)

Shortly after the beginning of the 14th century, France’s Vitry (Ph. de Vitri, 1291-1361) theoretically summarized the new music of the early 14th century and published it under the title “Ars Nova,” leading music of this period to be called Ars Nova. Later, “Ars Nova” came to be used as a term for the music of the entire 14th century.

The Notre-Dame school ceased its activities around the middle of the 13th century, but the music of the subsequent period until Ars Nova is called Ars Antiqua (old art). This does not mean that its content is old; it simply means music of the preceding age when viewed from the Ars Nova era. During Ars Antiqua, mensural notation developed further, and a new musical form called the motetus reached its heyday.

body.t: Musique sérielle (French), Serial Music (English), Serielle Musik (German)

The manipulation of a tone row containing all 12 semitones in one octave is called twelve-tone technique; total serialism applies this manipulation of tone rows to all sonic events, including duration, intensity, and timbre. It is also called integral serialism. Total serialism, begun by O. Messiaen in “Mode of Values and Intensities” (1949), spread through the avant-garde music world through L. Nono, P. Boulez, K. Stockhausen, B. Maderna, and others who appeared at the Darmstadt Summer Courses for New Music in the early 50s. In the United States, M. Babbitt, E. Carter, and others adopted twelve-tone technique and total serialism as an extension of the European tradition, building an academic American contemporary music scene distinct from experimental music. Behind the rise of these compositional techniques based on a kind of automatism lay the modernist view of art that all art proceeds according to its own internal laws. Meanwhile, some criticized total serialism, questioning the audibility of series applied to parameters other than pitch. If atonality and twelve-tone technique are regarded as the destination of progressive development in music history, total serialism was both the culmination of that development and a dead end. In the 70s, post-serialist composers such as B. Ferneyhough wrote works with complex textures following serial procedures, putting forward compositional techniques after total serialism. Later, the ideas of total serialism would be applied to algorithmic composition.

body.t: The theremin (Russian: Терменвокс, Termenvoks) is the world’s first electronic musical instrument, invented in 1920 by Russian inventor Lev Sergeyevich Termen

. In Russian and English it is also called Thereminvox (Терменвокс; Thereminvox), meaning “Theremin’s voice.” In English it is spelled Theremin or Theramin. This derives from the French-style spelling used by the inventor and is pronounced something like “teremin” or “seremin.” In Japanese, the spelling “teremin” was used for many years in music books
. Around 2000, Masami Takeuchi and others independently began using the spelling “terumin,” which also spread through the film of the same name released in 2001.

body.t: The thing-in-itself is what Kant, said to synthesize continental rationalism and British empiricism, postulated in Critique of Pure Reason when examining experience itself as something behind experience and a necessary condition for making it possible.

Responding to Hume’s claim that “nothing can be known except what is experienced through the senses,” Kant held that “something producing experience,” the “thing in itself,” must be presupposed, but that such “things in themselves” cannot be experienced. Things in themselves cannot be cognized and do not depend on our subjectivity for their existence. Nor do they follow the law of causality.

According to Kant, there is no evidence whatsoever that the world of things-in-themselves exists. We do not know whether an intellectual order like the “thing-in-itself” exists, but subsequent experience will probably justify it.

The skill and art of craftspeople﻿
A perfect fusion of intellect, technology and art﻿
A desperate stratagem: a scheme to deceive an enemy even by causing suffering to oneself or one’s allies.﻿
Techne is the origin of “technique” and “technology.”
Latin ars was ancient Romans' translation of Greek techne and is the origin of “art.”
Techne is applied to virtually all human-made products, from arts such as painting and sculpture to medicine, architecture, rhetoric, and cooking.﻿
Until the Renaissance, art and artisans' skills were deeply connected.
From the 18th-century Age of Enlightenment onward, art came to be regarded as distinct from artisans’ techniques and handiwork.﻿
In ancient Greece, knowledge and abilities accompanying human making generally were respected and collectively called techne.

body.t: Evaluation board for a single-chip 60GHz millimeter-wave sensor with long-range antenna.

The IWR6843ISK is an easy-to-use 60GHz millimeter-wave sensor evaluation kit based on the IWR6843 device with a long-range antenna. The IWR6843ISK can also be used to evaluate both the IWR6843 and IWR6443 devices. This board allows access to point-cloud data and receipt of power through its USB interface.
Millimeter-wave tools and software support this kit, including mmWave Studio (MMWAVE-STUDIO) and the millimeter-wave software development kit (MMWAVE-SDK).

Additional boards can provide extra functions. For example, the DCA1000EVM allows access to raw sensor data through the LVDS interface. MMWAVEICBOOST provides software development and tracing functions through TI's CCS.
Combining IWR6843ISK and MMWAVEICBOOST enables interfacing with TI’s microcontroller (MCU) LaunchPad™ development-kit ecosystem.

body.t: A TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) magnetic sensor array is a technology for detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity and precision. It detects magnetic fields using the TMR effect—the property that resistance changes when the magnetization directions differ across a tunnel between 2 magnetic materials. Arranging multiple TMR elements side by side enables a TMR sensor array to detect magnetic fields over a wider area or measure particular directions and strengths in greater detail.

An MR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) sensor array unit is a unit comprising an array of magnetic sensors using the TMR effect. The TMR effect is a phenomenon in which electrical resistance changes according to differences in magnetization direction in ferromagnetic tunnel junctions. This property is used in sensors detecting magnetic-field direction and strength.

TMR sensor array units feature 360° angle measurement, high angular accuracy, low power consumption, and redundancy. Products optimized particularly for automotive and industrial applications also exist.﻿

TMR sensors have higher MR ratios (resistance change rates) than AMR (Anisotropy Magnetoresistance) or GMR (Giant Magnetoresistance). In TMR elements, the MR ratio reaches 100%, allowing highly sensitive magnetic detection.
Applications of TMR sensor-array units are progressing in fields requiring highly accurate angle measurement and magnetic-field detection.

body.t: Among technologies measuring and visualizing (imaging) brain activity (brain function), fNIRS, which uses near-infrared light, is attracting attention as a method supporting brain-function research because it enables functional brain imaging under conditions close to natural environments. Exploiting its ability to measure brain function noninvasively and with few restraints, fNIRS is used in a broad range of research: basic research such as “functional brain mapping,” linking brain function and structure, as well as medical, rehabilitation, sports-medicine, psychology, education, and engineering research and industrial fields including automobiles and cosmetics. Another major feature is its compatibility with other measurement methods, enabling simultaneous measurement. fNIRS is also sometimes called near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), optical topography, or “optical topo.”

body.t: Elixir (Japanese pronunciation: erikusa) is a dynamic, functional programming language running on the Erlang virtual machine (BEAM). Influenced by Ruby and Clojure, it has Ruby-like syntax. Strong in concurrent and distributed processing, it uses Erlang's powerful concurrency model.
Functional programming: Incorporates concepts such as immutability and higher-order functions.
Dynamic typing: Types are determined at runtime, allowing flexible development.
Runs on Erlang VM (BEAM): Inherits the Erlang VM's characteristics such as concurrent processing, distributed processing, and fault tolerance.
Concurrency: Concurrent processing based on the Actor model can be implemented easily.
Distributed systems: Also suited to building distributed systems and used for applications requiring high availability.
Ruby-like syntax: developers familiar with Ruby syntax may find it relatively easy to learn.﻿
Macros: metaprogramming using macros is also possible.﻿

body.t: —What is the origin of the name op.disc?

body.t: πTon/2 is a sound installation that intervenes in the continuity of the researches of Cod.Act on mechanical and sound organicity. It results from an experience on the deformation of an elastic form and its incidence on the evolution of a musical work.

The object is a flexible ring closed on itself. It is set in motion by torsional engines located inside its body. πTon, by twisting and waving on itself, moves in a very natural and unpredictable way.

The origin of the music created by πTon is a deep sound of bass clarinet. It evolves according to its movements and is diffused by loudspeakers located inside its body. When πTon moves slowly, its contractions and dilatations produce deep sensual sounds that evolve like deep breathes. When the movements become fast, nervous and brutal, the creature develops acid and sharp sound along the tube, like a nervous flow.

body.t: Has a Japanese wife. 2009-Now Sony CSL Researcher. Alexis André explores unprecedented creative activities by applying the latest digital media. He regards the creative process itself as art and bases his work on the idea that creators focus on interaction with this process. His overarching theme is defining next-generation entertainment relevant to digital natives as well. His research areas include computer-generated/assisted art, procedural design, computer graphics, HCI (human-computer interaction), computer vision, game psychology, and game design. His work has been exhibited at the Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM) and the international conference SIGGRAPH, and he has collaborated with numerous artists, from Open Reel Ensemble to Aomori University’s men’s rhythmic gymnastics team produced by Issey Miyake. He is also the originator of Sony’s experiential toy platform toio.

Born in 1982. Based in France and has also lived in Tokyo for over 20 years. Works across a broad range of artistic expression and, as part of this, opens new horizons of entertainment using generative methods. His creative activities are deeply rooted in generative and interactive art, exploring the intersection of art and technology. Major works include collaborations with ISSEY MIYAKE and “EōN,” an app for generative music and images created in collaboration with electronic musician Jean-Michel Jarre. He has presented works in various settings, including interactive installation exhibitions in Tokyo and art events around the world.

body.t: The goal of the Wiener filter is to compute a statistical estimate of an unknown signal using a related signal as an input and filtering it to produce the estimate. For example, the known signal might consist of an unknown signal of interest that has been corrupted by additive noise. The Wiener filter can be used to filter out the noise from the corrupted signal to provide an estimate of the underlying signal of interest. The Wiener filter is based on a statistical approach, and a more statistical account of the theory is given in the minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimator article.

body.t: Aiko Tezuka was born in Tokyo in 1976. Graduated from the Department of Oil Painting, College of Art and Design, Musashino Art University in 99, and completed the oil painting course in its Graduate School of Art and Design in 2001. Seeking a way to elucidate painting’s irreversible structure, she focuses on weaving and embroidery, whose production processes can be rewound, creating works through a distinctive method that exposes their structure by unraveling threads. In her early work “Pulling Out Warp Threads—Five Colors” (2004), in which she extracted and bundled only the green, red, blue, black, and yellow warp threads from a classical-style fabric, she revealed that a complex pattern is formed by weaving just 5 colors, while attempting to unravel the basic structure of painting, which produces various tones by layering primary colors. Her dismantled and reconstructed works reveal not only structure but also the time of those who spun the threads and the history dwelling in the fabric.

body.t: To explain the origin of the masses of several particles, including weak bosons, Peter Ware Higgs of the University of Edinburgh proposed a theory based on spontaneous symmetry breaking in 1964. This theory is called the Higgs mechanism.
The Higgs mechanism introduces a scalar field called the Higgs field, simultaneously introducing its corresponding scalar particle.
. This is called the Higgs particle. The Higgs particle is a boson with spin 0 and charge 0.

Experimental verification of whether the Higgs particle corresponding to a theoretical model containing the Higgs mechanism exists is key to determining whether the model reflects reality. In a broad sense, the term Higgs particle refers to a particle appearing in the Higgs mechanism, but it is often used specifically for the Higgs particle of the Standard Model (Weinberg–Salam theory). In the Standard Model, weak bosons (W±,Z) are held to acquire mass through the Higgs mechanism, while quarks and leptons are also held to gain mass through interactions with the Higgs field.

body.t: In 1983, Rubbia's research team accomplished a discovery of the century, finding 2 new types of elementary particle called “W bosons and Z bosons.” The greatest discovery of his life, it was a feat revolutionizing not only his career but science as a whole. Yet perhaps not many people know what W and Z bosons are.

These elementary particles control the internal processes of stars such as the Sun. This is the world inside atomic nuclei, the smallest constituents of matter, at an ultramicroscopic scale smaller than one quadrillionth (10−15) of a meter. one quadrillionth corresponds to the diameter of a hair if the distance from Earth to the Sun is taken as 1.
Theoretical physics holds that everything in the universe (including human bodies) is governed by 4 fundamental interactions (forces acting between 2 or more objects).

The 1st is probably the best-known electromagnetic force, mediated by elementary particles called photons. The 2nd is gravity, an attractive force acting between all matter possessing energy and mass, but its details have not yet been explained.

The 3rd is the strong interaction, mediated by elementary particles called gluons. Stronger than the electromagnetic force, they are named for binding elementary particles together like glue to form protons, neutrons, atomic nuclei, and so on. The 4th is the weak interaction, key to explaining mysteries such as “Why are elements like uranium radioactive?” and “How does the series of nuclear reactions producing the Sun's heat and light begin?” The elementary particles mediating this weak interaction are the W and Z bosons.

body.t: AI researchers have long sought AI that continues learning indefinitely. One route is to have AI rewrite its own code (program) to encourage self-improvement. More than 20 years ago, Jürgen Schmidhuber proposed the Gödel Machine, a hypothetical self-improving AI. A Gödel Machine rewrites its own code when it can mathematically prove that a self-modification will lead to improvement, thereby solving problems optimally. This is an important concept in the field of “meta-learning,” in which AI learns how to learn.

However, the Gödel Machine remains a theoretical entity, since it rests on the unrealistic assumption that one can “mathematically prove” that a self-modification brings improvement. We therefore devised a more practical approach in collaboration with Professor Jeff Clune's laboratory at the University of British Columbia. Using principles of open-ended algorithms resembling Darwinian evolution, it explores self-modifications leading to better performance on the basis of experience rather than mathematical proof.

body.t: Music consists of repetitions of short or long rhythmic cycles (metric cycles of 2–256 beats).
At the end of a large cycle, the deepest enormous gong (Gong Ageng) sounds, marking a division.
Particular gongs or metal percussion instruments strike different beats at different speeds.
Large gongs group instruments playing fine subdivisions (ketuk, kempyang, etc.), organizing structure like punctuation.
The slowest pulses (longest cycles) are handled by low gongs, fast pulses by small gongs.
Main instruments: Gong Ageng (huge gong), Kempul (suspended gong), Kenong (large horizontally placed gong), Ketuk/Kempyang (small metal percussion instruments).

body.t: Pelog is a major 7-note scale used in Indonesian gamelan music (in practice, 5 notes are often selected from it), meaning “beautiful.” Characterized by distinctive unequal intervals combining whole tones and semitones, it produces an exotic sound resembling the Okinawan scale and is prevalent in Bali and elsewhere.
Tone series: 1 octave consists of 7 notes (usually 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), but in 1 piece, 5 notes are often selected and played according to the pathet (mode).
Intervals: Unlike Western equal temperament, small intervals (around 100 cents) and large intervals (around 300 cents) coexist, making an unequal-interval scale with 100–300-cent spacing.
Resonance: a slightly poignant or exotic sound resembling the Okinawan (Ryukyuan) scale.
Regional differences: Intervals are not fixed, because villages differ in their sense of intervals.
Difference from slendro: contrasted with gamelan’s other representative scale, “slendro (an evenly spaced 5-note scale),” pelog mainly consists of 7 notes (or 5 selected from them).
Many gamelans heard at tourist destinations, such as Bali's gamelan gong kebyar, use this pelog scale.

body.t: Pelog selisir is one of the most representative and common scales (note series) in traditional gamelan music of Indonesia's Bali and Java islands.
A mode formed by extracting chiefly 5 notes (pentatonic) from the 7-note pelog scale, extensively used in “gamelan gong kebyar” and other forms synonymous with Balinese gamelan.
5-note scale (pentatonic): Select and play 5 notes from the 7-note pelog system.

Structure (approximation): expressed approximately in Western scale terms, it resembles (tonic, minor 2nd, minor 3rd, perfect 5th, minor 6th). Characterized by a melancholy, exotic resonance suggesting a slight resemblance to Japan’s Okinawan (Ryukyuan) scale.
Representative instruments: Mainly used in Gamelan Gong Kebyar, and most music tourists hear in Bali is based on this scale.
Pitch structure: narrow intervals and wide intervals coexist within 1 octave, producing distinctive fluctuation.

body.t: The “Perpetual Storytelling Apparatus” is a drawing machine illustrating a never-ending story by the use of patent drawings.

New visual connections and narrative layers emerge through the interweaving of the story with the depiction of technical developments.

body.t: The pompidou series, its 4th edition in 2022.

In 2017, the Centre Pompidou initiated a new event entitled Mutations/Creations, focused on the prospect and interaction of digital technology with creation; a realm shared by art, innovation and science. At the crossroads between fields, combining research, art and engineering, this annual event is co-organised by the Musée national d’art moderne and IRCAM, and calls on art, architecture, design and music.

This platform for solo and themed exhibitions acts as a critical observer and analytical tool of the impacts of creation on our society. How do various fields of creation use digital technology to open new industrial perspectives? How do they examine the social, economic and political effects, or the ethical limits of such industrial developments? What form do the mutations in the fields of music, art, design and architecture take, relative to techno-scientific progress?  At the heart of Mutations/Creations, the artist encounters the engineer, the philosopher encounters the designer, scientific innovation and technology draw inspiration from new thought, design and production processes.

In close synergy with the exhibitions, IRCAM presents Vertigo, its annual forum supported by the European Commission’s STARTS programme. This event host meetings, performances and shows in a dialogue between music, the arts, engineering, scientific research and new technology. The multitude of exchanges between creation, research and teaching is embodied by numerous partnerships with universities, research laboratories, and schools of art, architecture or design.

body.t: Born in 1937 to a family running a construction business in Genoa. After 2 years at the University of Florence, graduated from the Polytechnic University of Milan in 1964. From 1970 to 1977, jointly directed the architectural practice “Piano & Rogers” with Richard Rogers. They jointly developed the design for the Centre Pompidou, won through an architectural competition
. From 1977 to 1980, jointly directed Piano & Rice & Associates with structural engineer Peter Rice. In 1981, established Renzo Piano Building Workshop in his hometown of Genoa.

Major works would include the Centre Pompidou, which shocked the international scene; the passenger terminal design for Kansai International Airport, the greatest achievement in engineering and structural design in 20th-century architecture; and the Daimler City master plan for the redevelopment of Potsdamer Platz in Berlin. All respond to the technical challenges demanded by enormous buildings while also considering such matters as an international airport's symbolism and the surrounding historical context in Berlin.

body.t: As part of the REACH project in the Music Representation team at IRCAM, Somax for Live brings the real-time interactive capabilities of Somax2 directly into Ableton Live.

Developed by Manuel Poletti in collaboration with Marco Fiorini and Gérard Assayag, this new integration bridges advanced symbolic AI improvisation with a widely used digital audio workstation, opening new creative workflows for composers, performers, and producers.

Implemented as a collection of Max for Live devices, Somax for Live allows users to interactively co-create with the system within Live’s native environment, combining the temporal and stylistic modeling of Somax2 with the flexibility of Live’s clips, automations, and control interfaces. This tight coupling between musical intelligence and production tools encourages a fluid dialogue between human and machine musicianship, enabling adaptive accompaniment, generative composition, and exploratory performance practices within an accessible and modular setup.

This presentation will showcase the architecture, interaction paradigms, and artistic use cases of Somax for Live, illustrating how the REACH project advances hybrid human–AI co-creativity in contemporary music-making.

body.t: The SCHAEFFER dataset (Spectro-morphogical Corpus of Human-annotated Audio with Electroacoustic Features For Experimental Research) is a compilation of 1000 raw audio files accompanied by human annotations and morphological acoustic features. The audio files adhere to the concept of Sound Objects introduced by Pierre Schaeffer, a framework for the analysis and creation of sound that focuses on its typological and morphological characteristics. Inside the dataset, the annotations are provided in the form of free text, while the labels are pre-chosen from a list of classes, making the sound description fit into a suitable framework for digital analysis.

body.t: I head the data analysis core facility at the Paris Brain Institute (ICM). Our facility provides bioinformatics support for the analysis and management of neuroscience data, from multi-omics and spatial transcriptomics to AI in microscopy and neuroimaging analysis. We promote and support open science practices and, based on open science principles, ensure that valuable research data comply with the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable), making them findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable.

I am scientific coordinator of “Brain Body Digital Music Instrument,” a collaborative project with MSH Paris Nord, University Paris 8, CICM/MUSIDANSE, Soixante circuits, and Goldsmiths, University of London, funded by the French National Research Agency (ANR). This project develops open-source software and hardware for sound synthesis and composition using neuroelectrical signals (EEG, EMG).

Since 2009, I am working on interdisciplinary art research, within the research collective OuUnPo, the art organization Vision Forum, the research collective 1+1=3, and the EEGsynth association, wherein we develop multisensory neurofeedback performances and produce contemporary sound experiments and workshops. We develop an open-source platform for brain-computer-interfaces, and organize art, science and sci-art events.

body.t: “Cybernetic Serendipity” was an exhibition organized and held by curator Jasia Reichardt at London’s ICA (Institute of Contemporary Arts) in 1968, pioneering later art using computer technology.

The exhibition title reflects the influence of mathematician Norbert Wiener, who explained automatic control and feedback through “cybernetics” theory in engineering, physiology, and cultural terms. “Serendipity” means “accidentally discovering something unexpected.”

Reichardt assessed the exhibition as combining technology and the pioneering possibilities it opens with the immaturity of technology's reception in art: “It deals with possibilities rather than achievements, and in that sense is premature and optimistic. For so far computers have not revolutionized music, art, or poetry in the same way they have revolutionized science.”

body.t: Jean Baudrillard's thought pointed out that “reality” in contemporary society has been replaced by signs and images (simulacra). The following elements can be identified in an “alternative life” or way of living based on his perspective.
Contemporary society is surrounded by “genuine-looking fakes (simulacra)” produced by consumer society and media.

An alternative way of living: Deliberately find value in “meaningless” or “useless” things within a reality where everything is consumed and symbolized. Live autonomously with “narratives” stripped away, without following media-presented “models of desire.”
Use things for their actual functions and experiences rather than buying them for brand value or status (signs).

An alternative way of living: Stop presenting a “well-regarded self” through social media and advertising, and value experiences in physical spaces and places (asylums) simply for “being,” without anyone's evaluation.
Generative AI, VR, and social media create the “hyperreal,” more real than reality.

An alternative way of living: Value real experiences involving physical embodiment rather than shutting oneself into digital space. Leave the world of information and images and recover bodily pain and sensations.
As alternatives to “consumption,” Baudrillard valued non-symbolic-exchange relationships such as incalculable “seduction” that does not dominate others and unilateral “giving.”
Alternative way of living: stepping away from a calculating life (reckoning gains and losses) and choosing an unpredictable, seductive, passionate (eros) way of life.
Consumer society conceals “death” and “limits,” seeking eternal youth and perfection (= signs).
Alternative way of living: by accepting finitude and taking death and limits as real parts of life, one conversely lives “now, this moment” in the true sense.

body.t: Italian Futurism (Futurismo) was an avant-garde comprehensive artistic movement arising in Italy in the early 20th century (from 1909), celebrating speed, machines, violence, technology, and war, and seeking to destroy traditional art and social institutions. Beginning with Filippo Tommaso Marinetti's “Futurist Manifesto,” it expressed the dynamism of automobiles and industrial cities in painting, sculpture, architecture, and music.

Praise of speed and machines: As exemplified by the famous phrase “A racing car is more beautiful than the Winged Victory of Samothrace,” industrial society's speed and mechanical beauty were regarded as ultimate beauty.
Destruction of tradition and rebellion: Thoroughly rejected past cultural heritage, including museums, libraries, and academies.
Dynamism (powerful movement): Sought to express temporal continuity, movement, and light on canvas rather than static appearances.
Synthesis of the arts: sought to transform all areas of life, including literature, music, architecture, photography, fashion, and theatre, as well as painting and sculpture.
Alignment with politics: Affirmed war as “the world's only hygiene,” later inclining toward the Fascist movement.

Its background lies in technological evolution and the emergence of large cities challenging established values as Italy, then an underdeveloped country, rapidly industrialized in the early 20th century. The movement influenced Russian Constructivism and Dada, but opinions on its value as an artistic movement are divided because of its glorification of war and political extremism.

body.t: Video art is an artistic genre dealing with images and sound. It may use video equipment as its display (exhibition/screening) medium and electromagnetic recording media—formerly videotape, now DVDs and the like—for recording. This distinguishes it from works using screens and film. It began in the 1960s; the number of makers grew rapidly from the 1980s, when equipment became cheaper, and since the 1990s it has increasingly been encompassed within media art through to the present.

body.t: “The Invisible Museum in the Telephone Network” in 1991 was an event using the telephone network to exchange diverse cultural information and expand the museum’s function as an “information field.” “on the Web” not only constructed a “visible museum” within the rapidly expanding “internet” but also combined performances using ISDN lines with installation exhibitions and other activities. In the “Net Gallery,” works were presented using the latest browser software, including Netscape Navigator, Hot Java, and VRML Viewer, allowing audiences to enjoy real-time interaction with the works.

Holding an exhibition on a network does not mean transferring to the internet works and artists' actions developed in existing media. Nor is it certain whether these fit within the existing framework of “art.” Everything is a process, and it has only just begun. Understanding artists' works and actions on networks where Euclidean spacetime cannot apply requires an entirely new “recognition.” “on the Web” also called the audience's own “network literacy” into question.

body.t: The title pH derives from the chemical term for the hydrogen-ion concentration index, and the performance comprises 13 scenes following binary oppositions (question/answer, image/word, fact/fiction, public/private, real/unreal, etc.).

A vast amount of footage shot from various viewpoints and angles at various performance venues was edited by Dumb Type's Teiji Furuhashi into a video work going beyond mere documentation. It won the Sole d’Oro (Golden Sun) award at TTVV-Riccione (Italy) and the Best Stage Recording award at IMZ Dance Screen 92 (Germany).

body.t: “Open Water—Water (*) Opens” is a project seeking to revitalize Tokyo as a 21st-century water city by reaffirming the role rich waterways have played in Tokyo's history and uncovering water's possibilities through art's creativity.

Edo/Tokyo, once called a water city, was a city crossed in every direction by waterways and broadly open toward the water. When land routes took over the central role in transport and logistics during the period of rapid economic growth, water receded behind the city and grew distant from our lives. Yet Tokyo remains a city rich in water. We want to look once again at Tokyo's rivers and sea and create opportunities to encounter the richness of water. “Open Water—Water (*) Opens” aims to create opportunities through art for people to engage with Tokyo's water.

body.t: Taylor–Couette flow is a fluid phenomenon arising when the inner cylinder rotates in the gap between concentric cylinders. At low speeds it is simple annular flow (laminar flow), but increased rotation generates axially periodic ring-shaped vortex rows called “Taylor vortices” through centrifugal instability; at still higher speeds it becomes turbulent, making it a classic, important fluid-dynamics phenomenon.

body.t: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a technique in which a large language model (LLM), before generating an answer, retrieves relevant information from external knowledge sources such as internal company documents and databases and constructs its answer based on that information. It enables accurate answers based on up-to-date and specialist information without retraining the model, and is strong in reducing hallucinations (falsehoods) and identifying information sources.

body.t: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard technology announced by Anthropic that seamlessly connects AI models (LLMs) with external data and tools. It standardizes connections between different AI tools and databases like “USB-C” and is attracting attention as a technology dramatically improving the efficiency of building AI agents and automating work.
Standardized integration: Removes the need for individual development previously required for each API, connecting various tools (Slack, GitHub, databases, etc.) to AI through common procedures.
Productivity improvement: AI becomes able to obtain and manipulate real-time external information, making development of agents specializing in particular tasks easier.
AI’s “USB-C”: once a tool is created to the MCP standard, any AI model (Claude, ChatGPT, etc.) can use it.
MCP host: an AI application interacting with the user (example: Claude for Desktop).
MCP client: intermediary between host and server.
MCP server: Connectivity to data sources and tools.

body.t: Opioid receptors are 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Morphine and endogenous peptides (endorphins, etc.) bind to them to produce strong analgesic and sedative effects.
Mainly 3 subtypes exist: mu, kappa, and delta, with mu receptors chiefly responsible for analgesic effects.
Mu (MOP) receptor: Mainly causes strong analgesia, respiratory depression, constipation, euphoria, and dependence.
Kappa (KOP) receptor: Involved in analgesia, sedation, withdrawal symptoms, or discomfort.
Delta (DOP) receptor: involved in analgesia and emotional regulation (antidepressant/anti-anxiety effects).

body.t: Yuko Hasegawa, Artistic Director, Museum of Contemporary Art (MOT), Tokyo
Hélène Meisel, Research and Exhibition Officer

The Dumb Type exhibition is the first monographic exhibition in France of this magnitude dedicated to this art collective. Formed in 1984, Dumb Type, in its early stages, was made up of about fifteen Kyoto City Art College students from different fields: visual artists, video artists, choreographers and performers, as well as architects, graphic designers, sound engineers and computer scientists who combined to invent a new, fundamentally pluridisciplinary type of performing art.

In English, dumb can mean “mute” or “stupid”. Teiji Furuhashi (1960- 1995), the central figure of the group, explained in an interview the critical approach suggested by the name “Dumb Type”: openness to the West and the economic bubble that culminated in the 1980s made Japan an increasingly superficial society, devoted to the media, consumerism and technology, in which every individual is “overwhelmed with information, without being aware of anything”, and where desires stand side by side with despair.

In reaction to this era and to the multiplication of theatricality and gimmicks, Dumb Type has created an experimental theatre in which the performers’ bodies serve to support the images, sounds, sets. Sanitised and unrelenting, the technology that proliferates in Dumb Type pieces formats the bodies and challenges the mind.

The first political gesture of Dumb Type lies in choosing to work as a collective; the desire for several people to work together was aiming for a total interdisciplinary approach, abandoning categories and academic hierarchies. This system is clearly visible in the hybrid nature of the group’s projects, where live performance and multimedia installations are interwoven. A new form of theatricality is taking shape, haunted by immersive technology, controlled by omnipresent data. Very active until the early 2000s, the company has regularly performed in museums and theatres in Japan, Europe and the United States, where some of its members have lived at times. Active on the international scene, Dumb Type examines the mutation of identities and communication in a globalised world.

The collective removed all dialogue from its early works, but the silent performers were surrounded by quotes from articles or lyrics of pop songs. New media and the digital revolution have transformed our intimate confession or direct addresses to the audience. behaviour, our subjectivity, and more broadly our humanity. Yet, at the heart of these data flows, the strobe lights and electronic music, a lively sensitivity was clear. This existential dimension can be seen in Dumb Type with the inclusion of more popular and fragile forms, such as karaoke, talk show, cabaret, drag performance, intimate confession or direct addresses to the audience.

In 1990, for one of its first projects, Dumb Type transformed the theatre stage into an immaculate pit, where the performers’ bodies are regularly swept by a machine with a giant scanner. PH borrows its title from the ”potential of hydrogen” used in chemistry to measure the acidity of a solution; the texts that punctuate the piece, however, also evoke the “potential Heaven/ Hell” of a Japanese society locked in a middle state, a harmful juste milieu, which Furuhashi compares to limbo. The following pieces will send shock waves through this cold neutrality. In S/N (1994), Furuhashi announced that he was HIV positive, displaying labels with the words “male”, “Japanese”, “homosexual”, “HIV +”. Phrases projected on stage counter this brutal categorization: “I dream of losing my gender”, “I dream of losing my nationality”, “I dream of losing my blood”. Videos of nude torsos filmed through targets complete this clinical treatment of the body. As with pH, the title S/N refers to a measure used in science: in acoustics, the signal/noise ratio measures the interaction between signal and noise, which influences the quality of transmission of information. The arrival of the compact disc in 1982 marked the transition from analogue recording to digital, where there is no longer any background noise. For Furuhashi, this elimination of ambient noise is symptomatic of a society that ignores all that it does not want to see or hear.

As part of its Japanese Season, the Centre Pompidou-Metz is presenting five major Dumb Type installations, including a new installation produced for the occasion. Some of these works are the respective productions of three of the very first members of the collective – Teiji Furuhashi, Ryoji Ikeda and Shiro Takatani – who, alongside their work in the collective, continued to produce solo projects. Archives and testimonies are also presented in the exhibition and retrace the genealogy of the group, before and after the death of Teiji Furuhashi in 1995. This understanding, both physical and documentary, of a selection of works from Dumb Type allows these striking creations to be considered in a new context, while placing them in perspective within the current context of a society still dominated by an excess of information and consumption.

body.t: Secularization is the process by which religious institutions, customs, and beliefs lose social significance. As society increasingly prioritizes scientific, rational, and secular perspectives over religious belief, separation of religion and state, the weakening of religious authority in public life, and a shift toward private, individualized belief systems advance. Main aspects of secularization. Social change: a shift from religious influence in public life (law, education) to a secular, rational worldview. Declining authority: religious organizations are losing influence over everyday life, social behavior, and political decisions. Privatization: religion tends to become a personal matter rather than a defining element of society. Modernization: closely associated with industrialization, urbanization, and the rise of scientific and secular explanations of the world.

body.t: FORTRAN IV, introduced by IBM in 1961 and later standardized as FORTRAN 66, introduced foundational language IF logical expressions, statements, and complex arithmetic expressions DATA for numerical, scientific, and engineering calculations. Designed for punched cards, it adopted fixed-format coding (using columns 7–72 for code). Key aspects of FORTRAN IV: Standardization: It was the first standardized Fortran to be widely adopted and paved the way for FORTRAN 77. Syntax: Emphasizes uppercase letters and numeric statement labels. Data types: Supported logical expressions, Boolean variables (.TRUE. or .FALSE.), and COMPLEX numbers. Subroutines: Frequently used subroutines and function procedures to avoid repeated coding. Input/output: Frequently used in combination with READ and WRITE statements to process data on tapes and cards.

body.t: “Bright Aquarium” is a two-person exhibition by Kosuke Nagata and Yusuke Oiwa. Both artists take approaches that exploit the tendency of humans to find some relationship between juxtaposed objects. Nagata mainly uses the characteristics of video and photography to make works in which virtual images and physical things short-circuit; Oiwa, meanwhile, thinks through language and acting to make works in which meanings appear and are then corrected. They share a concern in that their works are designed to gain their own dynamism through being exhibited and exposed to people's eyes and consciousness. As the 2 works are themselves “juxtaposed,” relationships will be found in this movement with further dimensionality.

An important panel discussion at the ICA in 2013 discussed how artists navigate a “post-net” world and considered how the proliferation of the internet shapes not only technology but identity, branding, and social media.

body.t: This book rereads Jean-Jacques Rousseau's classic “The Social Contract,” particularly its concept of the general will, as something implementable in today's information-technology environment, and discusses the possibilities of contemporary media and democracy alongside the resulting proposed general will.
The paperback's end includes a dialogue with political scientist Shigeki Uno, author of Democracy in the Age of the “Self” (Iwanami Shoten, Iwanami Shinsho, 2010), also quoted in the main text.

After publishing “Ontological, Postal,” Hiroki Azuma distanced himself from Japanese scholarly contemporary thought while publishing works such as “Otaku: Japan's Database Animals.” While announcing that he would eventually update his discussion of Derrida, he focused his activities for nearly 10 years on contributing to literary magazines, television appearances, and cultivating young critics.

Meanwhile, in the web world, Azuma used Nico Nico Douga and Twitter to reformulate Jean-Jacques Rousseau's general will, the origin of Derrida, using new media. There was also criticism asking him to stop discussing political issues involving actual human life and death through frivolous media (at Japan Policy School's 2nd commemorative symposium before its opening).

body.t: Technological Utopianism / Techno-utopianism is an optimistic belief or ideology that exponential technological progress automatically resolves every social problem (poverty, disease, labor, conflict, etc.), ultimately realizing a perfect society (utopia).
This is a form of “technological determinism,” based on the view that technology is the principal factor determining social structures and human culture.
Excessive trust in technology: closely related to “solutionism,” the belief that AI, digital technology, and automation solve every problem.
Optimistic future predictions: Considers technological progress to bring human happiness and worldwide fulfillment.
Connection with accelerationism: seeking to surpass the limits of current capitalism and social systems by maximizing and accelerating technological development.

body.t: Libertarianism is political and economic thought holding that each individual's freedom should be respected to the maximum and government intervention minimized, provided others' rights are not infringed. Its major characteristics are prioritizing individual self-determination and ultimately aiming for “small government” or “privatization of everything.”
Iwasaki Foundation, a general incorporated foundation
Regards individual freedom of choice as absolute, based on the premise that “one’s body and the products of one’s labor belong to oneself.”

Argues that government’s role should be limited to national defense, diplomacy, and maintaining order. Considers social security, public education, economic regulation, and the like impediments to individual freedom and market competition.
Besides seeking market-fundamentalist economic freedom, broadly supports diverse individual choices in private life (social freedom), such as same-sex marriage, abortion, and drug legalization.

body.t: In the 1990s, some entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley's information-technology industry vocally supported an ideology combining Marshall McLuhan's thought with elements of radical individualism, libertarianism, and neoliberal economics, spreading it through publications such as Wired. Based on 1960s counterculture and techno-utopianism, this ideology mixed New Left and New Right beliefs through a shared concern with anti-statism.

Supporters believed that in post-industrial society or post-capitalism, use of information and knowledge based on the knowledge economy would promote growth and wealth creation, and the traditional power structure of the state would be replaced by individuals linked through virtual communities.

Critics argue that the Californian Ideology strengthens corporate power rather than individuals, increases social inequality, and retains a strong American-centered perspective. Barbrook argues that the digital elite following this ideology embrace a form of reactionary modernism. According to him, “American neoliberalism appears successfully to have achieved the contradictory goals of reactionary modernism: economic progress and social stagnation. Precisely because the long-term goal of liberating everyone is never achieved, the digital elite’s short-term domination endures.

“The Californian Ideology,” also called “The California Ideology,” is an essay written in 1995 by British media theorists Richard Barbrook and Andy Cameron of the University of Westminster. Barbrook describes it as “a critique of dotcom neoliberalism”

. In this essay, Barbrook and Cameron argue that the rise of network technologies in 1990s Silicon Valley became linked to American neoliberalism, appearing as a hopeful technological determinism that fused contradictory left-wing and right-wing political beliefs.

This essay was first published in Mute magazine in 1995 and subsequently posted to the nettime internet mailing list for discussion. Its final version appeared in Science as Culture in 1996. This critique has since been revised repeatedly in different versions and languages.

Salon’s Andrew Leonard called this essay “one of the sharpest critiques of neoconservative digital hype.” Wired publisher Louis Rossetto, meanwhile, criticized it as showing “a profound misunderstanding of economics.”

Based on 1960s counterculture and techno-utopianism, this ideology mixed New Left and New Right beliefs through a shared concern with anti-statism.

body.t: Art for art's sake separates art from practical purposes such as politics, morality, and religion, treating “the beauty of art itself” as the sole absolute value. With the French “l'art pour l'art (art for art's sake)” as its ideal, it originated in 19th-century Europe.
💡 Main characteristics and history of art for art’s sake
Absolutizing beauty: Art is considered an end in itself rather than a means of moral justification or conveying lessons.

Historical background: spread in the mid-19th century, chiefly among literary figures such as Baudelaire and Théophile Gautier, as a reaction against rationalism and materialism brought by the Industrial Revolution.

Development in Japan: It was also imported into Meiji-period Japan, strongly reflected particularly in early works by writers such as Ryunosuke Akutagawa and Junichiro Tanizaki as an attitude pursuing beauty's ultimate heights.
In Japan from the modern period onward, the spirit of art for art's sake developed and changed in various forms.
Shirakaba school: valued individual emotions and artistic values alongside humanitarianism.
Taro Okamoto of “Art is an explosion”: He rejected practicality and beauty (prettiness, comfort), advocating art as a means of burning one's life.

body.t: “Biomedia,” proposed by Eugene Thacker, is an interdisciplinary concept referring to the contemporary condition of biology in which biotechnology and digital media merge. He focused on processes whereby biological data and bodies themselves are manipulated and recoded through information technology.

The mediatization of biology: Thacker points out a state where DNA sequences, proteins, cells, or whole organisms are treated as informational code (data) and function like information-processing systems.
Fusion of materiality and information: It shows biological and bodily materiality being converted into information and visualized by computer science and informatics, becoming manipulable “media.”
Biotechnology’s digital nature: in his 2004 book “Biomedia” and elsewhere, he argues that biotechnology’s essence lies in digitizing life rather than mere technological intervention.

body.t: Reverse-simulation music is a method proposed in 2002 by composer Masahiro Miwa, redefining concepts of contemporary composition, performance, and musical experience. It works backward from results (sound waves) to design causes (scores, performances, processes), using automatic-performance technology and chance to realize “music that might have been possible.”

A process of “working backward”: Instead of the usual “composition → performance,” first find the desired sounds or structures, then design actions and rules (methods resembling “spells”) to produce them.
Human–computer collaboration: Computer simulations and algorithm-based automatic performances (or methods giving performers precise instructions) are used.
Methodism: Emphasizes the process of “how the sound was produced” over the result.
Institute of Advanced Media Arts and Sciences
“Matari-sama” (from 2002): A representative early work using bells and castanets, evoking Shinto rituals and local performing arts.
“Four bits Counters”: a work performed collaboratively by computer and human.
Institute of Advanced Media Arts and Sciences
In 2013, the Museum of Fine Arts, Gifu held “The World of Reverse-Simulation Music,” and its activities are discussed in music education and research as well as contemporary music.

body.t: Time-based Media Art is contemporary art whose works unfold and change over time, including film, video, audio, computers, and performance. It encompasses video, sound, and light installations and developed from the 1960s onward.
Importance of time: Unlike static paintings and sculptures, appreciation requires time, and change forms the core of expression.

Dependence on technology: because works depend on technical elements such as video equipment, computers, and sound systems, preservation presents particular challenges and requires updating technology with the times.
Diverse media: Includes film, video (analog and digital), sound, performance, and interactive installations.
Conservation/restoration: Because equipment ages quickly, this field requires “restoration” such as updating exhibition equipment or digitization while maintaining artists' intentions.
This genre is rapidly growing in importance in contemporary art, and accurately documenting and exhibiting artists' intentions is considered essential.

excerpt.t: Time-based Media Art is contemporary art whose works unfold and change over time, including film, video, audio, computers, and performance. It encompasses video, sound, and light installations and developed from the 1960s onward.

body.t: Self-reference is the property of a sentence, utterance, symbol, or system indicating or referring to “itself.” Studied in logic, philosophy, mathematics, computer science, literature, and other fields, it is investigated as a source of contradictions (paradoxes) and a basis for advanced recursive systems (self-referential systems).
Main characteristics and examples of self-reference
Definition: a symbol or description having “itself” as its referent.
Self-reference paradox: Logical contradictions caused by self-reference. A famous example is the liar paradox: if “This sentence is false” is true, it becomes false, and if false, it becomes true.
Literature/art: A technique of referring within a work to the work itself (for example, Don Quixote addressing readers of Don Quixote within the story).
Technology and sociology: Recursive processing in computer programs and “autopoietic” structures in which social systems monitor and observe their own workings.
Liar paradox: “I am lying right now.”
Russell's paradox: Does “the set of sets not containing themselves” contain itself? (Collapse of logical hierarchy.)
Mathematics and logic: The concept underlying Gödel's incompleteness theorem (“This sentence cannot be proved”).
Law: The property of law defining its own validity and grounds.

body.t: The Omega Point (Omega Point) is the ultimate future point that cosmic evolution eventually reaches, integrating high intelligence and consciousness. Well-known concepts include Teilhard de Chardin's “sacred convergence point” and Frank Tipler's physics-based theory of “the end of the universe when computational capacity becomes infinite.”
Main characteristics and related concepts are as follows.
Evolution of “complexity = consciousness”: Claims that life and matter become more complex through evolution and simultaneously heighten consciousness.
Integration of cosmic consciousness: The idea that at the end of this process, individual consciousnesses merge and converge on the divine center, the “Omega Point.”
Noosphere (sphere of wisdom): It becomes the ultimate destination in the process whereby, after the physical biosphere, a “sphere of wisdom” consisting of humanity's mind forms over the entire Earth.
Physics of immortality: assumes computing power increases infinitely during the Big Crunch (the contraction and ending of the universe).

Resurrection within a simulation: the theory that, because all information in the universe is preserved and reproduced, resurrection of the dead and effectively “eternal life” become possible within the laws of physics.
Global brain: A vision of society's future in which all humans and AI on Earth are networked and function as a single intelligence.
Technological singularity: The turning point when AI surpasses human intelligence and rapid evolution occurs.
This concept is discussed as a theory interpreting the future of consciousness and life from perspectives of evolution, cosmology, AI, and information theory.

body.t: Born in Karl-Marx-Stadt in former East Germany in 1965 and now based in Berlin, Carsten Nicolai produces works moving between art, music, and science, focusing on the properties and patterns of human perception, light, sound, and natural phenomena. Nicolai, also active as a musician under the name Alva Noto, holds his first solo exhibition at a Japanese art museum in about 15 years. Titled “Parallax (the visual effect in which an object looks different when viewed from 2 different points),” it explores the roots of his expression.

The exhibition presents works meticulously remodeled to fit the museum’s exhibition spaces, including 6 projects such as an 18m-long projection work and a sound installation using an atrium. The dynamic display highlights the delicate beauty of the artist’s expression while providing an experience that appeals to viewers’ bodies.

body.t: A work that realizes unprecedented visual expression by treating the different concepts of space, color, and time symmetrically within a higher-dimensional space where they are unified. If each pixel of video data is regarded as a point with spatial coordinates given by 6 numerical values—X and Y for space, R, G, B for color components, and T for time corresponding to the frame number—all pixels in the video can be considered a set of points floating in 6-dimensional space. Applying an arbitrary rotation transforms color gradations, curves, and their changes over time into one another, merging them together, while relationships between points are not destroyed by rotation; at a rotation angle of 0 degrees, it returns to the original video. This work is the latest in the project (as of 2018/2) inspired by the word “dimension,” encountered in conversations with researchers in string theory, particle theory, and theoretical physics during a residency in 2016 at the Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe (IPMU), within the University of Tokyo Institutes for Advanced Study. It uses video obtained through interval shooting around the ALMA telescope in Chile’s Atacama Desert.

body.t: An installation manifesting potential futures contained within artificial intelligence (AI) trained on large quantities of news articles.

While virtual reality (VR) has attracted attention recently, events in the real world that seem to dissolve the boundary between reality and fiction are also not uncommon, as symbolized by terms such as alternative facts and fake news. By generating fictional news that might occur in the near “future” from a probabilistic language model trained on “past” news, this work attempts to illuminate the uncertain “present.”

Countless news articles mapped according to semantic distance appear within the 3-dimensional space projected on the screen. New news continually arriving from Twitter is mapped within this 3-dimensional space. Simultaneously, new text = new news is generated from their semantic neighborhoods and the spaces between them and other news.

Inspired by AI generating almost infinitely diverse sentences from mere sequences of numbers, this work can be called a process of excavating news that “already is” yet “does not yet exist,” embedded in language models' vast high-dimensional vector spaces, based on news actually happening.
Through these news items that “might have been” or “might be possible,” the work unsettles viewers' boundaries between reality and fiction, past and future.
For technical details and project background, see the article written on Medium.

body.t: A new work produced for the exhibition “ART+COM/Rhizomatiks Research: ‘Poetics/Structures’ of Light and Motion.”

5 rectangular solids with mirrored sides move through the space, self-propelled through radio control and optical tracking technology. Moving straight, rotating, and synchronizing their movements, they somehow suggest dancing.

The projector imagery covering the entire space includes portions projected directly onto the floor and portions reflected off the object’s mirror surface onto the floor. Although the mirror’s angle and distance relative to the projector imagery change continually as the cart moves and rotates, both portions continue to be projected onto the floor as consistently correct, undistorted images.

This work takes as its motif anamorphosis, a technique used since the 15th century in which the original image is drawn distorted so that a correct image can be obtained only from one particular viewpoint or angle. It is well known through trick art, for example, where an image that should be flat appears pseudo-three-dimensional when viewed from a certain angle.

In performances and other contexts, Rhizomatiks Research sets the viewpoint of a camera filming the venue at the same position as that of a virtual camera in computer graphics, then deforms the CG imagery accordingly in real time to make the footage filmed by the camera appear to have depth. Without compositing or head-mounted displays, this visual staging makes the subject seemingly appear to enter the image.

In this work, motion-capture cameras track the carts' movements, from which the mirrors' angles are analyzed. Distorted images are generated in real time and projected onto the carts' mirror surfaces so that, at those angles, the reflections appear as correct images. The layered images, fragmented by multiple mirror surfaces and further divided into RGB light components, are structurally integrated through the carts' movements.

body.t: LIGO (pronounced “lie-go,” English: Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) is a large-scale physics experiment and facility for detecting gravitational waves, whose existence Albert Einstein proposed in 1916. Its English name literally translates as “Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory.” The research was jointly established in 1992 by Kip Thorne and Ronald Drever of the California Institute of Technology and Rainer Weiss of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and is a collaborative research project involving scientists from both institutions and other universities and institutions. Researchers involved in research planning and analysis of gravitational-wave astronomy data form an organization called the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, with over 900 scientists worldwide participating

. LIGO was established by the US National Science Foundation (NSF), with major contributions from the UK's Science and Technology Facilities Council (English version), Germany's Max Planck Institute, and the Australian Research Council (English version)
. In September 2015, following improvements costing 200 million dollars over 5 years, the “world's largest gravitational-wave facility” was completed at a total cost of 620 million dollars
. LIGO is the largest and most ambitious project established by NSF

The essence of LIGO facilities lies in their ability to detect extremely small relative strains of 10-21 through the principle of the Michelson interferometer. This strain of 10-21 is often popularly described as “a strain the size of the diameter of a hydrogen atom (1.1 ×10-10 m) relative to the distance between Earth and the Sun (an astronomical unit, 1.5 ×1011 m).”

body.t: This exhibition, “supersymmetry,” is the 3rd presentation of a new work at YCAM and the first in 6 years, following the 2004 concert “C4I” and the 2008 exhibition “datamatics.” First, looking back at your previous works, please tell us how you arrived at this new work.

“C4I” incorporates every idea I conceived during my preceding 10 years of activity with Dumb Type, a kind of “scrapbook” scattered with all the elements that would develop afterward. Looking back now, some parts, such as landscape footage I shot with my own camera, seem somewhat verbose as expression. That “verbosity” was stripped away in the subsequent “datamatics” series, and by the “test pattern” series, the expression consists solely of black and white, that is, the binary “0 and 1.”

body.t: The work title “Chijikinkutsu” combines “geomagnetism” and “suikinkutsu (water-harp cave).”

“Geomagnetism” is the Earth's magnetism, a force humans cannot feel although it is always present everywhere on Earth. However, compasses using geomagnetism were useful long before the Age of Discovery, and today are built into smartphones as electronic devices. Research has also examined geomagnetism's relationship to the behavior of migratory birds, honeybees, and certain bacteria. Beautiful auroras are also closely related to geomagnetism. In his book, the 16th-century scientist William Gilbert wrote that the magnetic Earth is like a living creature, but even today its principles have not been fully explained.

The other element, “suikinkutsu,” has been an ornament in traditional Japanese gardens since the Edo period: a device for enjoying the resonant sound of water droplets falling into a buried jar near a washbasin. Since ancient times, Japanese people have had a distinctive sensibility that accepts sounds such as insects and wind in pine trees as nature as it is, and this delicate sensitivity gave rise to such devices. Just when I was making this work, I happened to visit a favorite temple in Kyoto. The temple stands in the most secluded part of the mountains. It has a garden with large Japanese white pines and a suikinkutsu in one corner. Hearing its sound, I felt that it resembled my work. Later, this expanded the work’s concept.

The concept of this work of mine does not come from the positivism of science and technology on which media art depends, nor from the constructive Western musical theories underpinning some sound art. It is to incorporate the effects of geomagnetism, normally treated in science, and develop them into delicate sounds within the context of Japanese views of nature, creating a sound installation. It consists of several materials: water, sewing needles, glasses, and copper wire. Sewing needles float on water through surface tension; the needles, magnetized beforehand, point north through geomagnetism, and sound generated by current flowing through copper wire becomes audible. The system uses MIDI, with data sent from a music-sequencer application on an iPad distributed to each coil by a specially designed controller that supplies the current.

I incorporate many elements into the work, and it is drawn by the magnetism and strikes the glass, producing sound. From the cups placed on the four sides of the exhibition space, rather than randomly, I sought to pare down the elements into a minimal expression. To consider what this minimality means, let us take taste as an example. In Japanese cuisine, “umami” is the most important taste, but until recently sweetness, sourness, saltiness, and bitterness were thought to be the four tastes. Much Western cooking has pursued depth of flavor by layering flavors, while Japan has taken a different approach, drawing out “umami” by using as few elements as possible. This is a pursuit of purity without extraneous flavors. Elements I did not add to this work include color, LED light, and sound amplification. As a result, the sound stood out and viewers could concentrate on it; it also led them to notice that the needles in the cups were related to geomagnetism.

Because geomagnetism acts on a needle floating on the water's surface in a round cup, it resembles a small Earth. Minute sounds sharpen viewers' senses; the quieter the sound, the sharper the senses become. Gradually, sound feels internal rather than external.

body.t: The CRT monitor installed in the center of the venue shows 4 glowing neon tubes positioned at equal intervals throughout the space. A swinging pendulum with a magnet is suspended from the ceiling. Every time the pendulum passes, the image on the monitor becomes distorted. Magnetism distorts the image, endlessly varying its color and form. Meanwhile, an antenna fitted to the television detects the magnetic field of the magnet and connects to audio equipment as a device analyzing electromagnetic waves. By converting fluctuations in electromagnetic waves into audio signals, viewers can perceive them as “sound.” This work makes it possible to capture through sight and hearing electromagnetic waves that humans cannot sense in everyday life.

body.t: 8 monitors with a 16:9 aspect ratio are connected in a horizontal row to form one overall image. Within this elongated image, an image the size of 1 monitor slowly moves from end to end, crossing the monitors. Ahead of the leading edge of the moving image, however, numerous colored linear images appear as though the 1-pixel-wide image at its tip has been stretched, giving the impression that the image is being woven out of these lines as it advances. Meanwhile, the trailing edge of the moving image is fixed in place 1 vertical pixel at a time, so that the still image appearing when it reaches the display's edge becomes what might be called the temporal trace of the camera's movement.

The work displays three different modes of imagery: linear bands of color that will be composed into landscape footage, moving landscape footage, and still images in which the displaced footage has been fixed. It presents a visual experience through a method distinct from the two ways of recognizing space: human vision and the camera as an optical device attempting to grasp space based on that vision.

For example, attempting to capture space by reproducing planar subjects with lines, like a scanner or photocopier, describes it as an image without vanishing points or depth, unlike perspective images based on linear perspective. It also captures the world through a method different from human vision.

body.t: Music and visual art have evolved in close relationship with one another. Examples from the early 20th century include Kandinsky, who aimed for a synthesis of the arts in which works evoked various senses, and Klee, who sought to visualize music with symbolic precision. The rich realm of sensibility and expanded expression made possible by crossing hearing and vision were investigated in more experimental forms by John Cage and others in the 60s.

Now, with the development of digital technology, images are decomposed into pixels and processed as symbols and numerical values, and sound is composed visually on PC displays: art and music are converging even in their creative processes. A generation of creators treating video, images, and sound equally on a single computer attempts diverse expressions through a more closely integrated sense that might be called “new synesthesia.”

With musician Ryuichi Sakamoto as general adviser, this exhibition introduces diverse works arising from the intersection and coordination of these two forms of expression, questioning the fundamental meaning of seeing and listening in “our time.”

Ryuichi Sakamoto collaborates with Seigen Ono, who creates some of the world's foremost sound designs, and Shiro Takatani, 1 of Dumb Type's founding members, exhibiting 2 new installations. Don't miss silence spins, inspired by Japanese tearooms and listening to an infinite universe from a small space, and collapsed, using 2 pianos and lasers.

Presents works previously unseen in Japan by internationally active contemporary artists. Introduces many internationally diverse expressions, including Florian Hecker's three-dimensional sound installations and Christine Ödlund's scores and music generated from plants' danger signals.

Through Kandinsky’s and Klee’s paintings and graphic scores by John Cage and Toru Takemitsu, among others, it introduces how artists and musicians have explored relationships between music and visual art from historical as well as contemporary perspectives.
What is the Tokyo Culture Creation Project?

The Tokyo Culture Creation Project is a project implemented by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and the Tokyo Metropolitan Foundation for History and Culture in collaboration with arts and cultural organizations, arts NPOs, and others toward realizing “Tokyo as a global city of cultural creation.” By forming cultural-creation hubs throughout Tokyo and providing creative experiences for children and young people, it establishes an environment in which many people actively participate in creating new culture, while creating and communicating new Tokyo culture to the world through international festivals and other initiatives.
