body.t: Tablature (commonly called tabs) is musical notation using numbers and symbols instead of notes to specify concrete bodily actions: “which string” of an instrument to play at “which fret (position).” Used since 16th-century lute music, it is now familiar as convenient notation allowing players to visually understand playing positions on guitar, bass, shamisen, and other instruments. Main characteristics of tablature: Structure: For guitar, it uses 6 lines (staff lines) corresponding to the 6 strings, with numbers indicating fret numbers. Advantage: Even without knowledge of music theory or reading music, players can perform intuitively by looking at fingering (finger movements). History: Used from around 1507 for lute and keyboard instruments, and widely employed through to modern popular music.

body.t: The Frontal pole cortex is an evolutionarily new brain region (Brodmann area 10) located at the very front of the cerebral frontal lobe. It is known for governing advanced human functions such as thinking, planning, and “metacognition,” objectively viewing one’s own state. Its main functions and characteristics are as follows. Metacognition (knowing one’s ignorance). It objectively evaluates whether one “knows or does not know” one’s own knowledge and memories. Goal achievement and sustained behavior. It is involved in the ability to carry out plans toward distant future goals (such as maintaining health) and sustain behavior. Higher-order decision-making. It plays a central role in appropriately switching between multiple tasks, making social judgments, and forming long-term outlooks. This region is most highly developed in humans and is an important part deeply involved in everything from everyday task management to achieving long-term life goals.

A research group including the Department of Integrative Physiology at the University of Yamanashi Faculty of Medicine and the Department of Neuropsychiatry at the University of Tokyo Hospital revealed that the brain’s frontal-pole–temporal-lobe network becomes active when a sound that had been occurring at equal intervals fails to occur. Following review by the University of Yamanashi’s Animal Experimentation Committee, the study used electrocorticography (Note 3), which comprehensively measures neural activity through numerous electrodes placed on the cerebral cortical surface of Japanese macaques (genus Macaca), primates like humans, to examine activity in the temporal lobe associated with hearing and the frontal lobe thought to be involved in higher-level prediction formation.

body.t: This artwork appropriated one million Facebook profiles and posted 250,000 of them on a custom-made dating website with profiles sorted by social temperament, which was estimated through trained artificial intelligence analyzing facial expressions. The dating website, Lovely-Faces.com, provided a stage for anybody to interact with Facebook users’ personality traits such as smug, easy going, or sly. The project took place over five days of thrilling personal, media, and legal reactions, which became a global mass media performance. During the performance the artwork received over a thousand mentions in the international press, eleven legal threats, five death threats, and several letters from the lawyers of Facebook. which had to confront this artistic intervention made with its appropriated material and as a result of its security flaws. The project addressed surveillance, privacy, and the economy of social media monopolies as well as performing art interventions within global media.

body.t: A video made by attaching a laser projector and camera to a computer-controlled industrial robot arm and filming the entire sequence in one shot while projecting computer graphics onto miniature models in real time.

A staging method called projection mapping, which changes the surface textures of three-dimensional forms such as architecture by projecting imagery onto them, can create visual spaces with an unusual sense of presence and reality. Ordinarily, supports such as buildings and the imagery have a fixed relationship: the shape and position of the objects are determined in advance, and images produced to fit them are superimposed. In this work, however, not only the camera but also the miniatures onto which images are projected move rather than remaining fixed, and the CG generated changes accordingly. The miniatures are designed to move together through a single power source, and some can be positioned by the audience. The camera automatically creates signals for compositing as it films, making it possible to project imagery without fixing the projection targets.
Music: Etsuko Yakushimaru Metro Orchestra, “Boys, Come Back to Me.”

body.t: This exhibition views “environment” as something connecting reciprocal domains such as <generating>, <permeating>, and <reflecting>. Many movements, including land art and earth art, have used the environment as a setting or element of art, but this exhibition seeks new “environments” within media art's essential creativity and exploratory qualities. It is an attempt to open “environment” through information technology as something linking multiple domains, producing mutual environmentality = an “environmental sphere.” The concept of expressing “environment” as a transformation of space, rather than a materially added exterior, will carry a strong, quiet assertion today.

At the globally acclaimed Osaka Expo of 1970, attention focused on the activities of the American experimental group E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology), realized in the Pepsi Pavilion. Collaboration between artists and scientists and the participating artists’ innovative ideas produced pioneering, astonishing results exploring the relationship between environment and art. This exhibition regards the period from then to the present, its 40th anniversary, as a major turning point from a progressive view of science based on material productivity to invisible information capitalism, and critically examines E.A.T.’s ideas and achievements. By interpreting advanced ideas and initiatives in art and science, incorporating perspectives from contemporary information sociology and environmental creation, it reveals present-day realities and new environmental elements.

This exhibition was conceived around Fujiko Nakaya's “fog sculpture,” first presented at the Pepsi Pavilion of the Osaka Expo, and the thinking and expression of the late David Tudor, who handled the interactive sound there. The main venues inside and outside YCAM exhibit “fog sculptures” displaying various forms. A new installation incorporating Tudor's pioneering idea of soundscapes through environmental reflection is also unveiled. This can be called a collaborative attempt to create a new environment by Nakaya, artists including Shiro Takatani from the generation that grew up after the Expo, and YCAM staff. Using information technology, works incorporating diverse changes in human perception alongside natural changes give sensory form to an entirely new, critical “information environmental sphere.”

body.t: Japan Media Arts Festival supporting event, “Cyber Arts Japan—30 Years of Ars Electronica.”
To commemorate the 30th anniversary of the global media-art festival “Ars Electronica” (Linz, Austria), we will hold an exhibition focusing on Japan's art and technology and media arts.

Since its founding in 1979, the festival has had deep ties with Japan through numerous award winners and participants including Isao Tomita, Ryuichi Sakamoto + Toshio Iwai, and Maywa Denki. Focusing on works participating in the festival, this exhibition explores new possibilities linking art, science/technology, and society.

In this exhibition, with the support of Ars Electronica Linz, valuable video and work materials recounting 30 years of history will be exhibited for the first time. The exhibition, comprising approximately 25 projects and 50 works, consists of several parts. Alongside displays by past award winners and this year’s award-winning works, it will include a collaborative program with the Ars Electronica Center (Device Art exhibition), as well as an experimental network project connecting Linz and the Tokyo venue in real time to consider, dismantle, and reconstruct the Museum of the Future. Furthermore, topical media arts/media art will be presented through hybrid new fields such as visualization of literary works, digital public art, and space art.

As a supporting project of the concurrently held Japan Media Arts Festival (The National Art Center, Tokyo), this exhibition will be developed in coordination with related facilities in Japan, including NTT InterCommunication Center [ICC]. Alongside the “Experimental Workshop” display within the concurrent MOT Collection exhibition and the large mural “Entrance Space Project” by Takehiko Inoue, creator of “Vagabond,” it explores the current state of media arts and its pioneers. Through participatory works, events, and screenings, this exhibition will offer a valuable opportunity to reconsider what “Japan's expressive power” means and think toward the next generation.

body.t: Sekai Camera is augmented-reality software running on iPhone and Android. It was provided free by Tonchidot Corporation. All services ended on 2014/1/22. This article also describes its mobile-phone version, Sekai Camera ZOOM.

When Sekai Camera is launched, the scenery in front of the user appears on the screen through the built-in digital camera of an iPhone or Android device, with additional information (text, images, audio) called “Air Tags” associated with that place or object (buildings, signs, etc.) overlaid on it. Users can freely add Air Tags, which are shared among users.
Using it requires a smartphone such as an iPhone or Android and also requires holding up the device and looking at its display.

GPS identifies the current location. The built-in electronic compass also recognizes the camera's direction and displays Air Tags placed in that direction. Position-recognition accuracy varies with GPS reception strength.

Sekai Camera ZOOM is an EZ application running on KDDI and Okinawa Cellular's Android OS au smartphones and au mobile phones. In addition to Sekai Camera functions, it includes Twitter functionality. The service ended on November 30, 2011.

body.t: Taking images for 3D is simple: one merely changes position to obtain views from left and right. Methods therefore vary, including preparing 2 cameras with linked shutters, modifying the lens section to expose left and right images simultaneously on film in 1 shot, or changing position to take 1 more image.

Various viewing arrangements are also devised, such as binocular-like stereoscopic viewers, colored (or polarized or liquid-crystal shutter) glasses worn while viewing, and naked-eye stereoscopic viewing.

Fujifilm's “FinePix REAL 3D W1,” launching on August 8, is probably the world's first digital camera taking stereoscopic photographs with 2 lenses and image sensors built into 1 camera (I say probably because it may already exist in specialized photographic equipment).

body.t: Exploring the Future of Life (inochi) and Love—Da Vinci, Okyo, Damien Hirst
Text: Kazumichi Hashimoto (representation and culture studies)
Photo: Osamu Watanabe; courtesy of Mori Art Museum

Contrary to its subtitle, the exhibition space seemed overflowing with representations of “death.” This was my impression after viewing the exhibition as a whole, composed mainly of the London Wellcome Foundation’s collection of various objects relating to medical history, 3 anatomical drawings by Leonardo da Vinci reportedly including works shown in Japan for the first time, and various contemporary artworks. In early modern European anatomical drawings depicting bodies stripped of skin and cut open at the abdomen, it would be difficult to sense the breath of life, even if they included a mother’s body carrying a baby. Among the contemporary artists, too, Alvin Zafra performed a rough funerary rite of grinding down a skull on sandpaper, while Walter Schels juxtaposed portraits of subjects immediately before and after death. Even in the final section, entitled “Toward Eternal Life and Love,” what the rabbit genetically modified to emit green light (Eduardo Kac) offers a glimpse of is perhaps instead the ominousness of the future brought by biotechnology.
Alvin Zafra, “Argument from Nowhere,” 2000. Courtesy Osage Gallery
“Walter Schels, Life Before Death—Elmira Sang Bastian”

Yet we should also refrain from casually dismissing all these with the single word “death.” Why, for example, do bodies in anatomical books from the Renaissance onward, represented by Vesalius’s writings, stand up as skeletons and strike poses, or strip off their own skin and show their internal organs to us? Simply put, it is because they are “alive.” What was new in medicine at this time was the belief that the truth of life should be attainable by exploring the body, rather than reducing it to the Christian soul. Corpses were used for that exploration merely because cutting open a living body was impossible. The bodies in anatomical drawings demonstrate such impossibility succeeding only within an image.

What once should have represented “life” now appears instead as “death.” Ultimately, this is probably because both “life” and “death” are merely abstract concepts that change with the times. It is only individual, concrete bodies that are born and die. George Washington’s dentures, a prosthetic hand for a 16-year-old girl, a prosthetic leg for a wounded soldier reportedly made from airplane parts, a slightly bloodshot artificial eye… How closely can medicine, or art, accompany the bodies that these medical devices so vividly evoke?
Andreas Vesalius, a skeleton hanging from a rope.
From On the Fabric of the Human Body, 1555.

body.t: “Pure φ (pure φ)” is a video painting as an interface, projected onto a large screen serving as a canvas. If ordinary graphical user interfaces (GUI) realize interfaces as diagrams using symbols and icons, “Pure φ” expresses an interface as a picture, using the screen as a planar field for its canvas.

In front of the screen, 4 active digital cameras are installed as metaphors for eyes; optical flow obtained from the input of these 4 cameras sets a feedback loop of random dots in motion. Switching among multiple cameras corresponds to the multiple viewpoints of analytical cubism, projected onto a large screen like an all-over color-field painting.

The interface of flowing random dots can be called an abstract interface without concrete metaphors or functions. By scaling the screen to envelop the body and providing, at the viewer's position, a stage with gently graduated levels as a metaphor for the earth, it constructs an ecological-optics interface through the movement of texture as an ambient optic array. In an interface, the balance between transparency (window) and reflectivity (mirror) is particularly important. The noise flowing across the screen through optic flow corresponds to a mirror of movement, while Pure φ, presumably perceived apparently from it—that is, the sense of motion in which “you cannot see what is moving, but can see only movement”—corresponds to what is visible through the window of the screen.

In principle, just as countless objects can be reconstructed from 1 retinal image, space arising from the “visuomotor system” in body-centered coordinates is constantly generated and dissolved dynamically. Bodily movement (action) on a stepped stage changes the visual data entering the retina, and that change generates further new actions. The eye itself is the interface for obtaining environmental information, and interaction directly connecting action and vision arises from the dynamism of the direct visuomotor system, rather than an indirect perceptual system seeking constancy.

body.t: “Musica ex Machina (Japanese pronunciation: mujika ekusu makina / Mechanical Music)” is the name of a special exhibition held in 2007 at the University of Tokyo's Komaba Museum and a related research project. It is known for focusing on the historical relationship between music and machines and their possibilities.
What does the phrase “mechanical music” bring to mind for you?

Although music boxes and computers (desktop music production) differ in structure, they could be called “mechanical” in that a machine performs on the spot; music playback devices such as CDs, hard disks, and flash-memory players might also be described this way. However, in the exhibition we have prepared, we would like to consider the relationship between “machines” and “music” from a somewhat different perspective than you might imagine.

The idea of having machines play music automatically already appears in Aristotle's writings. Various mechanical structures devised in ancient Greece passed to the Middle East and showed new developments when reimported into Europe in the Middle Ages.

Church clocks using bells tuned to a scale to play a melody at appointed times can be regarded as representative automatic musical instruments of medieval Europe. The proliferation of such devices is thought to reflect the fact that music, in which various sounds are played in beautiful melodies, and clocks, which mark time precisely, both symbolized a universe operating with harmony and order.

Such thinking is probably why pipe organs with enormous, complex structures are indispensable in churches. An organ, which produces sound simply by supplying air and pressing keys, is also well suited to automatic performance. Automatic organs had already been invented in the 17th century, and small hand-cranked organs came to spread throughout many regions. This trend toward automating performance also generated interest in recording and reproducing performances in the mid-18th century. In this exhibition, we plan to use a computer to reproduce performance records from about 230 years ago.

In the modern era after the Industrial Revolution, machines became everyday presences. Machines also seem to have become indispensable to musicians, including metronomes that mark rhythms accurately. In the 20th century, some young composers began to recognize machine-like qualities as a form of beauty. The ideal of machine music was to express simply being a machine, neither the harmony of the cosmos nor imitation of humans, and this was also considered an appropriate attitude for a mechanized age. I. Stravinsky, P. Hindemith, E. Toch, and others participated in this movement, leaving works for the player piano, which represented the highest music reproduction technology of the time. After the war, C. Nancarrow continued composing for player piano, but since the 1980s new technology has made it possible to connect pianos and computers, and many new works have emerged. This exhibition and its related events introduce representative works for automatic pianos and their creative activities from the 1920s to the present.

At the center of this exhibition are works by Martin Riches (1942-). This British artist living in present-day Berlin has presented many Music Machines. “Flute Playing Machine,” “Serinette (bird organ),” and “Clock V,” introduced here, demonstrate that even as contemporary artworks they do not exist independently of the historical relationship between machines and music.

Although their mechanisms have become electronic, automatic pianos remain popular today. Concerts featuring modern automatic pianos are also planned during the exhibition (with cooperation from Yamaha Corporation). In addition, the automatic composition and accompaniment programs developed through our university’s research, also presented in this exhibition, will offer abundant insights into “music” and “machines (technology)” in the present and future.

For us living in contemporary society, music is utterly commonplace. We live without any awareness of how this thing called “music” exists in relation to “machines.” Yet what was “music” in the first place? With such concerns in mind, this exhibition attempts to begin in ancient Greece, trace historical transformations, and explore contemporary and future “music” using its relationship with “machines” as devices that play it as a key theme.

This exhibition was organized by the research group “The Role of Machines in Musical Culture: Multifaceted Analysis and Perspectives on Its History and Present State,” funded by a Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (principal investigator: Hermann Gottschewski, associate professor at this university).

body.t: On June 16, documenta 12, the 12th international exhibition, opened in Kassel, Germany. This time, Roger M. Buergel was brought in as artistic director and established the exhibition with his wife, Ruth Noack.

This time, 3 leitmotifs were presented as “3 Questions for Art and Its Audience,” with approximately 500 works and over 100 artists selected and exhibited, from works around the 14th century to today, an attempt differing from previous ones.
Is modernity our antiquity? (Is modernity a relic of the past?)
What is bare life? (What is mere life?)
Was tun? (What is to be done?)

What I would like to focus on here is the selected artists and works. First, there are hardly any exhibits by famous artists said to have driven “art history.” Meanwhile, works from before 2000 account for nearly half the exhibits. The invitation of considerable numbers of contemporary artists from Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia—especially China—also distinguishes it from past exhibitions described as “Western Europe/America-centered”; it appears instead to have been conceived as an attempt to reinterpret history to date.

Personally, Ai Weiwei caught my eye most in this exhibition. He exhibits an enormous object in a courtyard at the center of the specially constructed venue (incidentally, it was reported to have collapsed in heavy rain around June 20, and no prospects for restoration have been reported at this point).

The chairs seen throughout the venue are said to be chairs commonly found in China. Along with these 1001 chairs, he undertook a project to invite 1001 ordinary people recruited publicly in China to documenta 12. The invitees reportedly came from various social strata and understood almost no foreign languages. The interest of this project lies in the dramas that might unfold as such people travel to a small German city. Viewed this way, mischief such as in the following photograph may be one of the outcomes generated by the project, or perhaps Ai Weiwei's intention.

body.t: In the space, 2 loudspeakers face each other, filling the entire space uniformly with white noise. Standing between them, the noise disappears precisely at the midpoint, where silence takes over. Opposite-phase waveforms emitted by the symmetrically facing speakers meet directly, canceling each other's sound and creating a kind of “blind spot.”

“invertone” is an installation that allows visitors to experience the phenomenon of sound attenuation through mutual interference between phase-inverted sound waveforms in an anechoic chamber, a space covered in material that absorbs sound reflections. Its title combines “invert” (turn upside down) and “tone” (sound). In this work, sound, although invisible, is treated as if it were a fluid, immaterial “sculpture” made of frequencies. Frequencies appear as physical phenomena such as air vibrations and ripples in fluids, but we rarely have opportunities in everyday life to perceive and confront their existence. This work suggests that sonic phenomena involve physical and geometric mutual interference and indicates how human perception relates to this. The minimal space composed of repetitive sound-absorbing material and speakers, ready-made products, can also be said to speak eloquently of Nicolai’s distinctive aesthetic.

body.t: OuBaPo is a French comics-creation group established in 1992. It creates experimental works by imposing various formal limitations called “constraints” (contraintes) on comics (bande dessinée). “OuBaPo” abbreviates “Workshop of Potential Comics” (OUvroir de BAnde dessinée POtentielle), and its name and methodological approach follow “Oulipo,” the experimental literary group founded in 1960 by Raymond Queneau and others.

Around the end of the 1980s, bande dessinée artist Lewis Trondheim had gained a reputation through experimental works including Le dormeur (The Sleeper) and Psychanalyse (Psychoanalysis), made entirely from copies of a single panel, and Bleu (Blue) and La nouvelle pornographie (The New Pornography), labeled “abstract comics,” which removed meaning and words from the works and consisted solely of sequences of abstract shapes. After finishing Psychanalyse, encouraged by fellow cartoonist Jean-Christophe Menu, Trondheim also attempted to create stories based on just 4 wordless panels drawn by Menu. Combining these 4 panels (often using only one type of panel), Trondheim produced 20 sets of 4-panel comics, then asked Menu to draw 4 new types of panels; this is how Moins d'un quart de seconde pour vivre (A Quarter of a Second to Live) came about. The results of Trondheim’s experimental comics production, resembling Oulipo’s literary experiments, formed the basis for the establishment of Oubapo.

Menu, Trondheim, 6 other cartoonists, and comics historian Gilles Ciment met frequently at the Nawak studio frequented by Parisian artists (“Nawak” is slang meaning “nonsense”), discussing comics created with constraints over drinks. Thus OuBaPo was established in 1992 under Ou-x-po with the motto “Constraints free the artist's soul,” and announced in publications of L'Association, the independent comics publisher with which Lewis Trondheim was involved.

During the 10 years after its founding, the 9 founding members met 3 times annually, creating various constraints and continuing to produce works. OuBaPo created a board game called Scroubabble. It is based on Scrabble, but uses comics panels instead of letters. OuBaPo's first collection, OuPus 1, was published in 1997, and 3 further collections were published from 2003 to 2005. Several exhibitions of works have also been held in Paris.

In 2005, Trondheim and Menu fell out over the group's direction, and Trondheim left in autumn 2006. Subsequently, one founding member left in 2007 and the aforementioned Ciment left in 2008, each over differences with Menu. In November 2010, representative members of Oubapo attended Oulipo's 50th-anniversary celebration in Rennes and performed ScrOUBAbble before an audience.

body.t: Oulipo is a literary group established on November 24, 1960, at the initiative of mathematician François Le Lionnais (French version). Its full name is “Ouvroir de littérature potentielle” (Workshop of Potential Literature). Taking the literature of Alfred Jarry, Raymond Queneau, Raymond Roussel, and others as its ideal, it pursued new literary possibilities through the development of language-play techniques. It is characterized by encouraging texts to proliferate themselves by mechanically and mathematically transforming and altering quoted texts, and is strongly influenced by Surrealism's “exquisite corpse.”

body.t: Commodore BASIC (also called PET BASIC or CBM-BASIC) is a dialect of the BASIC programming language used in Commodore International's 8-bit home-computer product range, widely used from the PET (1977) through the Commodore 128 (1985).

The core is based on 6502 Microsoft BASIC, and thus shares many features with other 6502 BASICs of the time, such as Applesoft BASIC. Commodore licensed BASIC from Microsoft in 1977 on a “one payment, no royalties” basis. This was because Jack Tramiel rejected Bill Gates’s offer of a fee of 3 dollars per 1 machine, saying “I’m already married,” and refused to pay more than 25,000 dollars for a perpetual license.

The original PET version closely resembled the original Microsoft version, with only minor changes. The same applied to BASIC 2.0 for the C64, also found on the C128 (in C64 mode) and other models. Later PETs included BASIC 4.0, similar to the original version but with several added commands for operating floppy disks.

body.t: Transcoding is one of the 5 principles defining new media proposed by media theorist Lev Manovich in his book “The Language of New Media.”
Manovich explained that computer-generated and computer-processed “new media” have a two-layer structure in which cultural logic and computer logic influence each other.
Transcoding means converting from one format to another. In Manovich's context, it means a phenomenon in which the following 2 layers intermingle.
Cultural Layer: aspects such as meanings, narratives, genres, and compositions understood by humans (examples: films, encyclopedias, stories).
Computer Layer: computational aspects such as packets, data structures, and algorithms (examples: files, functions, databases).

According to this theory, contemporary media culture is understood as traditional “cultural logic” being rewritten and reconstructed (transcoded) by “computer logic”: computer data structures and algorithms.
Besides transcoding, Manovich lists the following principles.
Numerical Representation: all elements consist of digital code (0 and 1) and are mathematically manipulable.
Modularity: Elements such as images and sounds exist as independent “modules” that gather to form a larger work.
Automation: Numerical representation and modularity allow computers to automatically perform much media creation and editing.
Variability: Rather than one fixed finished product, infinite variations (for example, personalized websites) can be generated depending on data combinations.
Transcoding: through the above processes, media are converted from cultural logic into computer logic.
Manovich's perspective goes beyond mere technological theory and provides an extremely important guide in contemporary media studies, including analysis of Instagram visual culture and digital art.

excerpt.t: Transcoding is one of the 5 principles defining new media proposed by media theorist Lev Manovich in his book “The Language of New Media.”

body.t: I think that the artists grouped under the term “post-internet” began reconsidering the traditional problem of representation—the relationship between image and object, as demonstrated in Joseph Kosuth's “One and Three Chairs”—in a situation mediated by the internet as another space distinct from physical space. “Post-internet” can be described as closer to a matter of thought, like “speculative realism,” than to a periodization. At its center is the New York artist Artie Vierkant. In 2010, Vierkant wrote a text titled “The Image Object Post-Internet” and began the project “Image Objects” ★4. Images taken of artworks displayed in museums and galleries reach more people through the internet than the artworks themselves as objects. Focusing on this, Vierkant attracted attention by processing documentation images of his works in Photoshop and publishing them online as images presenting strange physical spaces and objects.

body.t: IWASAKI Hideo + Oron CATTS + Juan M. CASTRO
Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria that grow by absorbing metals and minerals dissolved from substrates.

They slowly promote the biological deposition of such minerals, transforming landscapes. “Biogenic Timestamp” is a project investigating the relationship between geological time and biological time. Drawing on the breadth of time-based artistic practices and new developments in synthetic biology, we explore different aspects of the material expression of temporality and arrangement, studying cyanobacteria as model organisms. The concept of time (and its manipulation) embodied by cyanobacteria and their by-products offers fertile ground for exploring various modes of time-based artistic practice.

This project includes artistic research at several sites of biological and biogenic-geological significance, and laboratory work exploring possibilities for human-induced biogenesis. Considering biogenic structures of geological and anthropogenic origins, our artistic research offers alternative uses and critical interpretations of synthetic biology. (IWASAKI Hideo + Oron CATTS + Juan M. Castro)

body.t: Meta AI created the first database revealing structures of the metagenomic world on the scale of hundreds of millions of proteins. These proteins exist in soil microbes, the deep ocean, and even our bodies, far outnumbering the microbes constituting animals and plants. Yet they are the least understood proteins on Earth.

Deciphering metagenomic structures can resolve longstanding evolutionary-history mysteries and discover proteins potentially useful for curing diseases, cleaning environments, and producing cleaner energy.

Predicting structures at this scale requires a breakthrough in protein folding speed. We trained a large language model to learn evolutionary patterns directly from protein sequences and generate accurate structure predictions end to end. Predictions are up to 60 times faster than the current state of the art while maintaining accuracy, and our approach can scale to much larger databases.

We are now sharing our model, research paper, a database of more than 600 million metagenomic structures, and an API allowing scientists to easily retrieve specific protein structures relevant to their research.

body.t: Zero-shot prediction is a technique in which an AI model predicts or classifies unfamiliar tasks or concepts using only its previously learned knowledge, without any additional training (fine-tuning) or specific training examples. It also handles unlabeled data and makes full use of foundation models (such as GPT and CLIP) pretrained on vast amounts of data. Key points of zero-shot prediction: No additional training required: There is no need to retrain the model for unseen classes or tasks. Generalization of knowledge: Based on existing knowledge, it understands and associates things it sees for the first time (images or text) through context. Versatility: It is applied in a wide range of fields, including image classification, object detection, time-series analysis, and natural-language processing. Main applications: Image and natural-language processing (CLIP): Correctly classifies even images it has not learned from based on descriptions such as “a running brown horse.” Time-series prediction (TimeGPT): Applies past patterns to predict future numerical values even for datasets absent from the training data. Natural-language processing (LLM): Like ChatGPT, solves tasks it has never been instructed to perform using only natural-language instructions (prompts). Difference from few-shot learning: Zero-shot: 0 examples (completely unknown). Few-shot: Makes predictions after receiving 1 to several specific examples (for example, including “this is the translation of this English sentence” in the prompt). This technology enables highly accurate use of the latest AI models even where specialized datasets are unavailable.

body.t: A protein language model (Protein Language Model: pLM) is an AI technology that treats amino acid sequences as natural-language “sentences” and extracts the grammar and regularities behind them through large-scale deep learning. This technology makes it possible to predict and design protein three-dimensional structures and functions instantaneously. How protein language models work: This technology applies natural-language processing models (LLMs), processing amino acids as follows: Characters (tokens): The 20 types of amino acids are treated as the alphabet or words of natural language. Grammar (context): By reading large quantities of protein sequences, the model learns evolutionarily conserved sequence rules and motifs (word sequences) with particular functions. Representation (embedding): From the order of amino acids, features describing how the protein folds (its 3-dimensional structure) and what it does are mapped into a vector space. Major representative models: Just as natural language has GPT and BERT, powerful models have been developed and released in the protein field. ESM (Evolutionary Scale Modeling): A representative model developed by Meta (formerly Facebook) and others. It learns large quantities of evolutionary data and accurately predicts how amino acid mutations affect protein function and stability. ProtTrans: A group of models applying the architectures of many large language models (such as T5 and BERT) to protein sequences. AlphaFold: Synonymous with protein structure prediction, it incorporates deep learning and language-model-like approaches to generate highly accurate three-dimensional structures directly from amino acid sequences. Applications: AI drug discovery: Designing new proteins (drug candidates) that bind to molecules associated with target diseases from scratch. Enzyme design: Artificially producing new industrially useful functions, such as increasing the activity of enzymes that break down plastics. Mutation effect prediction: Rapidly assessing diseases caused by genetic mutations and mechanisms of drug resistance.

body.t: Directed Evolution is a technique that reproduces Darwinian evolution (mutation and natural selection) in a test tube to artificially improve biomolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids. It attracted worldwide attention as a technology dramatically improving desired functions when it received the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Dr. Frances Arnold and others). Basic steps of directed evolution: A cycle for causing “evolution” within a short time in the laboratory.
Creating genetic diversity: Introduce random mutations into target genes to produce many mutants (a library).
Screening and selection: Select only mutants with high desired performance (activity, stability, etc.) from those produced.

Amplification and improvement: Repeat the cycle of amplifying selected genes, adding further mutations, and selecting them many times. Differences from conventional “rational design”: Conventional protein engineering has mainly used “rational design,” calculating and predicting protein structures with computers and other tools to modify them. Rational design: Effective when structures are clear, but complex mechanisms are difficult to predict. Directed evolution: Even when structures are unexplained, evolutionary mechanisms can elicit unexpectedly excellent functions. Main applications: It can create new, industrially useful molecules that do not exist in nature. Environment and industry: Improving the efficiency of plastic-degrading enzymes; producing biofuels.

Medicine/pharmaceuticals: improving antibody drugs for diseases, searching for new drug candidates. Chemistry: developing artificial enzymes promoting reactions previously possible only with chemical catalysts.

body.t: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA, mDNA) is DNA within mitochondria, cellular organelles. From the position that mitochondria originated in endosymbiosis, it is sometimes called the mitochondrial genome.

Mitochondrial DNA mainly contains information on mitochondrial proteins and so on, and is replicated when mitochondria divide. Some information required by mitochondria is contained in nuclear DNA, and mitochondria cannot exist independently outside cells. Conversely, cells can extract the energy they need using oxygen through the action of mitochondria, and cells themselves cannot survive without mitochondria. These facts provide circumstantial evidence for the hypothesis that mitochondria originated in endosymbiosis.

Diseases caused by mitochondrial abnormalities, generally called mitochondrial diseases, include those originating in abnormalities of mitochondrial DNA and those originating in abnormalities of nuclear DNA. Mitochondrial DNA polymorphisms are thought to relate to individual differences in susceptibility to obesity. Furthermore, recent reports suggest that mutations in mitochondrial DNA affect cancer's metastatic potential. (Hayashi et al, 2008)

body.t: “In Defense of the Poor Image” by German filmmaker and theorist Hito Steyerl is a highly important essay in media theory published in 2009. In this essay, rather than dismissing the compressed, low-resolution, noise-filled “Poor Image” on the internet as merely an inferior copy, she defends it as a symbol of democratic media in contemporary society. Its central arguments are as follows: Compression and movement: poor images are low-resolution and deteriorate each time they are copied, compressed, and accelerated on the internet. Yet this deterioration instead makes them a “ghost of an image,” something anyone can share. Revolt against hierarchy: perfect high-resolution (hi-res) images are often controlled and monopolized by large capital, power, and propaganda. Rough-quality images, meanwhile, spread across borders and serve as a “visual proletariat (masses)” accessible to everyone. Access and affect (emotion): poor images emphasize producing emotions (empathy and political solidarity) through “seeing and sharing them” more than possessing a perfect and beautiful form.

body.t: For contemporary people connected to smartphones, connecting to the internet constantly and everywhere completes our personalities. This article uses body painting to examine our physical definition and embodiment in a world of networked information devices.

Each work in this portrait series displays a nude, shaved person painted entirely in a single color on an LCD whose entire surface apart from the onscreen human is painted the same color. These boundaries are removed, and background and foreground become the human body and the electronic display's body, each covered in paint of the same color. The subject therefore becomes a sense of ambiguity and confusion, raising questions about defining the depicted individual as human or as representation.

Apart from these formalist aspects, this work also addresses the question of “existence” in media. The human body has a fairly well-understood horizon of longevity, but the horizons of longevity of data, paintings, and art remain debatable. The diverse timescales of body art, figurative painting, and media art interact as the work seeks common ground concerning the present and existence itself.

body.t: Donald Judd's “Specific Objects” is an essay he published in 1965 and the artistic concept proposed in it. It refers to clearly defined three-dimensional objects that directly engage particular materials and spaces, belonging to neither conventional “painting” nor “sculpture.” Main characteristics of Specific Objects: Escape from categories: Completely rejecting traditional notions of painting (canvas and frame) and sculpture (figurative or abstract objects placed on pedestals). Introduction of industrial materials: Employing industrial and ready-made materials such as aluminum, iron (Cor-Ten steel), Plexiglas, and plywood. Geometric composition: Using simple geometric forms such as boxes and pipes, excluding the artist's emotions and brushwork (matière). Engagement with space: Emphasizing the work's presence by integrating it with its location (walls, floors, etc.) rather than treating it as a standalone work. Significance and influence: This concept became a theoretical pillar of the minimalism (minimal art) emerging in America. Judd presented artworks as autonomous “real objects” in themselves, rather than things that produce “illusions (deceptions or fictions).”

body.t: “Image Objects,” proposed and produced by Artie Vierkant, is a representative concept in post-internet art that blurs the boundary between digital images circulating online and actual sculptures and paintings, overturning the physical value of a work into image consumption in the digital age. The main characteristics and mechanisms of “Image Objects” are as follows: Intersection of the real and digital: Abstract sculptures and relief works are made, photographed, and digitally processed using Photoshop and other tools. Reproduction of images: The processed digital images (screenshots, etc.) are treated as if they themselves were the original work and circulate on the internet. Variation of physical objects: Three-dimensional objects placed in exhibition spaces are positioned as merely one of the “physical variations” of those digital images. Through this experiment, viewers are asked, “What is a real artwork?” and “What does it mean for us to experience and consume art?” You can read more about Vierkant's works and detailed concepts in an explanatory article on artscape. Would you like to explore the background further, or specific series (such as changes in the works over the years)? If you tell me about the following points, I can provide more specific information: Art-historical backgrounds related to post-internet art; examples of other representative post-internet artists; the specific production processes and exhibition formats of his works. Please let me know what angle you would like to explore.

body.t: While affirming technology as a “progressive force,” Takaaki Yoshimoto discerned that it was moving toward “nullifying (flattening)” human sensibility, time, and space. He saw information society and electronic technology as opportunities to create independent individuals who no longer need to rely on physical collective fantasies (such as nations or religions). The direction of technology as interpreted by Takaaki Yoshimoto. Images and the nullification of time. Using images from artificial satellites (Landsat), among other examples, he noted that technology has a gaze that instantly erases the “temporal and spatial thickness” of Earth’s surface and the distinction between “inside and outside.” He predicted an age when everything would be flattened into images and information. Liberation from collective fantasy and the expansion of self-fantasy. Digital information technology dilutes external grand narratives (collective fantasies) such as nations and organizations. Consequently, he foresaw a future in which individuals would be liberated while becoming more prone to shutting themselves within their own worldviews (self-fantasies). Absolute trust in science and technology. Partly informed by his scientific background (Department of Electrochemistry, Tokyo Institute of Technology), he took a pragmatic position on issues including environmental problems and nuclear power, maintaining that “the direction of science and technology itself cannot be reversed” and that they should ultimately be resolved through the power of technology.

body.t: Neutral monism (Japanese pronunciation: churitsu ichigenron; English: Neutral monism) is a position on the mind-body problem in the field of philosophy of mind. It posits a single kind of intermediate substance, neither material nor mental, as the world’s ultimate reality. Opposing materialism and idealism, it takes a position between them. It is also translated into Japanese as chusei ichigenron.

body.t: Speculative Realism is a current in contemporary philosophy that emerged in the early 21st century. It shares a position that criticizes the premise of modern philosophy (correlationism) that human “thought” and “being” are inseparable, and attempts to reconsider “reality” itself, which exists objectively whether or not humans perceive it. Main arguments and characteristics: Criticism of correlationism: Philosophy since modernity has been preoccupied with “how humans perceive the world.” In response, it attempts to speculate about “the history of the universe before humans existed” and “independent things.” Object-oriented ontology (OOO): An approach proposed by Graham Harman and others that considers all nonhuman things (objects, animals, concepts, technologies, etc.), as well as humans, to have their own existence on an equal footing with humans. This current was decisively influenced by Quentin Meillassoux's book “After Finitude” and brought about a major paradigm shift, particularly in continental philosophy.

body.t: Born in Melbourne in 1944. A pioneer in media art who has conducted numerous experiments with artistic forms using new media since the late 1960s. Through active collaboration with engineers and programmers, he has produced many works encompassing new meanings and perspectives on technology, from performance, sculpture, and video to interactive expression involving audiences. In 2015, with support from Shanghai's Chronus Art Center, he released the archive website “Jeffrey Shaw Compendium 1966 - 2015,” encompassing half a century of works, writings, and criticism. From 1991-2009, he was the first director of the Institute for Visual Media at ZKM, a public media art center in Karlsruhe, Germany. He currently serves as dean of the School of Creative Media at City University of Hong Kong.

body.t: “Re‐move,” by the pseudonymous artist Lia, allows users to manipulate a series of generative video works balancing organic forms and the rawness of fin-de-siècle Viennese abstraction. Created in Macromedia Director, the work was newly restored as part of the Net Art Anthology.

Each work in Re‐move finds its own balance among the artist’s formal choices, user interaction, chance, and algorithmic processes. They therefore convey the idea that the computer is an interplay of different processes rather than an artistic tool in the conventional sense. By balancing responsiveness, randomness, and repetition, the generated, evolving abstractions ensure that the underlying processes shaping them remain legible despite their complexity.

body.t: The “Museum of Accidents (Museum of Contingencies),” proposed by French thinker Paul Virilio, is a conception in which “major accidents” and “disasters,” inseparable from the development of science and technology, paradoxically reveal the essence of that civilization. The core ideas of the “Museum of Accidents”: Accidents as the shadow of technology: Virilio understood the invention of any new technology or vehicle (e.g., trains, aircraft, nuclear power, the internet) as equivalent to simultaneously inventing “entirely new accidents caused by them (derailments, crashes, meltdowns, cyberterrorism).” A mirror reflecting civilization: He argued that exhibiting the wreckage and records of the catastrophes behind technological progress and dazzling achievements, rather than those achievements alone, was essential for accurately understanding the light and shadow of modern civilization. Putting it into practice at the Fondation Cartier pour l'art contemporain: Based on this thinking, Virilio held the special exhibition “What Happens (Ce qui arrive)” at the Fondation Cartier pour l'art contemporain in Paris from 2002 to 2003. It featured exhibitions on enormous disasters such as the 9.11 terrorist attacks and technological catastrophes. If you would like to learn more about Virilio's thinking or are looking for related books, the following information offers ways to explore further: His representative work “Speed and Politics,” and “The Accident: Accidents and Civilization,” which discusses accidents and civilization; the exhibition catalogue “Ce qui arrive” from the Fondation Cartier pour l'art contemporain. Please feel free to tell me which points you would like summarized in more detail, or whether you would like to know about applications to the relationship between accidents and contemporary AI or technology.

body.t: Although sculptures and three-dimensional works are generally made of hard materials by carving stone or wood or casting metal, this term refers to sculptures and three-dimensional works created using soft, plastic materials such as fibers like cloth and thread, rubber, or fat. Soft sculpture as a trend in contemporary art is said to have begun with Claes Oldenburg, a leading Pop Art artist known for public art and installations that reproduce ordinary everyday objects on a gigantic scale. His “Soft Bathtub” (1966) and “Lipstick (Ascending) on Caterpillar Tracks” (1969), among others, are made from vinyl and cloth and therefore deflate unless participants pump air into them; the very process of transformation as gigantic everyday objects distort under gravity is presented as the work. Other examples include Christo’s works wrapping famous buildings in enormous fabric, Joseph Beuys’s sculptures using fat and felt, and Yayoi Kusama’s works covering furniture and boats in phallic cushions made from cloth stuffed with cotton; however, these are often discussed in terms of the variability and ephemerality arising from the materials rather than their softness. The cloth works of Satoru Shoji, moreover, should probably be regarded as spatial expression through cloth rather than as objects.

body.t: is a framework for analyzing and predicting media’s (technology’s) effects on society and humans from 4 aspects. Effects arising when introducing technologies or artifacts are organized through the following 4 questions.
Enhancement: What does it expand, enhance, or accelerate? (Example: Cars extend and enhance the function of feet.)
Obsolescence: What does it render outdated and cause to decline? (Example: Cars cause walking and horse-drawn carriages to decline.)
Retrieval: what from the past does it recover or revive? (Example: the car retrieves the lost freedom of individual movement.)

Reversal: when pushed to its limit, what does it reverse into? (Example: excesses of a car-based society, such as traffic congestion, deprive people of freedom of movement and reverse into a state “slower than walking.”) These 4 elements do not oppose one another but function as “laws of media” acting simultaneously on one another. Details are explained at length in McLuhan’s book “Laws of Media.”

body.t: Cybernetic art and cybernetic serendipity are artistic expressions that apply the concepts of cybernetics, which emerged in the 1940s. They refer to works in which a system autonomously receives changes in the environment or viewers and responds and interacts through light, sound, movement, and so on. Characteristics and history of cybernetic art: Interaction with the environment: A “feedback loop” in which humans and machines (computers) influence each other forms the core of the work. Historical roots: The “Cybernetic Serendipity” exhibition held in London in 1968 is considered a milestone that brought this genre to worldwide attention. Representative artists: Examples include Nicolas Schöffer, who made sculptures responding to space and environment, and Tsai Wen-Ying (Chinese name: Cai Wenying), known for works using strobe lights and vibrations. Contemporary developments: Today's interactive art, media art, and AI-based generative art are rooted in the ideas of cybernetic art and are further evolving into VR and robotics.

body.t: Nam June Paik is an artist representative of the high-technology era who introduced the new expressive form of “video art” into contemporary art and developed it into “media art,” giving contemporary people dreams and visions and opening a new, rich world of creation. At a time when technology, hitherto pursued for utilitarian purposes, is changing our senses and receptor systems, Paik argued that technology needs to be humanized through art, transforming television from a medium supplied to us one-way into a means of human expression. “Good Morning, Mr. Orwell” was his first attempt. A real-time two-way communication project using satellite broadcasting, it is satellite art in the form of a live satellite broadcast between New York and Paris. The New York and Paris recordings that day featured Joseph Beuys, Laurie Anderson, John Cage, John Sanborn, Merce Cunningham, Yves Montand, Peter Gabriel, Thompson Twins, Philip Glass, and others, and were also broadcast in the United States, France, West Germany, South Korea, and elsewhere. The first work in the satellite trilogy.

body.t: Hybrid Art is art created by fusing multiple different forms, media, and techniques, including painting, sculpture, digital technology, biology, and science. It refers to an expressive method combining tradition and innovation to create new visual values and experiences. Representative examples of fusion include the following styles. Digital × analog: Combining hand-drawn analog textures with digital technology such as Photoshop or AI-generated images. Science × art: “Bioart,” which applies biotechnology and robotics to art. Historical styles: For example, art combining Japanese and Western approaches by mixing the techniques of Meiji-era Japanese painting and Western painting. Public cultural institutions and galleries in Japan also hold projects focusing on this method. For example, Fuchu Art Museum has held a “Hybrid Art Lab” as a media-art experimental workshop, making this a field attracting attention.

body.t: will hold “E.A.T.—Experiments in Art and Technology” in ICC Galleries A and B from Friday, April 11, 2003, to Sunday, June 29.

E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology) is a group formed in the mid-1960s around engineer Billy Klüver, then at AT&T’s Bell Telephone Laboratories, together with painter Robert Rauschenberg, Robert Whitman, and others.
Based in New York, conducted numerous experiments connecting art and technology across diverse expressive genres, including visual art, dance, electronic music, and video.

Representative projects include the 1966 event “9 Evenings: Theatre and Engineering,” involving as many as 40 engineers; organizing the 1968 “Some More Beginnings” exhibition at the Brooklyn Museum; and the “Pepsi Pavilion” at the 1970 Osaka Expo. At its peak, it had several thousand members.

E.A.T.'s activities can be considered pioneering for the later expressive genre of performance and collaboration in a broad sense, and are said to have provided the foundation for establishing the Center for Advanced Visual Studies at MIT in 1967.
Although its activities as a large organization effectively ended in the mid-1970s, E.A.T.'s concepts and spirit have greatly influenced the field of “art and technology” from the 1980s onward.

This is Japan's first exhibition comprehensively introducing these E.A.T. activities through contemporary documents and other materials. Particularly centered on Billy Klüver's footsteps, it exhibits his collaborations of the time with Rauschenberg and others, also introduces new works by E.A.T.-related artists, and clarifies its historical significance, directly connected to the principles of ICC's current activities.

body.t: “Ecosophic” is a term based on the concept of “ecosophy (ecology + philosophy)” proposed by thinker Félix Guattari. It refers to thinking and artistic approaches exploring ecological connections and coexistence encompassing society, the human mind, and technology, as well as the natural environment. Through books by Yukiko Shikata (media art curator), a leading figure in this field in Japan, and others, it became widely known in the contexts of art and social criticism. Its main characteristic is connecting the following 3 elements: Environmental ecology (relationships with the natural environment); social ecology (social systems and communities); mental ecology (individual psychology and consciousness). If you would like to explore the ecosophic concept or related art projects further, which of the following information would you like? Details or reviews of Yukiko Shikata's book “Ecosophic Art”; examples of specific artists and works embodying this thinking; relationships between environmental issues, technology, and ecosophy.

body.t: Born in Moscow, Russia, in 1984. Lives in Kyoto.

Interested in human landscape perception and narrative creation, and the relationship between walking and imagination. Walking and interacting with people in various places, she explores stories hidden in the land and expresses them through video, photography, writing, and drawing. Alongside making works and writing, she regards “walking,” making paths in the world, as a form of expression and organizes walking and mapmaking events.

After studying classical music and Japanese literature in Moscow, she moved to Japan in 2012. She completed the doctoral program in Intermedia Art at the Graduate School of Fine Arts, Tokyo University of the Arts. PhD in Fine Arts. Her sole-authored book (a collection of works) is “When an Apple Falls from a Tree, a Sound Is Born” (torch press, 2016). Recent major solo exhibitions include “Days With the Wind | Walking the Island on Windy Days,” Takamatsu Artist-in-Residence 2020 (2021, Megijima, Kagawa), “The Road Goes Along the Peninsula” (2018, Shiretoko Peninsula, Hokkaido), and “On Teto’s Trail,” Gallery Trax (2017, Yamanashi); group exhibitions include “FACES,” SCAI PIRAMIDE (2021, Tokyo), “Land and Beyond | Tracing the Voice of the Earth,” Pola Museum Annex (2021, Tokyo), and “KENPOKU ART” (2016).

body.t: “7000 Oaks (7000 Eichen)” is a historic environmental art project begun in Kassel in 1982 by German contemporary artist Joseph Beuys. It is known as a representative work of “social sculpture” aimed at urban greening and social transformation. Project details: Year begun: 1982 (the international contemporary art exhibition “documenta 7”). Location: Urban Kassel, Germany (subsequently expanded worldwide). Concept: Planting 1 oak sapling together with 1 basalt (black stone) column standing alongside it. Characteristics as art: Citizen participation and economics: Soliciting donations to purchase and plant 1 oak and 1 basalt stone created a mechanism through which citizens and companies could participate in the project. Social sculpture: Beuys advocated the concept that “every human being is an artist,” viewing the process of restoring and constructing relationships between people and the natural environment as one great “sculpture.” Passage of time: By incorporating “time” through growing trees and weathering stones, it made environmental change visible.

body.t: The exhibition “Sky & Game: Eventstructure Research Group 1967-1982” is the first retrospective of the artist collective Eventstructure Research Group (ERG), providing an extensive overview of their works. The group was founded in 1967 by Dutchman Theo Botschuijver, American Sean Wellesley-Miller, and Australian-born Jeffrey Shaw, and was active in the 60s, 70s, and 80s of the last century. It focused on creating temporary art in public spaces centered on play and interaction through installations using air and technology. The group constantly challenged boundaries through large-scale inflatable installations, often adding audiovisual elements that elicited immediate physical responses from audiences. Visitors were always participants, and thus authors created through the work; the work was a structure that you could take in, change, and adapt as you wished, a work as an experience, as an event. The main ideas behind the interventions were to interrupt everyday routines, step off habitual paths, encourage citizens' participation and interaction, and especially to (re)introduce play into society.

The name Eventstructure Research Group (ERG) derives from the concept of “event structure” coined by British conceptual artist John Latham, and was used to describe the relationship between structure (spatial and static) and events (dynamic and temporary). Although its name sounds somewhat formal and academic, ERG was nothing of the sort. The group's ideas appeared in the theoretical essay “Concepts for an Operation Art,” published in the journal Art and Artists in 1969. ERG opposed the dominant methods of the art world at the time, and was overly attached to fixed objects that could have only decorative functions. According to ERG, art's essential functions (revolution, self-action, and calls for social change) had disappeared. ERG's works were therefore deliberately temporary and always situated outside museum walls so that the traditional art world could not control them. Moreover, the authorship of each group work was intentional and entirely collective only in the broadest sense. Not only everyone in and around the group but also users authored the work.
The exhibition “Sky & Play: Eventstructure Research Group 1967-1982” displays original archival materials (drawings, sketches, material studies, aerial art, video materials, and photographs).
Curators: Rosa van Rumpt and Jorn Konijn

body.t: Mishaguji worship is an ancient Japanese form of nature worship (spirit worship) passed down chiefly in the Suwa region of Nagano Prefecture. Without a particular image, gods are said to inhabit stones, trees, snakes, and so forth, and it is considered an extremely ancient form of faith continuing from the Jomon period, before the imperial court’s mythological system became established. Main characteristics of Mishaguji worship. Diverse names and identity: depending on the region, it is called by various written forms and names, including “Mishaguji,” “Misakuchi-no-kami,” “Ishigami,” and “Shakuji.” Originally, it is said to have referred to the “mysterious power” itself dwelling in all things rather than to a particular deity. Foundation of Suwa worship: an extremely important presence underpinning rituals such as the “Ontosai” still performed at Suwa Taisha. The priestly Moriya family, which once governed the Suwa region, had served since ancient times as priests worshipping Mishaguji. Syncretism with boundary gods and stone-god worship: according to research by folklorist Kunio Yanagita and others, it is conjectured to have spread throughout Japan through associations with “Sai-no-kami” and “Dosojin,” who protect village boundaries, and with “Shakuji” worship venerating natural stones resembling reproductive organs.

body.t: The “Jomon Venus” is a clay figurine designated a National Treasure, approximately 5000 years old (Middle Jomon period), excavated from the Tanabatake site in Chino, Nagano Prefecture. Characterized by flowing curved beauty depicting a pregnant woman and a heart-shaped face, it was Japan’s first Jomon-period artifact designated a National Treasure. Characteristics and history. Discovery and excavation: excavated in nearly complete form in 1986 at the Tanabatake site in Chino. A major characteristic is that it was found carefully preserved, unbroken, in the center of the settlement. Design and form: total height 27 centimeters, weight 2.14 kilograms. Mica (kirara) is mixed into the clay, and its entire body was once painted red. Purpose: believed to have been used in rituals praying to the mysterious power of women to nurture life, including prayers for safe childbirth and flourishing descendants. Current exhibition location. The Jomon Venus is currently held and exhibited at the Togariishi Museum of Jomon Archaeology in Chino, Nagano Prefecture.

body.t: A “Klein bottle” is a special surface in topology devised in 1882 by German mathematician Felix Klein, “with no distinction between front and back and no boundary surface.” Overview and characteristics: A three-dimensional version of the Möbius strip: It is the “Möbius strip,” made by twisting a strip 1 time and joining its ends, turned directly into a solid form in three-dimensional space. Following its surface eventually brings you to its back, ultimately making front and back indistinguishable. Closed space: There is no inside (front) or outside (back) of the bottle; it consists of just one surface. Thus, even if water is poured in, it cannot be filled through its spout. Possible only in four-dimensional space: Making this shape in the real three-dimensional world requires it to pass through itself. A complete form requires four-dimensional space.

body.t: Multispecies anthropology is a new research trend in cultural anthropology that moves beyond conventional “anthropocentrism” and regards the world as being constructed through the entanglement of not only humans but all other species (multispecies), including animals, plants, fungi, and viruses. The core of multispecies anthropology. Entangled life and coexistence. Humans do not live alone but are beings who “live together” within relationships with other species. It moves beyond dualisms of humans and animals, nature and society, focusing on the coexistence of all living organisms. Expansion of agency (subjectivity). Rather than granting privileged agency only to humans, it considers animals, plants, natural environments, and even nonliving things to have their own capacities to act and respond. Multispecies ethnography. Through actual fieldwork, scholars depict how humans and other living beings influence one another and share worlds of experience through “thick description (ethnography).”

body.t: is a four-character expression describing something visibly aged over many years, exuding charm and historical dignity. It is used to convey a positive sense of beauty and depth acquired with age, rather than merely being worn out.
Patina: Aged coloring developed over time, or the atmosphere it produces.
Sozen: Refers to an old-fashioned appearance or a bluish-looking appearance.
Used for buildings, artworks, antiques, streetscapes, etc.
“Walking through the back alleys, one finds rows of old wooden buildings imbued with antique dignity.”
“I found an antique hanging scroll imbued with the dignity of age at an antiques market.”
“Koshoku koko”: antiquated, tasteful, and possessing an elegant aroma.
Elegant tranquility: Being quietly secluded, refined, and calm.

body.t: Anthropological art (such as the anthropology of art) is a discipline or approach that explores, from the perspectives of human history and culture, “Why do humans form relationships with the world through art?” and “How is art a system that moves society and cognition, rather than merely an object of appreciation?” The following 2 major currents can be identified. 1. Alfred Gell's “Art and Agency”: British anthropologist Alfred Gell separated artworks from aesthetic evaluation and understood them as “tools with the power (agency) to move people within social relationships.” Index: Materials and signs that influence human cognition and behavior, from African fetishes and Polynesian tattoos to contemporary art. Nexus theory: Analyzes the social networks and cognitive processes that emerge between artworks, makers, and recipients. 2. Shinichi Nakazawa's “Anthropology of Art”: In Japan, thinker Shinichi Nakazawa proposed this as an extension of “symmetrical anthropology.” Symmetrical intelligence: The workings of the mind that encompass logical contradictions and produce fundamental human imagination, such as myth and art. Led by institutions such as Tama Art University's Institute for Anthropology in Art and Design at Tama Art University, human creative activity spanning tens of thousands of years is studied through perspectives crossing art and anthropology. This field's most distinctive feature is thus its dismantling of the modern Western framework of “paintings displayed in museums” and its reconception of art as universal techniques through which humans express themselves and communicate.

body.t: Invisible forces and processes producing influence and transformation within human and nonhuman communities actively shape the ecosystems in which we live.

Sound, signals, vibrations, and bodily fluctuations reveal existential interrelationships between matter and immateriality—that is, the corporeal and incorporeal—and represent knots within the endless movement through which matter and energy constitute the world through bodies and objects.

They also emphasize the complex processes of acquisition, industrialization, and change our environment undergoes, defining more complex relations between nature and the artificial. Borrowing Marco Armiero's words, this can be called the “Wasteocene”: the age of waste.

Contemporary criticism emphasizes the existence of energetic fluxes capable of reconstructing artistic processes in all their forms (Douglas Kahn). These themes form the basis of this year's edition of Liminaria/Interferenze. Through critical and performative spaces, the festival aims to reconsider the possibilities of art itself and explore the infinite phenomena of energy, viewed as a complex of invisible forces shaping every transformation of matter.

Liminaria / Interzona will continue building this discussion around rural, remote, and liminal environments, central pillars for creating futuristic imaginings, and potential scenarios for energetic policies toward collectives.
Local communities, experts, artists, and curators gather opinions on these themes together, attempting hybrid co-curation with the region, those living there, and those passing through.

body.t: “ANALAPOS” is a distinctive echo instrument created in 1970 by sound art pioneer Akio Suzuki. Its structure connects the bottoms of 2 iron cans like a string telephone; striking or rubbing the body manipulates reverberations, producing rich resonances in space. Main characteristics of ANALAPOS: Structure: The bottoms of 2 iron cans (cylinders) face each other, with a spring-like string stretched between them. Playing method: Striking or rubbing it with hands or sticks produces sound, generating resonance and echoes to perform distinctive spatial music. Roots: It emerged from the process of Suzuki's self-study events of “throwing” sounds into space and “tracing” their echoes, which he has conducted since the 1960s. One of his representative works over his many years of creative activity, it has been widely performed and exhibited at contemporary art exhibitions and performances in Japan and abroad.

body.t: Themed around “environmental observation through art,” this work makes the entire space function as a single apparatus for environmental observation. Carsten Nicolai continually pursues cutting-edge activities in visual and sound art and also works as a musician under the name Alva Noto. Marko Peljhan is an activist involved in projects related to art and technology around the world and known for the polar mobile laboratory project “Makrolab,” focusing on telecommunications and weather-observation systems. The long-awaited new work “polarm,” the first collaboration in 10 years between these 2 independently active artists, has finally been unveiled.

In this project focusing on the presence of “radiation,” the properties of radiation and electromagnetic waves on Earth are observed through various devices in the space, converted into light and sound, and further expressed through video and audio. Another “environment = <environment as an unknown polar region>,” ordinarily imperceptible and seemingly situated between the Earth's environment and the information environment, between real space and information space, becomes manifest.

To mark the unveiling of the long-awaited new work, a symposium and live performance were held at the opening. Alongside the artists, participants included the “polar” project’s curators Kazunao Abe (YCAM) and Yukiko Shikata, and guest Andreas Broeckmann, a Berlin-based art historian and curator who, following V2 (Rotterdam) and TESLA, directed “ISEA2010RHUR” and is currently director of Dortmunder U (Dortmund).

body.t: This is an unknown, enormous ocean covering an entire planet in Stanisław Lem's science-fiction novel “Solaris.” Depicted as an “intelligent ocean” that reads and materializes human memories and the unconscious, it has become an enduring theme in science fiction questioning contact with alien intelligence. Main points about the “ocean of Solaris”: Extraordinary properties: The entire planet consists of a single living protoplasm and is said to possess intelligence so great that it can produce local distortions of space-time. Contact with humanity: Scientists attempt to communicate with the ocean, but it reads the human unconscious (memories and guilt), “materializing” forgotten pasts and lost people and making them appear. Philosophical themes: It is a story probing failures of communication and human nature, suggesting that however far humanity advances science, it ultimately arrives at “understanding humans themselves.”

body.t: The “monolith” in “2001: A Space Odyssey” is a mysterious black slab that appears at turning points in humanity's evolution and awakening. Functioning as a tool or information terminal of extraterrestrial intelligent life, it gave apes the intelligence to use tools, and the excavation of one buried on the Moon prompted humanity's expansion into space. The monolith's main appearances and roles: The Dawn of Man (about 4 million years ago): It suddenly appears before starving apemen. Waves emitted by the monolith awaken their “wisdom to use tools” and “fighting spirit.” The lunar surface (the 2000s): It is excavated at the lunar Clavius base as the “Tycho Magnetic Anomaly.” Humanity's touching it and its emission of a signal beyond the solar system trigger the story. Near Jupiter (the Discovery): In the final phase of the Jupiter exploration, it appears before the protagonist, Captain Bowman, as a doorway in space and leads him into an unknown dimension. The monolith's shape and characteristics: The mystery of its proportions: It is a distinctive geometric body whose length, width, and height are precisely in the ratio \(1:4:9\) (the squares of 1, 2, and 3 respectively). Physical properties: Its surface is completely jet black, with a texture that seems to absorb its surroundings. It is an artificially created, extremely advanced tool and has no ego or will of its own.

body.t: “Omiwatari” is a natural phenomenon seen at Lake Suwa, Nagano Prefecture, and elsewhere. In severe winter, the lake surface freezes completely, and ice contraction and expansion cause cracks and high, mountain-range-like ridges. A seasonal feature of Suwa winters, with observation records extending over 600 years from the Muromachi period.

body.t: “Anthropocene” refers to a new, current geological epoch (a proposed chronological division) in which humanity’s economic activity and environmental destruction have fundamentally changed Earth’s natural systems. It is widely discussed in contemporary society as a concept expressing global climate change and ecosystem crises. Basic information about the Anthropocene. Japanese pronunciation: jinshinsei (or hitoshinsei). English name: Anthropocene (antoroposen). Proponent: German atmospheric scientist Dr. Paul Crutzen (proposed in 2000). Background and characteristics of the term. Departure from the Holocene: the current official geological epoch is the “Holocene,” which began approximately 11,700 years ago when the ice age ended. However, because traces of human activity (radioactive materials from nuclear tests, plastics, greenhouse gases, ash from fossil fuel combustion, and so on) have become clearly inscribed in Earth’s strata, it is considered that a new age has begun. Starting point: a prominent view places its beginning in the “Great Acceleration” (rapid increases in population, energy consumption, environmental burdens, and so on) around the 1950s. Geological status: although the concept itself that “humanity has had a decisive impact on Earth” is widely accepted in academia, its adoption as an official geological epoch was rejected once by an international body in 2024/3, and debate continues. Social impact and related books. In Japan and around the world, the concept has become a key term for reconsidering environmental problems and the form of the economy. In particular, economist Kohei Saito’s book “Capital in the Anthropocene” became a bestseller and attracted considerable attention by proposing a reassessment of capitalism and a transition to “degrowth communism” to overcome the environmental crisis.
