body.t: “Fog Sculpture” is a “sculptural” work created by spraying water at high pressure through special nozzles to produce large amounts of artificial “fog.” Influenced by the site’s terrain and weather, the generated fog fluctuates and disperses, covering everything and enveloping the surrounding landscape in a white world. It is considered a mediating “sculpture” resonating with nature: viewers can enter it and bodily experience the continually drifting fog that visualizes slight changes in the weather.

body.t: “The Phenomenon of Man,” the major work of Pierre Teilhard de Chardin (paleontologist and Catholic priest), is a sweeping philosophical and theological work that integrates scientific evolutionary theory and Christian faith, arguing that humanity is the pinnacle of cosmic evolution and has a direction toward the future. Its core ideas and key points are as follows. 1. The process of cosmic evolution: The universe is understood to have evolved from inorganic matter to life and then to the human mind (consciousness), becoming increasingly complex and advanced. Teilhard considered the increase of “spirit (internal energy)” within matter to be the driving force of evolution. 2. Humanity's position and the “nooenos”: Humans are not simply animals; they have the capacity for “reflection” (reflective consciousness), thinking and knowing that they are thinking. He argued that humanity's emergence formed a “layer of mind (nooenos/noosphere)” covering the Earth. 3. The Omega Point (the endpoint of convergence): Cosmic evolution was held to move toward and converge on a single point through the powers of integration and love, rather than dispersing. He called this ultimate destination of evolution, the absolute center that is the goal of history, the “Omega Point,” and identified it with the concept of God. 4. Publication and influence: This thinking, which combined science and religion from a distinctive perspective, was not accepted by the Catholic Church during his lifetime, and was published in the 1950s after his death (1955). It has subsequently been reevaluated as a pioneering vision for later thinkers, environmental movements, and even contemporary AI and theories of digital networks (collective intelligence).

body.t: Born in Nagoya in 1936, Shusaku Arakawa abandoned his artistic activities in Tokyo and moved to New York in 1961, “a little farther away.” Working from Yoko Ono's studio, through exchanges with many artists including Marcel Duchamp he met poet Madeline Gins (1941–2014), who became his partner. The problem they addressed was <What is meaning?> We are always <feeling/thinking> something, but much of this concerns <meaning> mediated by <words>.

The 2 undertook an exhaustive investigation of that <meaning>. After 25 years, the result, completed as an ongoing project, was “The Mechanism of Meaning.” The work comprises 81 large two-dimensional works and 44 drawings, together with photographs and models, for a total of 127 pieces. On this occasion, when a major series that can be called their life's work is presented in its entirety, why not go a little further, beyond the meaning of seeing?

body.t: Information Closure / Informational Closure refers, in discussions of systems, networks, or logical frameworks, to a property or state in which information circulates only within a particular boundary and is completely cut off from the outside, or in which new information from outside does not change its state. Its usage and nuances differ by field. The main 3 contexts and their formulations are as follows. 1. Information closure in systems theory and cybernetics. In biological systems and complex systems science, it is treated as a property necessary for a system to maintain itself. Self-referentiality: rather than receiving raw external data as it is, a system transforms and processes information according to its own internal rules. Boundary with the environment: a state in which, even when physically influenced by the external environment, the processing of information (meaning and interpretation) is completed within the system (a concept close to autopoiesis theory). 2. Information closure in cognitive science and sociology. Used to explain cognitive distortions in individuals or groups, or social phenomena. Echo chamber phenomenon: a state in which only opinions and information matching one’s own circulate, and the exclusion of dissent reinforces particular beliefs. Cognitive closedness: a psychological tendency to reject objective external facts or counterevidence and attempt to explain everything in the world solely through internal logic. 3. Information closure in computer science and logic. A rigorous concept used in rules of data processing and inference. Closure of operations: the property that when particular operations or inferences are performed on information in a set, the resulting new information is necessarily also contained in the same set.

1. Information Closure Theory of Consciousness (neuroscience/cognitive science): A hypothesis proposed by neuroscientist Ryota Kanai and others explaining the mechanism of consciousness through information theory. Essence: Consciousness arises when information from the external environment, past memories, and so on is separated within a system (such as the brain) by a particular boundary (information closure), forming a self-contained whole. Non-Trivial Information Closure (NTIC): The theory's central concept, referring to a state where information processing inside the system is independent of the outside world and involves complex information integration (nontrivial loops or processing). Systems with nonzero NTIC are assumed to possess consciousness.

body.t: Chaitin's constant (Japanese reading: Chaitin no teisu; English: Chaitin's constant) is a concept in algorithmic information theory, a field of computer science, and informally is a real number expressing the probability that a randomly selected program halts. It emerged from Gregory Chaitin's research. Also called halting probability (Japanese reading: teishi kakuritsu; English: Halting probability).

There are infinitely many halting probabilities, but they are usually represented by Ω as though they were 1. Because Ω depends on how programs are encoded, discussion without specifying an encoding scheme is sometimes called Chaitin's construction.

body.t: A busy beaver is a type of Turing machine studied in computability theory. The name derives from an English idiom meaning “workaholic.” A busy beaver starts processing with a blank tape and runs as long as possible, but ultimately halts. This gives an upper bound on the time and space (tape) length that a class of halting Turing machines can consume.

The busy beaver function quantifies this upper bound and is an example of a noncomputable function. It can be proved that this function grows faster than any computable function. The concept was first introduced under the name “busy beaver game” in Tibor Radó’s (English-language article) 1962 paper “On Non-Computable Functions.”

body.t: Confirmation bias is a cognitive bias: a psychological process in which people collect only information supporting their preconceptions or opinions and ignore or exclude contradictory information to affirm them.

body.t: (Constraint Satisfaction Network) is a network model for finding solutions satisfying multiple constraints in artificial intelligence and computer science. Overview: Components: 3 elements—variables, the ranges of their values (domains), and constraint relationships between variables. Representation: A graph structure with variables as “nodes (points)” and constraints as “edges (lines).” Purpose: To find combinations of variables (solutions) that satisfy all constraints simultaneously. Representative network models: CPN (Constraint Posting Network): A model that flexibly adds and changes constraints. Boltzmann machine: A neural network that changes states probabilistically and maximizes constraints. Hopfield network: A model that converges to a state (solution) minimizing an energy function. 🛠 Specific applications: Sudoku and crosswords: Rules against duplicate numbers or letters in cells serve as constraints. Map coloring: The constraint that adjacent regions must not be colored the same. Timetables and shift creation: Scheduling that considers room availability and work preferences.

body.t: Decision Field Theory (DFT) is a dynamic cognitive model that mathematically explains the process through which humans choose among options while wavering over time. Unlike traditional economic theories, it can predict not only the “outcome” of a decision but also the “time taken to choose (reaction time)” and “changes of mind.” Core idea: People repeatedly alternate between considering the advantages and disadvantages of each option, gradually accumulating evaluations (sampling). Fluctuation in preference: Over time, the inclination (preference) toward a particular option in the mind rises and falls like a wave. Crossing a threshold (Japanese reading: shikiichi): A choice is made the moment its accumulated preference first reaches a “boundary (threshold)” set beforehand within oneself.

body.t: Means “disappearing like smoke” in Italian and is a painting technique that removes outlines by blurring boundaries between colors and shading. Known for being perfected by Leonardo da Vinci, it produces the subtle expressions around the eyes and mouth in his representative work “Mona Lisa.” Characteristics and effects. No outlines: just as real objects have no clear lines, volume is expressed through gradients rather than lines. Smooth gradations: colors are mixed in such slight amounts that their boundaries are imperceptible, blending light and shadow. Atmosphere and vitality: creates softness as if enveloped in smoke or air and a skin texture that seems alive. How the technique works. Multiple thin layers: oil paints are made into a translucent varnish-like state and applied repeatedly in many thin layers. Light reflection: light passes through the many thin layers of color and reflects at the surface, producing distinctive translucency.

body.t: A coplanar plane (Coplanar Plane/coplanarity) refers in mathematics and geometry to a state where multiple points or lines all exist “on the same plane.”
The main characteristics and conditions are as follows.
• 3 points: Any 3 points in space always determine 1 plane, so they are necessarily coplanar.

• 4 or more points: Vectors are used to determine whether 4 points (A, B, C, D) lie on the same plane. If the scalar triple product of vectors \(\vec{AB}\), \(\vec{AC}\), and \(\vec{AD}\) is 0, these 4 points are coplanar.

body.t: The combination of “chaos” and “infinite speed” is discussed in several contexts, mainly chaos theory (deterministic chaos), physics (dynamical systems), or fictional and philosophical concepts.
Depending on the specific context, mainly the following 3 meanings are possible.
1. “Sensitivity to initial conditions” in chaos theory (the butterfly effect)
In chaos theory, trajectory diffusion is a phenomenon changing so rapidly that its speed feels “infinite.”
• Exponential change: In chaotic systems, tiny initial differences (differences in initial values) expand over time at exponential speeds (ferociously fast, nearly infinite).
• Unpredictability: Because this diffusion is so fast, predicting future states becomes effectively impossible (a chaotic state).
In statistical mechanics and dynamical systems, chaotic motion moves so as to fill every location in “phase space (the space representing states).”
• Infinite paths: Chaotic trajectories proceed through limited space while bending with infinite complexity.
• Effectively infinite speed: its property of seemingly spreading instantaneously throughout space (ergodicity or mixing) is sometimes expressed metaphorically as “chaos spreading at infinite speed.”
Focusing on actual physical “speed,” Einstein's theory of relativity means real matter cannot attain infinite speed (above light speed).

• However, in chains of quantum entanglement (nonlocality) and chaotic changes in space-time caused by inflation (rapid expansion) in the early universe, extremely rapid fluctuations suggesting “infinite speed”—exceeding light speed or spreading throughout the whole instantaneously—are sometimes discussed.

excerpt.t: The combination of “chaos” and “infinite speed” is discussed in several contexts, mainly chaos theory (deterministic chaos), physics (dynamical systems), or fictional and philosophical concepts.

body.t: Boundedness (Japanese reading: yukaisei) in chaos theory means the system's state (trajectory) continues to remain within a finite region of phase space without diverging to infinity.
The importance of boundedness in chaos
• Preventing divergence: Even if sensitivity to initial values irregularly separates trajectories greatly, they do not fly off infinitely throughout space.

• Necessary condition for chaos: phenomena that are merely irregular and unpredictable but whose variables diverge are not considered chaos; boundedness, continuing to wander within a finite range, is essential.
• Strange attractors: Because of boundedness, trajectories remain confined around particular limited, complex structures (attractors), tracing beautiful fractal shapes.

excerpt.t: Boundedness (Japanese reading: yukaisei) in chaos theory means the system's state (trajectory) continues to remain within a finite region of phase space without diverging to infinity.

body.t: Sensitivity to initial conditions in chaos means that even tiny differences in the starting state (initial conditions) lead to greatly differing subsequent results as time passes.
Characteristics of sensitivity to initial conditions
• Butterfly effect: Famous for the analogy that “tiny air disturbances as slight as a butterfly flapping its wings greatly affect weather such as typhoons far away.”

• Impossibility of long-term prediction: even in systems whose futures are fully determined by physical laws and the like (deterministic systems), tiny initial measurement errors expand rapidly over time, making accurate prediction of the distant future impossible.
• Familiar examples: Weather forecasts (accurate several days ahead, difficult weeks ahead), irregular motion of double pendulums, etc.

body.t: The reversal of Platonism is a philosophy advocated by French philosopher Gilles Deleuze, reversing Platonism's fundamental order.
• Superiority of Forms: Plato regarded the visible actual world (sensible world) as an imperfect copy (image) of “Forms (true originals).”
• Fixing the hierarchy: It strictly distinguished the original “model (copy)” from inferior “things resembling it but different (simulacra = bad phantoms),” placing truth and identity above them.
• Liberation of simulacra: Dismantles the fixed hierarchy of original and imitation, moving toward affirmation of the “simulacrum (semblance)” itself, a copy of a copy not obeying order.

• Primacy of difference: rejects thinking premised on the identity “A is A,” positioning “pure difference” irreducible to identity and “becoming (continual change)” as the first principles of existence.
• Transformation of thought: Creating a state in which thought is forced through intense encounters with sensory “signs/intensities,” rather than established frameworks of morality or reason.
If you like, I can also discuss the following:
• The specific progression of the discussion in “Difference and Repetition.”
• The influence of “simulacra” on art and contemporary thought.

body.t: "Airborne Newscasts" (Relational Architecture 20) is an interactive shadow play originally commissioned by the Chrysler Museum of Art to transform Norfolk’s public space. Participants block the light of two projectors casting their shadows on a 900 sqm wall, and these are tracked by computerized surveillance systems. Out of the shadows emanate billowing smoke which is mapped onto the wall and accumulates in it. Turbulent clouds of text evaporate from the “heat” of the tracked bodies. The text are live news cables from Reuters, Agencia EFE, Notimex, AlterNet, AP and other sources.

The opening of the project in Norfolk was just a couple of days after the Boston Marathon Bombing and out of respect for the victims the newscasts were replaced with poetry from salient authors such as John Ashbery, Kathy Acker, Wallace Stevens, Cedar Sigo, Adrian Matejka, Nicole Brossard, William Blake and others.

body.t: "Body Movies" transforms public space with interactive projections measuring between 400 and 1,800 square metres. Thousands of photographic portraits, previously taken on the streets of the host city, are shown using robotically controlled projectors. However, the portraits only appear inside the projected shadows of the passers-by, whose silhouettes can measure between two and twenty-five metres depending on how close or far away they are from the powerful light sources positioned on the ground. A video surveillance tracking system triggers new portraits when all the existing ones have been revealed, inviting the public to occupy new narratives of representation.

Samuel van Hoogstraten's engraving "The Shadow Dance" (Rotterdam, 1675) is the main source of inspiration for this work. Body Movies attempts to misuse technologies of the spectacular so they can evoke a sense of intimacy and complicity instead of provoking distance, euphoria, catharsis, obedience or awe.

body.t: “Frequency and Volume” (Relational Architecture 9) enables participants to tune into and listen to different radio frequencies by using their own bodies. A computerized tracking system detects participants' shadows, which are projected on a wall of the exhibition space. The shadows scan the radio waves with their presence and position, while their size controls the volume of the signal. The piece can tune into any frequency between 150 kHz and 1.5 GHz, including air traffic control, FM, AM, short wave, cellular, CB, satellite, wireless telecommunication systems and radio navigation. Up to forty-eight frequencies can be tuned simultaneously and the resulting sound environment forms a composition controlled by people's movements. This piece visualizes the radioelectric spectrum and turns the human body into an antenna. All the receiver equipment used and antennae are exhibited in an adjacent room.

The project was developed at a time when the Mexican Government was very active in shutting down informal or "pirate" radio stations in indigenous communities in the states of Chiapas and Guerrero. The question "who has access to the public space that is the radioelectric spectrum" is one that deserves attention and visualization tools not just in Mexico but also here in the developed world, where there is a remarkable assymmetry in the assignation of frequencies only to government or corporate interests to the detriment of community-building, experimental or artistic uses of the spectrum. This project was inspired by the "Manifesto for Antenna-Man" and the radio poetry experiments by the Mexican estridentista artists in the 1920s.

body.t: chat: Redefining shadows and sonic space
Of course. Based on the attached materials and exchanges with Abe, the core this time is quite clear.
**I think the core production theme is “redefining shadows as media connecting self-recognition, spatial recognition, acoustic feedback, and technological history, rather than mere visual effects.”**
These 4 axes initially seem important when reading the materials.

From Plato's cave, Christian painting, theater, film, and animation to doppelgängers, shadows have been treated as “proxies for substances,” “the self made other,” and “visualizations of the invisible.” The materials particularly emphasize that shadows have renewed their meaning with each appearance of new technologies such as film, animation, and interactive art, rather than developing independently.

In early interactive art, shadows were used as the body's most intuitive input data. Shadows are therefore a primitive yet powerful interface linking “embodiment” and “image processing.” The material emphasizes Lozano-Hemmer's linking shadows to social criticism and readings of public space rather than using them merely as visual effects.

ShadowUp is an experience of “bringing shadows out in three dimensions” rather than illumination. Its proprietary StereoLight and 3D glasses present different shadow images to the left and right eyes, forming three-dimensional images of shadows, reflected light, and transmitted light within space.

Especially interesting is the ability to treat shadows as “moving, touchable, searchable, transformable spatial phenomena” rather than “fixed images,” using fixed lights, handheld lights, caustics, mirror balls, robot arms, and so on.
4. Points connecting to future artwork proposals.
Combining Boulez/IRCAM/real-time feedback, 40Hz resonance, caves and rituals, spectra, and spatial audio discussed with Abe, the following is quite a strong direction.
A work treating shadows as input, sound as response, and space as a memory medium.

That is, it 3D-maps viewers' and objects' shadows, converting their shape, density, scale, and fluctuations into acoustic parameters. It also incorporates the space's own resonant frequencies and acoustic stimulation near 40Hz as external factors, creating a feedback loop in which shadows and sound alter each other.
In particular, the materials’ conclusion states that developing ShadowUp as international art requires social meaning, criticality, and connections with AI/data science, beyond simple shadow play.

This is quite important: connecting it with Keigo’s research and production would be stronger if extended beyond **“the beauty of shadows” to “modulation of self-recognition through shadows,” “changes in bodily state through spatial sound,” and “AI interpretation of shadows and sound.”**
The next thing to do is to take the materials
① Reference history ② Technical specifications ③ Work concept ④ Implementation proposal ⑤ Materials for the next proposal to Abe
It is best organized into 5 chapters for a presentation.

A work treating shadows as input, sound as response, and space as a memory medium. That is, it 3D-maps the shadows of viewers and objects and converts their shape, density, scale, and fluctuations into acoustic parameters. It also incorporates the space's own resonant frequencies and acoustic stimulation near 40Hz as external factors, creating a feedback loop in which shadows and sound change each other. Please research as thoroughly as possible whether any studies or works have already done this.

As far as I have researched, I have not yet found a representative work or study fully integrating the identical configuration: “3D shadow mapping → acoustic response → spatial resonance/40Hz → feedback loop.”
However, there are several quite close precedents.

The closest example is Rafael Lozano-Hemmer's “Frequency and Volume” (2003). It tracks participants' shadows, scans radio frequencies according to their positions, and controls volume according to their size. Thus, a “shadow = interface for manipulating sound/frequency” already exists. It is described as sounding up to 48 frequencies simultaneously, with bodily movements composing the sound environment.

The next closest example is the Japanese research/work “sonodial.” This interactive sound installation uses Kinect to acquire participants' 3D shapes, generates and projects artificial shadows, and changes the sound parameters of granular synthesis through their movement. It is quite close in terms of “3D-acquired body → shadow → sound generation.”

David Rokeby's “Very Nervous System,” though not involving shadows themselves, is also a classic precedent converting bodily movements into music in real time. Because body positions and movements are converted into multilayered sound, it is important in the lineage of “turning bodies/spaces into instruments.”

Lozano-Hemmer's Body Movies, 2001, is also important as an example connecting shadows with public space, memory, and otherness. Portraits photographed in the city appear within passersby's enormous shadows, using shadows as “media reflecting others' memories.”

Care is needed regarding 40Hz and cave resonance. Acoustic studies of ancient sites and caves frequently report resonances around 90–120Hz at places such as Malta’s Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum; it does not seem that 40Hz itself has been centrally demonstrated in ancient caves.

Meanwhile, it is true that 40Hz sensory stimulation attracts attention in research on brain gamma rhythms and Alzheimer’s, and MIT-related studies continue investigating the neuroscientific effects of 40Hz light and sound stimulation.
So the conclusion is that each element has precedents, but Keigo's proposal has ample originality.
What is particularly new is not merely “making sound with shadows,” but
Turning shadows into 3D data, converting them into sound generation, and incorporating spatial resonant frequencies and 40Hz stimulation into the feedback loop as “external factors.”

I think this could become quite a strong proposal by integrating Lozano-Hemmer-style shadows/public space, Rokeby-style body–sound interaction, sonodial-style artificial-shadow sound, and archaeoacoustics/neuroacoustics. chat

body.t: “Two Origins” (Relational Architecture 7) is an intervention in which the emblematic Place du Capitole in Toulouse was transformed by a projection of The Book of Two Origins, a 13th-century heretical manuscript compiling the theological beliefs of the dualist cathars. Once a vibrant community in several regions of Europe, the believers in the two origins of the Universe were virtually annihilated by the brutal crusades that gave birth to the Inquisition and France's expansion. The texts are illegible since they are projected overlapping each other on the same façade from two distant projectors; only when passers-by block one text with their bodies is it possible to read the other text inside their shadow.
Two Origins attempts to connect disparate planes of experience, inviting people to discover texts that have been covered-up by history and intolerance.
References for this work include research into the "minor histories" that characterise European trends of pluralism and dissent.

body.t: "Vectorial Elevation" (Relational Architecture 4) is an interactive art project originally designed to celebrate the arrival of the year 2000 in Mexico City's Zócalo Square. The website(

) enabled any Internet user to design light sculptures over the city's historic centre, with eighteen searchlights positioned around the square. These searchlights, whose powerful beams could be seen within a 15 kilometres radius, were controlled by an online 3D simulation program and visualized by digital cameras. A personalized webpage was produced for every participant with images of their design and information such as their name, dedication, place of access and comments. These web pages were completely uncensored, allowing participants to leave a wide variety of messages, including love poems, football scores, Zapatista slogans and twenty-seven marriage proposals. In Mexico, the project attracted 800,000 participants from 89 countries over the course of its two-week duration.

Vectorial Elevation alludes to Sol LeWitt's "art of instructions" as well as László Moholy-Nagy's paintings by telephone in 1922. Another precedent was the teleoperation of the Lindbergh searchlight in Los Angeles in 1928, activated when President Coolidge pressed a telegraph key at his desk at the White House.

William Kentridge presented the Charles Eliot Norton Lectures in 2012, entitled “Six Drawing Lessons.” Incorporating elements of graphic design and ranging freely from discussions of Plato’s cave to the Enlightenment’s role in colonial oppression to the depiction of animals in art, Six Drawing Lessons is an illustration of its own thesis of how art creates knowledge. Foregrounding the very processes by which we see, Kentridge makes us more aware of the mechanisms—and deceptions—through which we construct meaning in the world.

body.t: “Embodiment,” “4E,” and “Galla (Shaun Gallagher)” are central concepts in contemporary cognitive science and philosophy of mind. They express the idea that the body and environment, as well as the brain, play indispensable roles in cognitive processes.
“4E cognition,” proposed and organized by Shaun Gallagher, regards cognition through an approach composed of 4 “E”s:
Embodied: the idea that cognition is deeply rooted in bodily structure and sensorimotor functions, not only within the brain.
Embedded: Our cognition is “embedded” in physical and social environments and cannot function without interacting with them.
Extended: The view that external environments such as tools, smartphones, and notebooks also extend functions and abilities as parts of cognitive processes.
Enacted / Enactive: The idea that cognition and perception are not passive information processing but “action” itself, actively engaging the environment.

A shrine recounting Japanese religious history: nature/huge-stone worship/descent of heavenly deities/arrival of Buddhism/Shinto-Buddhist syncretism/separation of Shinto and Buddhism.
Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Ame no Hoakari Kushitama Nigihayahi no Mikoto (Nigihayahi no Mikoto)
(Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Ame no Hoakari Kushitama Nigihayahi no Mikoto)

Known since ancient times as a training site for Shinto practitioners and Shugendo, the grotto formed by numerous huge rocks becomes a broad cave in some places and a narrow hole barely large enough for a single person to pass through in others. The Amanogawa flows into it, becomes a torrent, and erodes the rocks; it is said that even those who know no special ascetic practices can undergo training simply by touring the grotto. This grotto is open to visitors. To preserve its original appearance, safety measures are kept to the minimum necessary, so visitors are requested to observe the following.
1. Wear ritual clothing (shirotasuki; available to borrow at the shrine office).
2. Change slippery shoes for straw sandals (ibid.).
3. Age restrictions (10 years or older, under 75).
5. Visits are unavailable at night, in rain, or during high water.
Visits to sacred rocks and rock-carved Buddhas
An ancient Japanese belief that huge or unusual rocks house divine spirits or receive their descent. Many rock-carved Buddhas are carved into rocks believed to house gods.

body.t: 1. Information Closure Theory of Consciousness (neuroscience/cognitive science): A hypothesis proposed by neuroscientist Ryota Kanai and others explaining the mechanism of consciousness through information theory. Essence: Consciousness arises when information from the external environment, past memories, and so on is separated within a system (such as the brain) by a particular boundary (information closure), forming a self-contained whole. Non-Trivial Information Closure (NTIC): The theory's central concept, referring to a state where information processing inside the system is independent of the outside world and involves complex information integration (nontrivial loops or processing). Systems with nonzero NTIC are assumed to possess consciousness.

Information Closure / Informational Closure refers, in discussions of systems, networks, or logical frameworks, to a property or state in which information circulates only within a particular boundary and is completely cut off from the outside, or in which new information from outside does not change its state. Its usage and nuances differ by field. The main 3 contexts and their formulations are as follows. 1. Information closure in systems theory and cybernetics. In biological systems and complex systems science, it is treated as a property necessary for a system to maintain itself. Self-referentiality: rather than receiving raw external data as it is, a system transforms and processes information according to its own internal rules. Boundary with the environment: a state in which, even when physically influenced by the external environment, the processing of information (meaning and interpretation) is completed within the system (a concept close to autopoiesis theory). 2. Information closure in cognitive science and sociology. Used to explain cognitive distortions in individuals or groups, or social phenomena. Echo chamber phenomenon: a state in which only opinions and information matching one’s own circulate, and the exclusion of dissent reinforces particular beliefs. Cognitive closedness: a psychological tendency to reject objective external facts or counterevidence and attempt to explain everything in the world solely through internal logic. 3. Information closure in computer science and logic. A rigorous concept used in rules of data processing and inference. Closure of operations: the property that when particular operations or inferences are performed on information in a set, the resulting new information is necessarily also contained in the same set.

body.t: The universe's greatest mystery: “The vanished antimatter.” Immediately after the birth of the universe (the Big Bang), matter and antimatter are thought to have been created in exactly equal numbers. Yet surveying the universe today reveals almost no antimatter in nature, and our Earth and stars are made only of matter. The mystery of “why only antimatter disappeared while only matter remained” is thought to relate to the physical phenomenon of “CP symmetry violation,” but has not yet been fully explained.

body.t: “Ki'in seido” (spirit resonance and lifelike movement) is a four-character expression describing paintings, calligraphy, writing, and other works overflowing with noble dignity and a vivid sense of life. Originating in ancient Chinese art theory, it has been regarded as the most important mindset in East Asian painting. Meaning and origins: Ki'in: Refinement and a wonderful atmosphere that seems to emanate from a work. Seido: Being so full of life that it seems about to move. Origin: It began as the first of the six basic rules for painting well (the Six Principles of Painting) listed in “Guhua Pinlu” (Japanese reading: Koga Hinroku; Record of the Classification of Old Painters), a treatise written by Xie He (Japanese reading: Shakaku), a painter of the Qi dynasty during China's Northern and Southern Dynasties period.

body.t: “De architectura” consists of 10 treatises on architecture and other technologies written by the ancient Roman engineer Vitruvius. Dedicated to Emperor Augustus. Also called “On Architecture,” “Architectural Theory,” or “Ten Books on Architecture.” In Japan, Keiichi Morita's translation was published as “Vitruvius's Books on Architecture.”

In fact, neither the term “golden ratio (1:1.618...)” nor its mathematics appears directly in “De architectura / Ten Books on Architecture,” written by the ancient Roman architect Vitruvius. However, the idea of “human bodily proportions” proposed in the book later became closely associated with the golden ratio during the Renaissance and developed into a standard of beauty. The key points of this relationship and its historical background are as follows. 1. The “human bodily proportions” taught by Vitruvius: In Book 3 of “De architectura,” Vitruvius argued that architecture (particularly temples) should imitate the proportions of the “human body,” a masterpiece of nature. He described harmony between body parts through integer ratios, such as “a palm equals the width of 4 fingers” and “the length of a foot is 4 times the palm.” He left the description that “when a healthy human lies on their back with arms and legs spread, they fit within a perfect ‘circle’ and ‘square’ centered on the navel.” 2. Da Vinci's integration with the “golden ratio”: The famous drawing “Vitruvian Man” faithfully visualized this description by Leonardo da Vinci during the Renaissance, nearly 1500 years later. While reproducing Vitruvius's thinking, da Vinci also incorporated geometric structures of the golden ratio (1:1.618) throughout this drawing of the human body. This led to “ancient architectural theory” and “mathematical beauty (the golden ratio)” being interpreted as contiguous concepts.

body.t: Superstring theory is a model for understanding the fundamental constituents of matter and is 1 of the theories and hypotheses of physics. It extends string theory, which regards matter's fundamental units as strings with 1-dimensional extent rather than infinitely small 0-dimensional point particles, by adding the idea of supersymmetry. It is also called super-string theory or superstring theory.

As a hypothesis that can unravel the form of the universe and the mechanism of its birth while simultaneously explaining the world beyond microscopic things such as atoms, elementary particles, and quarks, this theory is highly developed with almost no internal contradictions. However, sufficient experimental results supporting it have not been obtained. Moreover, the energy necessary for experiments demonstrating this theory is assumed to exceed what humanity can handle, leaving room for debate about its testability.

body.t: The frequency spectrum of pink noise is approximately a straight line on a log-log graph, with equal power in frequency ranges of equal width on that graph. In other words, the power in the frequency range from 40 to 60 Hz equals that in the range from 4000 to 6000 Hz. Human hearing actually has similar characteristics: whatever the original frequency, doubling it is perceived as rising 1 octave (changes of 40–60 Hz and 4000–6000 Hz are perceived similarly). Pink noise, with equal power per octave, is therefore often used as a reference signal in acoustic engineering. In terms of spectral density, it shows a decline relative to white noise of 3dB per 1 octave (10dB per 10-fold frequency increase) (density is proportional to 1/f). Pink noise is consequently also called 1/f (1 over f) noise.

body.t: (English: Phase vocoder) is a vocoder modeling audio signals through amplitude and phase in the frequency domain.
At the heart of the phase vocoder is the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), through the following stages.
Analysis: Conversion from time-domain representation → time–frequency representation (English version) by STFT.
Modification: Manipulating amplitude and phase of arbitrary frequency components.
Resynthesis: Frequency-domain representation → time-domain representation through inverse STFT.

A phase vocoder allows time-stretching and pitch conversion of audio signals through frequency-domain modification. Changing STFT analysis frames' temporal positions before resynthesis also changes the resynthesized result's evolution in time, for example enabling changes in sound timescale.

British composer Trevor Wishart (English version) created “Vox V()” (on the album “Vox Cycle (English version)”) based on phase-vocoder analysis/transformation of the human voice. American composer Roger Reynolds's “Transfigured Wind()” used a phase vocoder to time-stretch flute sounds.

Introduced as an algorithm maintaining horizontal coherence between phases of bins representing sinusoidal components. This original phase vocoder did not consider vertical coherence between adjacent frequency bins, so audio signals time-stretched by the system lacked clarity.

excerpt.t: (English: Phase vocoder) is a vocoder modeling audio signals through amplitude and phase in the frequency domain.

body.t: The phase-coherence problem is a major issue that must always be resolved when manipulating an STFT time-frequency representation (STFT representation). Using analysis windows (window functions) overlapping along the time axis causes individual signal components (sinusoids, impulses) to spread across multiple frames and STFT frequency bins (in frequency, this corresponds to “spectral leakage”). The temporal overlap of window functions is based on the fact that adjacent STFT (short-time Fourier transform) analysis results are strongly correlated (a sinusoidal component present in the analysis frame at time t is likely to continue similarly in subsequent frames).

All modifications made to an STFT representation must maintain “appropriate correlations” with adjacent frequency bins (vertical coherence) and time frames (horizontal coherence). This relates to the problem of signal transformation by the phase vocoder. Except when the synthesized sound is extremely simple, maintaining these “appropriate correlations” accurately is difficult. Since the invention of the phase vocoder, research has mainly sought algorithms that preserve vertical/horizontal coherence after modifications to the STFT representation. Amplitude coherence is only a minor problem for time-scale manipulation, since shifting analysis frames in time has only a small effect on amplitude. The problem of phase coherence, however, required consideration over a considerably longer period before suitable solutions were obtained.

In particular, it often refers to one with discrete time (times represented by subscripts).

body.t: Following just intonation strictly requires infinitely many scales

We provisionally defined 8 notes in the scale above, but this is insufficient. For example, defining 2:3 and 4:5 relative to B (495Hz) yields 742.5 Hz and 618.75 Hz. Repeating from 742.5 Hz ... actually produces an infinite scale.

This happens because however many times it is repeated, one never returns to the original note. If it returned like today's scale—do, re, mi, ..., do—it would stop there, but unfortunately “2 times,” representing a note an octave above, and “3 times” and “5 times,” producing beautiful chords, are prime numbers, so it never returns however one tries.

excerpt.t: Following just intonation strictly requires infinitely many scales

body.t: Why are there 12 notes in the first place? The conclusion is that this number allows theory and practice to find just the right compromise.

Using the Pythagorean theory mentioned above, we keep producing notes with the simple frequency ratio 1:3 and would ideally stop on reaching a note exactly 1 octave higher. However, as noted above, 2 and 3 are prime numbers, so even infinite repetition never returns to the original number.
Calculating whether a compromise is possible somewhere, the 12th iteration gives a note close to the original. The error then is 23.46 cents (1 cent is 1/100 of a semitone).

Mathematically, this happens because there is a theory about powers of 2 and powers of 3 becoming close… But leaving that aside, Pythagoras accepted these 23.46 cents and determined this point to be 1 octave.
Incidentally, the next time it approaches the original note—I forget exactly—was something like 30 or 40, I think.
Thus, there being 12 notes is not the result of a perfect theory but a compromise between theory and practice.

excerpt.t: Why are there 12 tones?

The sound's distinguishing features are, first, synthesizer timbres resembling the beeping (= bleep sounds) suggested by its name, distorted “acid house”-style basslines, and rhythmic sounds and developments characteristic of “Chicago house,” combining into an intuitive sound stimulating the senses of the human brain and body.

“Bleep house” can be described as an evolved sound formed around the sound of artists such as LFO, whose releases on the prestigious UK techno label Warp took the 90s by storm (the sound known as “bleep techno”), and the “acid house” and “Chicago house” movements originating in Chicago, US, from the 80s, with the addition of laptop production and other practices arising from “click house,” popular over the last few years.

body.t: “Vinyl brake” (Japanese pronunciation: vainaru bureki) is one technique used by DJs and music producers when operating turntables. It creates a brief stop during analog-record playback, temporarily halting the rhythm or beat to add rhythmic changes or effects.

When spinning a record on a turntable, DJs commonly stop or turn the disc by hand. Because stopping it at a consistent speed is difficult this way, a “vinyl brake” is used to control temporary stops more precisely.

“Vinyl brake” is a method of temporarily stopping a record by placing a vinyl disc on a turntable, putting a finger at its center, and lightly pressing the finger while the record turns. This makes it possible to temporarily stop the flow of music or add effects. Many DJs master this technique as an important element of DJ skill and creative staging.

body.t: The Poisson distribution used in statistics and probability theory is a discrete probability distribution representing the number of times an event occurs within a fixed period. body.t: FM synthesis is a type of sound synthesis method for generating music and sound effects. FM abbreviates Frequency Modulation. FM synthesis was originally invented by John Chowning in 1967.
FM synthesis generates sound using multiple oscillators, modulating the frequency of 1 oscillator with another oscillator’s frequency. This frequency modulation can produce complex, rich timbres.

Typical FM synthesis uses 2 waveforms: a carrier wave and a modulator wave. The carrier wave is the sound actually heard, and the modulator wave is used to change its frequency. The higher the modulator wave's frequency, the higher the carrier wave's frequency also becomes.

FM synthesis can create complex timbres using simple waveforms. Combining several operators (combinations of oscillators and modulators), for example, can reproduce chime sounds, metallic sounds, bell sounds, and more.

FM synthesis was adopted by Yamaha in the digital synthesizer “DX7” during the 1980s and achieved great success through its rich timbres and flexibility. It remains an important method used in music production and sound-effect generation.

body.t: The carrier wave is a concept used in communications and signal processing.

Viewed as a physical wave, a carrier wave is a fundamental high-frequency wave for carrying other information. By modulating data or information, this wave is converted into a signal carrying information. In other words, the carrier wave itself contains no information; its waveform functions as a “carrier” transmitting other signals.

For example, in radio broadcasting, television broadcasting, and wireless communications, information such as sound and images is modulated onto a carrier wave and propagates through the air. At the receiving end, the original information can be extracted by demodulating the carrier wave.

Carrier waves are normally high-frequency, with wavelengths chosen according to the bandwidth required to carry information. Because high frequencies allow efficient information transmission, many communication systems choose high frequencies for their carrier waves.
Carrier waves are also sometimes used as basic sounds in speech and music synthesis. In FM synthesis, combinations of carrier and modulator waves generate complex timbres.

excerpt.t: The carrier wave is a concept used in communications and signal processing.

body.t: Grid world is a concept used in computer science and artificial intelligence (AI).

A grid world represents an environment of square cells called a grid arranged in a fixed configuration. In a 1-dimensional grid world, cells form a single row along a straight line. Each cell represents a particular location and is uniquely identified by it.

A 1-dimensional grid world is a very simple environment used mainly as a testbed for reinforcement learning and optimization algorithms. An actor called an Agent aims to achieve a goal while moving within the grid world and receiving rewards on cells.

For example, the objective is to reach a particular cell in a 1-dimensional grid world, and the agent learns how to achieve it by choosing its actions. The agent decides actions considering its current position and rewards, aiming to find an optimal strategy.

A 1-dimensional grid world is extremely simple, making problems easy to analyze and helping understand and evaluate algorithms. The concept may also be extended to more complex 2- or 3-dimensional grid worlds.

body.t: A chirp signal is a signal whose frequency increases over time (“up-chirp”) or decreases over time (“down-chirp”). It is sometimes used synonymously with sweep signal. Commonly used in sonar and radar, it is also employed in other applications such as spread-spectrum communication. When used in spread spectrum, it is often generated and demodulated using surface-acoustic-wave devices such as RAC (reflective array compressors). In optical systems, increases or decreases in pulse-signal dispersion due to the dispersion characteristics of optical transmission-path materials can sometimes turn ultrashort laser pulses into chirp signals. The name chirp derives from the English word for birdsong.

body.t: New Academism is a term coined

by mass media to describe as a social phenomenon the boom in new forms of knowledge outside existing academic frameworks, when works by Akira Asada and Shinichi Nakazawa became bestsellers in the mid-1980s; it has no strict definition. It basically referred to a trend arising alongside the importation into Japan of contemporary Western academic currents such as semiotics, structuralism, poststructuralism, and postmodernism.

It is characterized by interdisciplinary thought crossing existing academic divisions, sometimes adopting free expression departing from traditional scholarly argumentation and conventions. Journalism, therefore, rather than scholarly societies or academic journals, was its main arena. However, almost all its thinkers held university positions.

Factories built in the early 1950s with East German technical assistance and later repurposed are concentrated here, housing many artists’ studios and residences and galleries established from China, Japan, and other countries. As an artists’ community, it is often compared to New York’s Greenwich Village or SoHo.

Since the Ullens Center for Contemporary Art (Ullens Center for Contemporary Art) opened in 2007 in the renovated “Factory 798,” this area has become a central contemporary-art district of Beijing, China.

body.t: A branch of mechanics, considered part of continuum mechanics.

Its subfields broadly divide into fluid statics, which treats states at rest, and fluid dynamics, which treats motion. (In Japan, however, some people do not clearly distinguish the 2.) In engineering, it is sometimes divided into hydraulics, dealing with water, and aerodynamics, dealing with air.

body.t: Rayleigh-Taylor instability is a phenomenon in which, when 2 fluids of different densities meet at an interface, a force acts from the denser fluid toward the less dense fluid, and disturbances grow from small irregularities at the interface, destabilizing fluid motion. It was identified by Rayleigh in 1883 and G. I. Taylor in 1950.

For example, if water and less-dense oil are separated with water above and oil below, the boundary is in unstable equilibrium, and a small disturbance instantly reverses their positions. This phenomenon, caused when a denser fluid pushes a less-dense one through gravity or similar effects, is Rayleigh-Taylor instability.

Rayleigh–Taylor instability is the greatest factor impeding spherically symmetric implosion in central-ignition laser fusion. It is also actively studied in material-mixing processes inside stars, such as supernova explosions.

body.t: Nonlinear optics (Japanese reading: hisenkei kogaku; English: nonlinear optics) is the field studying the diverse nonlinear responses (phenomena) of matter—that is, responses not proportional to the light's electromagnetic field—when very strong light interacts with matter. It developed with the advent of lasers, but nonlinear optical effects also play essential roles within lasers themselves, governing their characteristics. It is closely related to quantum optics.

Optical constants of materials, such as refractive index and absorption, can be regarded as constants when light is weak. When light becomes strong (requiring consideration of nonlinearity), they vary with light intensity. Phenomena originating in such nonlinearity of interactions between light and matter are called nonlinear optical phenomena.

A phenomenon in which incident light of a certain frequency causes matter to emit light at integer multiples of that frequency. It is a fundamental process among the earliest observed nonlinear optical effects; processes emitting light at 2 times (second-harmonic generation: SHG) and 3 times (third-harmonic generation: THG) the frequency are particularly important. Its main application is converting laser wavelengths to shorter wavelengths.

Under phase-matching conditions, incident light of multiple different frequencies causes a material to generate light at a combined frequency different from any of them. Also called sum-frequency or difference-frequency generation. Optical mixing can be treated as a generalization of optical harmonic generation, but is distinguished by having 2 incident lights of different frequencies.

Difference-frequency generation is also associated with optical parametric amplification. Discovering these phenomena made it possible to convert light into various frequencies. The Manley–Rowe relations are used when considering them.

A phenomenon where the sum of the frequencies of 2 emitted lights equals the incident light's frequency. It is sometimes discussed alongside optical mixing from the perspective of frequency conversion. Optical parametric amplifiers, optical parametric oscillators, stimulated Raman scattering, coherent Raman scattering, stimulated Brillouin scattering, stimulated Compton scattering, four-wave mixing, etc.

A phenomenon in which multiple photons are simultaneously absorbed or emitted, producing a transition to an eigenstate corresponding to the sum or difference of their energies. Generally, n-photon transitions have parity rules of even–odd between initial and final states when n is odd, and even–even or odd–odd when n is even. In the simplest case, n=2, there is two-photon absorption, in which 2 photons are simultaneously absorbed, and Raman scattering, in which 1 photon is absorbed and 1 emitted. Stimulated Raman scattering and coherent Raman scattering are nonlinear optical processes, but ordinary Raman scattering (spontaneous Raman scattering) is not classified as a nonlinear optical process. It is used in highly sensitive, high-resolution spectroscopy and isotope separation, among other applications.

A phenomenon in which a medium's refractive index, normally independent of light intensity, acquires a distribution within the medium because of intense incident light. By extending the discussion to a complex refractive index, 2-photon absorption can also be treated as a nonlinear refractive-index change. The phenomena are diverse: a beam converges to a point within the medium (self-focusing), its frequency is modulated (self-phase modulation), or transmitted-light intensity depends on the history of incident-light intensity (optical bistability). Self-focusing can destroy optical components and is therefore an important technical issue for high-power lasers; self-phase modulation is important for ultrashort laser pulses and optical-fiber information communication technologies, while optical bistability is important for optical switching.

A phenomenon in which a medium’s refractive index varies depending on the electric field applied to it. A type of nonlinear refractive-index change. Called the electro-optic effect, with the Pockels and Kerr effects known as second- and third-order nonlinear optical effects. Used in variable-focus lenses needing no moving parts, among other applications.
TBD. Studied as a method for realizing adaptive optics.

Since nonlinear optical effects appear in all materials, their subjects include not only ordinary gases, liquids, and solids but also plasmas, living organisms, and particle beams. Nonlinear optics studies phenomena themselves and has broad applications, including optoelectronics for generating, controlling, and measuring light; nonlinear spectroscopy exploring material properties through nonlinear optical effects; and laser engineering using this knowledge and these techniques.

body.t: Nonlinear biology (Japanese reading: hisenkei seibutsugaku) is a branch of nonlinear science covering fields from molecules to species populations. Although it overlaps considerably with mathematical biology, its characteristic may be its active emphasis on the nonlinearity of models

Prior studies include Alan Turing's theory of morphogenesis using a reaction-diffusion model and Hodgkin and Huxley's action-potential model. The vast accumulated work on nonlinear-network models classified as systems neuroscience could probably also be classified as nonlinear science.

The current task in this field is consciously applying general methodologies of nonlinear science proposed by Yoshitsugu Oono and others, such as phenomenology and renormalization, to biological problems; however, because the gap between experiment and theory is deep, Japan has no notable successful examples yet.

body.t: Nonlinear narrative (Japanese reading: hisenkei no katarikuchi; English: nonlinear narrative, disjointed narrative, disrupted narrative) is a storytelling technique used in literature, film, and other media. Examples include events described out of chronological order, indirect causal relationships, parallel plots, inserted dreams, and plays within plays. It is used for purposes such as imitating structure and reproducing memory.
“In medias res,” starting a story midway rather than from its beginning, has existed since antiquity and was established in Homer’s epic “Iliad” in the 8th century BCE

. The Indian epic “Mahabharata,” created around the 5th century BCE, tells most of its story through flashbacks. Among the medieval “One Thousand and One Nights,” “Sindbad,” “The City of Brass,” and “The Three Apples” use both in medias res and flashbacks; this is said to have been inspired by the “Panchatantra”
From the late 19th to early 20th century, modernist writers Joseph Conrad, Virginia Woolf, Ford Madox Ford, Marcel Proust, William Faulkner, and others used avant-garde nonlinear narration.

body.t: A complex system (Japanese reading: fukuzatsukei; English: complex system) is a system in which multiple interconnected factors combine to show some property as a whole (or behavior derived from that property), while its overall behavior is not evident from the individual factors or parts

For these, narrow-scope and short-term predictions are not impossible based on empirical elements, but it is difficult to understand the grounds for such predictions by reducing them to more fundamental laws (reductionism). There are two types of system complexity: disorganized complexity and organized complexity

. Essentially, this distinction calls complexity arising from a multitude of factors “disorganized,” while describing a system’s display of emergence (even if it may in some cases have extremely limited factors) as “organized.”

Complex systems are by no means unusual: many systems interesting and useful to humans are complex. Examples of complex systems as models for studying systemic complexity include ant nests, human economies and societies, weather phenomena, nervous systems, cells, organisms including humans, and modern energy and communications infrastructure.

Complex systems are studied in diverse fields including natural science, mathematics, and social science. The 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for pioneering research into climate systems as complex systems.
This was the first Nobel Prize awarded to complex-systems science. See also the article on complex-systems science.

body.t: According to Hesiod's “Theogony,” this is a primordial deity that existed at the beginning of the world. When the world (universe) began, a place (chora) was needed in which things could secure existence; Chaos first existed as an empty “place,” or gap, and within it things such as the earth (Gaia) came into being. Hesiod also calls Chaos a chasm (cleft). Following the emergence of Chaos, Gaia (Earth) was born, followed by Tartarus, the deepest depths of the dark underworld. The exceedingly beautiful Eros (primordial love) was also born. However, these primordial gods are not considered children of Chaos. Erebus (gloom) and dark Nyx (Night) were born from Chaos. Aether (upper air) and Hemera (Hēmerā; daylight) were further born from Nyx. Hesiod sings that the world began in this way.

body.t: Chaos theory (Japanese reading: kaosu riron; English: chaos theory; German: Chaosforschung; French: théorie du chaos) studies phenomena displaying complex behavior found in some dynamical systems, considered unpredictable because of numerical errors. Also called chaotic dynamics.

Unpredictable here by no means means random. Although its behavior follows deterministic laws, solutions cannot be obtained by integration, so numerical analysis must be used to learn its future (and past) behavior. However, sensitivity to initial values requires information of infinite precision at a given time, and errors arising during numerical analysis (inevitably, because computers cannot handle infinitely many digits) also amplify the discrepancy between obtained values and true values. It means prediction is therefore practically impossible.

The Lorenz equations are nonlinear ordinary differential equations first studied by mathematician and meteorologist Edward Lorenz. They attract attention for having chaotic solutions for particular parameter values and initial conditions. In particular, the set of chaotic solutions of the Lorenz equations is called the Lorenz attractor. Often used to explain the so-called butterfly effect, the sensitivity to initial values of deterministic simultaneous ordinary differential equations was met with surprise and sparked research into chaos.
Solution trajectories of the chaotic Lorenz equations.

body.t: There are ouroboros types in which 1 creature forms a ring and consumes itself, and types in which 2 creatures form a ring and consume each other. In the 2-creature type, 1 has a plain appearance with nothing added (though some versions wear a crown), while the other 1 has 1 crown, 1 pair of wings, and 1 pair of limbs.

Snakes symbolize “death and rebirth” and “immortality” through shedding skin and growing large, and their strong vitality enduring prolonged starvation. A snake eating its own tail thus gained symbolic meaning as something complete without beginning or end.
In Hellenistic cultural regions such as Alexandria in late antiquity, it expressed ideas that world creation was all and one, perfection, and the world spirit.
In alchemy, used to symbolize the union of opposites (such as yin and yang).
Carl Gustav Jung regarded it as symbolizing archetypes of the human psyche.

Its meanings also broadly include cyclicality (vicious cycles/eternal return), continuity (eternity/circular motion/death and rebirth/destruction and creation), primordiality (the origin of the universe), infinity (immortality), and perfection (omniscience and omnipotence); it has been used in many cultures and religions.

body.t: Object-Oriented Ontology (often abbreviated OOO) is a philosophical position holding that objects exist independently of human perception and questioning the central role of the human perspective in traditional philosophy.

In metaphysics, object-oriented ontology (OOO) is a 21st-century school influenced by Heidegger that rejects privileging human existence over the existence of nonhuman objects. This contrasts with what is called the “anthropocentrism” of Kant's Copernican revolution, accepted in most other current metaphysics. In most other metaphysics, phenomenal objects are said to conform to the subject's mind and thus become products of human cognition. Object-oriented ontology maintains that objects exist independently of human perception (as Kantian noumena) and are not ontologically exhausted by their relations with humans or other objects. For object-oriented ontologists, all relations, including nonhuman relations, are,

Object-oriented ontology is often considered part of speculative realism. This critiques post-Kantian philosophical inquiry's correlation between thought and being, outside which reality cannot be known. However, object-oriented ontology predates speculative realism and makes explicit claims about the nature and equivalence of object relations with which not all speculative realists agree. The term “object-oriented philosophy” was coined by the movement's founder, Graham Harman, in his 1999 doctoral dissertation, “Tool-Being: Elements in a Theory of Objectory.” In 2009, Levi Bryant rephrased Harman's original designation as “object-oriented ontology,” giving the movement its current name.

TIPS on recording brainwaves, for your reference!

Unfortunately, VIE’s sensor cannot avoid contamination by neck muscle electrical activity, so the raw waveform needs L-R or R-L processing. It is the simple karaoke (vocal removal) method popular around 20 years ago. It takes some effort, but I will describe how using “Audacity (Japanese version)” as an example.
*SS1–SS6 below are filenames of attached screenshots. Please consult them alongside the text.
(1) SS1 shows the recorded brainwave Wave file loaded; because it is raw, it contains electromyographic noise.
(2) Reserve space using “Tracks” → “Add New” → “Stereo Track,” then select the entire current track and copy/paste it (see SS2; this protects the original file).
(3) Select the copied-and-pasted track (2ch), choose “Tracks” → “Mix” → “Stereo to Mono,” and split it into 2 mono tracks.
(4) Select “either” of the 2 split tracks and choose “Effect” → “Invert” (positive and negative are exchanged).
*That is SS3; please compare the top and bottom (LR).
(5) “Select both” of the 2 split tracks, inverted and uninverted, and choose “Tracks” → “Mix” → “Mix and Render to New Track.”
(6) As in SS4, subtraction removes large noise, but whisker-like noise remains.
(7) Select this difference track and apply, for example, a steep low-pass filter like SS5 through “Effect” → “Classic Filters.”
(8) EEG components then emerge as in SS6, so afterward process this freely!

Solids have 2 types: crystals, with regularly arranged atoms, and amorphous (noncrystalline) materials, with irregularly arranged atoms. Generally, minerals such as ice, metals, and quartz have crystalline structures, while glass and similar materials have amorphous structures.

Metals are also cooled from a molten raw-material state, but in that state their atoms are neatly arranged. This state is called “amorphous.” Its characteristics include high strength, corrosion resistance, and abundant magnetic properties.

body.t: **Minimum-norm estimation** is a method seeking an “optimal result” using data. Particularly when several answers are conceivable, it selects the solution with the “smallest value.” Specifically used when determining model parameters (weights).
- When **data are full of noise**. For example, when sensor data or measurements are slightly inaccurate, it helps find solutions while considering noise.
- When multiple solutions exist and one wants to choose the solution with minimum norm (magnitude).
- Let observed data (results) be \( \mathbf{y} \), and their associated features (input data) be \( \mathbf{X} \).
- The aim is to find the parameters \( \mathbf{w} \) obtained using \( \mathbf{X} \).
- A common method minimizes the difference between observed results and model predictions (least squares).
- If there are multiple solutions giving similar results, minimum-norm estimation selects the one with the smallest “size.” This produces stable results.
- **Stability**: small changes in data do not greatly change estimated results.
- **Preventing overfitting**: Avoids the model fitting the data too closely (overfitting), enabling better generalization.
- **Signal processing**: Used to clean noisy signals, among other purposes.
- **Machine learning**: Used to obtain stable parameters when building a model.
Minimum-norm estimation obtains stable solutions even with inaccurate data, particularly useful when multiple solutions are conceivable. This enables more reliable models.

excerpt.t: **Minimum-norm estimation** is a method seeking an “optimal result” using data. Particularly when several answers are conceivable, it selects the solution with the “smallest value.” Specifically used when determining model parameters (weights).

body.t: “Ragtime” emerged from Black music in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, characterized by unprecedented syncopation of ragged (displaced) rhythms and occasional emphasis on offbeats.
The difference between ragtime and jazz is whether playing follows the score and whether there is improvisation.﻿

Ragtime is a musical style performed in saloons and similar venues mainly by African American pianists from the 1870s, characterized by playing according to the score. Pieces in 2/4 or 4/4 time feature rhythms with frequent syncopation. A common style has the left-hand accompaniment maintaining a steady 2-beat meter while the right hand plays rhythmic melodies.
Jazz, meanwhile, emphasizes improvisation, characterized by performing while creating music on the spot.

body.t: A Turing machine is a hypothetical computing device that defined “computation” in a paper published by Alan Turing in 1936. Its structure is simple: if this device performs a calculation and can output data, it is defined as computable; if data output is impossible, it is defined as uncomputable.

The astonishing thing about a Turing machine is its extreme simplicity. It has just 1 tape and 1 reading head. All it can do is move the head 1 character to the right or left, write characters on the tape, and read characters. With just these mechanisms, every algorithm can be implemented.

body.t: Revealed that ventral tegmental area dopamine (VTA DA) projects to the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
Dopamine is released in the BLA during stimulus-reward pairing.
Necessary and sufficient for associating identifying reward features with predictive cues, but does not assign general incentive properties to cues or mediate reinforcement.
Dopamine's contribution to learning has long been known.

These learning signals have conventionally been interpreted as caching general reward values in predictors and reinforcing corresponding policies that rely on past success rather than prospectively considering specific outcomes4,5,6. Adaptive decision-making, however, often requires such prospective consideration.

To ensure flexible behavior, humans and other animals not only learn predictive events' general values but also encode relations between these cues and identifying features of their associated outcomes.

Little is known about its function because it receives less attention than more common VTA DA projections to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex. BLA itself has recently been shown important in forming detailed identity-specific cue–reward memories.
Dopamine is released in the BLA during stimulus-reward learning.

Nor does it assign general incentive properties to cues to support nonspecific motivation. These data reveal that the VTA DA →BLA pathway contributes importantly to forming detailed, identity-specific cue–reward memories, fundamental components of internal models of environmental relationships (also known as cognitive maps) that support flexible decision-making.

body.t: Room impulse response (RIR) is an important concept in acoustical engineering, signal processing, and similar fields. It represents the response observed after sound from a source is reflected, scattered, and absorbed within a particular space.

Specifically, RIR is defined as follows: It shows the changes in time and amplitude when a short acoustic signal (impulse) emitted from a sound source reflects off indoor surfaces such as walls, floor, and ceiling, and these reflected sounds are recorded at an observation point (for example, a microphone's position). It is used to evaluate the acoustic characteristics of a particular space, develop acoustic simulations and speech-processing algorithms, and more.

RIR plays an important role in audio-signal-processing applications including recording and reproducing speech and music, noise removal, sound-field rationalization, and speech recognition and synthesis.

body.t: Another feature of the data shared across cultures is that response distributions tend to be symmetric across cyclic permutations (Fig. 3). For example, the modes at 1:1:2, 1:2:1, and 2:1:1 are roughly equally prominent within a given participant group. However, there was reason to expect that the most frequent permutations would be those in which the long interval occurs last43,44,45. This is because, when this configuration is played cyclically, the long interval provides a gap that helps group the pattern according to Gestalt principles43. Comparing the frequency of each cyclic permutation in each participant group, we indeed found a consistent tendency in this direction. Likewise, in 33 of the 39 groups, participants made their first tap immediately after the long interval. See Extended Data Fig. 3 (and “Analysis of cyclic permutations and symmetry” in Methods) for further analyses.

body.t: The TR-808 is a drum machine released by Roland in 1980, highly regarded as a classic. From its name “808,” it is colloquially called “yaoya” in Japan. Manufactured from 1980 to 1983, with 12,000 units produced. Its price at the time was 150,000 yen.

Born in Osaka in 1930. Opened Kakehashi Musen (an electrical appliance store) in 1954. Founded the electronic musical instrument manufacturer Ace Electronic Industries, Inc. in 1960 and a joint venture with the American Hammond company in 1968. Left both companies in 1972 and founded Roland. Released a succession of innovative electronic musical instruments, including world firsts. Received an honorary doctorate in music from Berklee College of Music in the United States in 1991. Established the Roland Foundation for Art and Culture in 1994 and became its chairman. In 2000, left his handprints and signature at Hollywood’s RockWalk in the United States in recognition of his enormous contribution to the music world through technological innovations in electronic musical instruments. Received the “Lifetime Achievement Award” from m.i.p.a, an organization of music/instrument magazines from countries around the world, in 2002. In 2005, received the title of honorary professor from China’s Central Conservatory of Music for his global contributions through the development of electronic musical instruments and his major influence on their spread within China. This was the first time the school had awarded an honorary professorship to someone other than a musician, and he was the second Japanese recipient after conductor Seiji Ozawa. In 2008, received an honorary professorship from the University of Glamorgan in Britain in recognition of his contributions to the music industry and music education. In 2013/2, jointly received the “Technical GRAMMY Award” from The Recording Academy with Mr. Dave Smith (former president of Sequential Circuits). This recognized his efforts to establish “MIDI” as a universal worldwide standard for electronic musical instruments regardless of manufacturer, and the MIDI standard’s subsequent contributions to the music industry. His book “Music Is My Life’s Work: Dreams Devoted to Developing Electronic Musical Instruments” (Ongaku no Tomo Sha) has also been published in the United States, Germany, Taiwan, and China. His motto is “Simple & Straight.”

body.t: Surfing entropy. “surf on entropy,” as Brian Eno said in an interview.

The idea was that what lies between a completely controlled state (cosmos) and endless chaos becomes the most interesting. A place where subject and object can switch, where one is both active and passive, and where controllable and uncontrollable things exist simultaneously. I think what Eno wanted to convey with “surf on entropy” was the bodily sensation of riding the entropy generated in that place as if surfing.

body.t: A painter active in the 5th century BCE.

According to Pliny the Elder's Natural History, Zeuxis and his contemporary Parrhasius (English version), who worked in Ephesus and later Athens, held a contest to determine who was superior. When Zeuxis unveiled his painting of grapes, they were reportedly so realistic that birds flew down and tried to peck them. However, when Parrhasius showed a picture hidden behind a curtain and Zeuxis urged him to draw it aside, the curtain itself proved to be a trompe-l'œil painting. Parrhasius won, and Zeuxis reportedly said, “I deceived birds, but Parrhasius deceived Zeuxis.” This story was often cited in 18th- to 19th-century painting theory to defend techniques that produce spatial illusions. A similar anecdote tells how, while Zeuxis was painting a boy holding grapes, birds once again tried to peck the grapes; he became very displeased and said that if he had painted the boy's figure more poorly, the birds would have been frightened and would not have approached.

body.t: Harmonic analysis is a field of mathematics concerned with representing functions and signals as superpositions of basic waves, studying Fourier series, Fourier transforms, and their generalizations. Problems can be analyzed by focusing on principal frequency (wavelength) components.
Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, harmonic analysis covered broad subjects with diverse applications in signal processing, quantum mechanics, neuroscience, and more.

“Harmonic” originally came from physical eigenvalue problems, denoting waves with frequencies that are integer multiples of another frequency (such as harmonic vibration frequencies in instrument strings), but is now used in generalized ways beyond its original meaning.

The classical Fourier transform on Rn remains an active research area, with particular interest in Fourier transforms of more general objects such as tempered distributions. For example, when appropriate assumptions are imposed on a Schwartz distribution f, one can consider translating those assumptions into assumptions about the Fourier transform of f. The Paley–Wiener theorem is one example.

Sometimes one image spread across the three screens, and sometimes separate images appeared on each of the three; used in several scenes, including the final departure for Italy, it achieved an overwhelming spectacle. However, “The Jazz Singer” (1927) was released in America in the same year as “Napoleon,” and with it cinema entered the era of talkies. Investment in large-screen systems was neglected, and consequently “Napoleon” was almost never screened in its complete form (in America this epic, with a running time of 5 hours, was merely shortened to 1 hour 20 minutes and released reprinted in a standard version; in Japan, too, only a 17.5-millimeter version was released).
