body.t: Max Vernon Mathews (1926/11/13 - 2011/4/21) was a scientist, inventor, and musician born in Nebraska, United States, and a pioneer of computer music.

After studying at the California Institute of Technology and Massachusetts Institute of Technology and earning a Doctor of Science in 1954, he worked at Bell Laboratories, developing the MUSIC-N series of music-programming languages (1957–), widely used for sound generation. He subsequently became a leading figure in digital audio and sound synthesis, and in research on human-machine interfaces associated with playing musical instruments.

The performance in 1951 by CSIRAC, a computer developed in Australia, was the world's first computer sound synthesis, but through the MUSIC-N series he developed, Mathews greatly contributed to subsequent music-programming languages and applications using digital technology worldwide.

In 1961, he added an accompaniment to “Daisy Bell,” the culmination of his colleague John Larry Kelly Jr.'s speech synthesis, and served as director of Bell Laboratories' Acoustics and Behavioral Research Center from 1962 to 1985. The center studies speech communication, visual communication, learning and memory, robotics, organized knowledge, analysis of subjectivity, physical acoustics, and more. He served as scientific advisor to France's Institute for Research and Coordination in Acoustics/Music (IRCAM) from 1974 to 1980, and as a professor at Stanford University from 1987 onward. Awarded the IEEE David Sarnoff Award in 1973.
Died in San Francisco of pneumonia on 2011/4/21
Max, a visual programming language widely used today by composers and media artists, is named after Mathews.

In 1988, drawing on research begun at the MIT lab, he developed Patcher, a control interface for the 4X, at IRCAM. He also ported it to Macintosh computers as personal research, and it was commercially released by Opcode under the name “Max” in 1990. Meanwhile, in 1989, as a researcher on IRCAM's “Musical Workstation” team, he developed Max/FTS for NeXT and the Ircam Signal Processing Workstation. From 1994, he became a faculty member and researcher in the music department at the University of California, San Diego (UCSD), and developed the freeware Pure Data in 1996. He currently serves as associate director of the university's Center for Research in Computing and the Arts (CRCA).

This movement, which “challenged classicism and the Enlightenment and asserted the superiority of emotion over reason,” was advanced by Goethe and Schiller, and later brought German Romantic literature to fruition with Novalis, the Brothers Grimm, and others. The following words are by poet Novalis (1772–1801), who could be called 1 of the leading early Romantics. I quoted them because I thought they expressed the Romantics' way of seeing things well.

The world must be romanticized. In this way one will find its original meaning once again. Whenever I give the common a higher meaning, the usual a mysterious aspect, the familiar the dignity of the unknown, the finite and infinite appearance, in this way I romanticize it.

As a musical form, a scherzo is a humorous, lively triple-meter piece developed in the Baroque period. In music history, it began to be used in middle movements of symphonies and chamber works from the 1780s.﻿
Characteristics of scherzos include the following.

The scherzo was adopted and developed by Franz Joseph Haydn, Beethoven, and others. Beethoven's scherzos are faster than Haydn's, and some pieces make their 3-beat meter unrecognizable. Chopin and Brahms also wrote scherzos as independent piano pieces.

body.t: Musique concrète, also translated as “concrete music,” refers to music produced using recorded sounds, and was begun in France in the 1940s by P. Schaeffer, a radio-station engineer. Instead of musical tones, recordings of human and animal voices, natural sounds, urban noise, and so on were electrically and mechanically altered and combined. In 44, Schaeffer created an experimental studio in a corner of the radio station and initially began producing music using records; in 48 it was first broadcast on radio. In 51, after P. Henry joined Schaeffer's activities, the Groupe de Recherche de Musique Concrète (GRMC) was established in Paris, leading to the production of many works. According to Schaeffer, the name musique concrète was chosen to contrast with traditional “abstract” music, rather than because it used concrete (Concrète, Concrete) sounds. Schaeffer considered “abstract music” to move from abstract ideas and conceptions toward concrete musical works, whereas “concrete music” moved from concrete sounds toward the expression of abstract ideas and conceptions. From the 60s onward, Schaeffer withdrew from actual production and concentrated on theoretical reflections on concrete music, including, for example, systematic consideration of listening to sounds with their sources unseen (“acousmatic” listening). In his later years, however, he left a painful interview summing up his life in concrete music as “a waste.” This interview is simply regrettable as the words of someone who pioneered an entirely new genre of music that had not previously existed; nevertheless, of course, the founder's later abandonment of its potential does not erase the importance of musique concrète as the first example to explore the possibilities of music using recorded sounds.

The symphonic poem was established by Hungarian composer Franz Liszt. Attempting to express nonmusical arts through music, Liszt named Tasso, composed as an overture in 1854, a “symphonic poem.” His symphonic poems include What One Hears on the Mountain, based on Hugo's poetry collection Autumn Leaves, and Les Préludes.
After Liszt's death, German composer Richard Strauss expanded the concept of the symphonic poem, composing works emphasizing more inward expression. Strauss called his symphonic poems “tone poems.”
Representative symphonic poems include the following.

body.t: Serial music (musique sérielle) is a compositional technique widely used in the 1950s.

Serial music composes by turning all sonic events—pitch (height), note value (duration), timbre, intensity (strength), and so on—into series and manipulating them through permutations. This expands Schoenberg’s twelve-tone system and is also called integral serialism.﻿
The chronology of serial music is as follows.
In 1949, O. Messiaen published the piano piece “Mode of Values and Intensities.”﻿
At the Darmstadt Summer Courses for New Music in the early 1950s, L. Nono, P. Boulez, K. Stockhausen, B. Maderna, and others spread serial music through the avant-garde music world.﻿
By the late 1950s, increasing theoretical complexity and the introduction of chance and tone clusters reduced works produced purely through series alone.﻿
In the 1970s, B. Ferneyhough and others presented works continuing serial music as post-serialist composers.
The thinking of serial music would later be applied to algorithmic composition.

body.t: Program music consists of instrumental or ensemble works with titles or texts whose content they seek to express. Its characteristic is a story prepared separately from the score and shared with listeners and performers.
“Absolute music,” contrasted with program music, means pure instrumental music concentrating on the construction of sound itself without direct connections to content such as paintings or literature.

A forerunner of program music was French composer Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique, presented in 1830. Its titles include “Dreams, Passions,” “A Ball,” “Scene in the Fields,” “March to the Scaffold,” and “Dream of a Witches' Sabbath.”

Program music was a suitable form for expressing personal worlds for Romantic composers who reacted against the formalism of Classical music. Explaining music through words opened the possibility of listeners hearing more precisely the world the composer intended to depict.
Program music does not include songs, operas, ballet music, and so on.

From the Renaissance onward, they increasingly took on the character of polyphonic sacred vocal works not based on the Ordinary of the Mass and were performed in worship.

Developing since the medieval Minnesänger period, it features not only poems set to melodies but piano accompaniments rich in musical ideas. Many composers have written Lieder, including Schubert, Schumann, Brahms, Wolf, Mahler, and R. Strauss.
Schubert's lieder texts include many by 8–9 poets such as Goethe, Schiller, Handel, Matthisson, Heine, and Müller.

body.t: The Dead Sea Scrolls are ancient documents found in caves around the Dead Sea, between present-day Israel and Jordan. Containing the oldest manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, they have great religious and historical significance.
Thought to date between around 250 BCE and 70 CE.
Many are written in Hebrew, also including documents in Aramaic, Greek, and Nabataean.﻿
Many are written on parchment, with some on cowhide or papyrus.﻿
They are thought to have been copied by followers of a Jewish sect called the Essenes.
The canonical text of the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament)
Old Testament apocrypha and the group of documents called “pseudepigrapha.”
Sectarian documents (rules and ritual books of the Qumran community, etc.).
New fragments were found in Cave 8 in the Nahal Hever wadi from late 2019 to early 2020.

body.t: German psychiatrist Hans Berger was the first to measure human brainwaves with an electroencephalograph. Berger was obsessed with researching telepathy. Professor Faisal Mushtaq, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Leeds in Britain, explains that Berger developed the electroencephalograph as a tool for measuring “psychic energy” and secretly used it on his own son, then in his 10s, early in his research. Mushtaq notes that Berger has been a controversial figure from then to the present because of suspected connections to the Nazi regime.

body.t: The word “mode” derives from the Latin modus, meaning “measurement,” “limit,” “regulation,” “method,” “style,” or “form.”
“Mode” as a fashion term derives from French “mode,” meaning “trend” or “fashion.”
From the 15th to 16th centuries, Italian fashions strongly influenced France and other countries.﻿
In the 17th–18th centuries, distinctive fashion developed under French court culture.
In 19th-century France, haute-couture designers modernized and generalized the traditions of aristocratic fashion.
In the 1970–80s, wearing DC brands such as Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto, which expanded from Japan worldwide, became known as “mode-style” fashion.
In fashion media, it includes nuances such as stylish and sophisticated, and is sometimes used to express an advanced style opposite to “conservative.”

body.t: What this experiment shows is that the sense of immersion seems to change with the degree of order in a work's design (shapes, in this case). The brain pays more attention and spends more time classifying moderate order than high (easily understood) order, so moderate order seems most suited to ambiguity, attracting interest, and making people think. But with low order (random, scattered, difficult), the brain apparently pays little attention and responds weakly --> it turns into noise or is ignored. So in the end moderate order really seems to be number 1 in terms of “leaving an impression”!

body.t: Simulationism (English: simulationism) is an art movement that spread chiefly in New York during the 1980s. Opposing the uniqueness (aura) of modern art, it is characterized by appropriating (borrowing) images from popular art using cut-up, sampling, remix, and other techniques. It is also called simulation art or appropriation art.

Behind this lies the condition of contemporary society in which the distinction between original and copy disappears and copies are consumed in large quantities, as Jean Baudrillard observed in “Simulacra and Simulation.” By appropriating images, simulationism reexamines originality, critically dismantles the authority and power of original works, and directs attention toward new relationships between images and social systems (gender, commercialism, race and identity, institutionalized art).

Representative artists include Cindy Sherman, who photographed self-portraits acting out scenes resembling film stills; Sherrie Levine, who copied Walker Evans's photographs and made them her own works; Richard Prince, who copied advertising photographs as his own works; and Jeff Koons, who displayed vacuum cleaners in glass cases as artworks.
In Japan, art critic Noi Sawaragi's arguments in his 1991 Simulationism: House Music and Appropriation Art greatly influenced artists and others.

body.t: Around August 1954, the Gutai Art Association was formed by young avant-garde artists in the Kansai region who had gathered around Jiro Yoshihara. Its founding members are often taken to be the 17 people whose works appeared in the first issue of its journal “Gutai”: Jiro Yoshihara, Shozo Shimamoto, Tsuruko Yamazaki, Masatoshi Masanobu, Michio Yoshihara, Chiyu Uemae, Toshio Yoshida, Sadami Azuma, Yutaka Funai, Shigeru Tsujimura, Hideo Yoshihara, Tamiko Yamada, Hiroshi Okada, Yoshio Sekine, Kei Iseya, Hajime Okamoto, and Toichiro Fujikawa. Shimamoto proposed the name “Gutai.” The following year, 1955, Kazuo Shiraga, Saburo Murakami, Akira Kanayama, and Atsuko Tanaka, who exhibited at the Shinseisaku Association exhibition and had formed a group called “0-kai,” joined. Sadamasa Motonaga joined that same year. Given these origins, the association was centered on a teacher-student relationship, rather exceptionally for a postwar art movement (art movement [English version]).

Under Yoshihara's instruction, “Do not imitate others. Create something that has never existed before,” which provoked a break in expression rather than a continuation of modern painting, the young artists presented innovative works in rapid succession, including the outdoor “Experimental Outdoor Exhibition of Modern Art to Challenge the Midsummer Sun,” staged among the pine trees of Ashiya Park in the scorching sun, and an international advertising-balloon exhibition on a department-store rooftop. They then vigorously developed activities including publishing their journal Gutai, holding “Gutai Exhibitions” in Tokyo (the first Gutai Exhibition at Ohara Kaikan (English version)) and the Kansai region, and presenting works on stages such as Sankei Hall in Umeda. Eventually, French critic Michel Tapié introduced Gutai widely overseas as “an example of Art Informel in Japan,” and it became highly regarded. (Meanwhile, its introduction as an abstract-painting group meant that subsequent activities centered on two-dimensional works, and early three-dimensional works and performances using the stage ceased.)

body.t: The glymphatic system is a recently discovered waste clearance system in the central nervous system of vertebrates, acting as a "pseudo-lymphatic" system for the brain. It facilitates the removal of metabolic waste products and other substances from the brain's interstitial fluid, primarily during sleep. This system is crucial for maintaining brain health and its dysfunction is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases.

A hydrophobic peptide accumulating in the brains of Alzheimer's patients. Measuring blood concentrations requires high sensitivity. Dementia patients in Japan are estimated at over 6 million, approximately 24 million worldwide, and projected to reach 80 million in 2040.

Studies using mouse models showed that stimulation with 40Hz light or sound promotes clearance of amyloid-β from the brain.
This stimulation is thought to activate the brain’s glymphatic system (its waste-disposal system) and promote amyloid-β clearance.﻿
40Hz stimulation is also expected to reduce brain atrophy due to Alzheimer’s disease and prevent cellular damage.﻿

body.t: An expressive approach that emphasizes the “process” of making a work rather than its final completed form as an artwork, focusing on the characteristics of materials and techniques. A tendency shaping expression from the late 1960s through the 70s, it can also be traced to elements of Abstract Expressionist painting such as Jackson Pollock’s dripping and Morris Louis’s staining. Tendencies emphasizing process and material characteristics converged and diverged from Minimal Art, Conceptual Art, and Performance Art, connecting to post-minimal tendencies. Major artists include Robert Morris, Richard Serra, Keith Sonnier, Eva Hesse, Bruce Nauman, Robert Smithson, Gary Kuehn, and Barry Le Va.

The Guggenheim Museum explains: “Process artists address matters involving the body, chance, improvisation, and the freely open-ended qualities of nontraditional materials such as wax, felt, and latex. Using these materials, they create unusual forms in irregular arrangements resulting from actions such as cutting, hanging, and dropping, or organic processes such as growth, condensation, freezing, and decomposition.” Morris advocated “Anti Form,” emphasizing process, time, and material properties, developing a distinctive theory of process art.

An exhibition representative of this tendency was “Anti-Illusion: Procedures / Materials,” organized by Marcia Tucker and James Monte at the Whitney Museum in 69. Artists exhibiting included Morris, who arranged diverse materials; Serra, who showed “Splashing,” scattering lead; Nauman, who exhibited a structure called “Performance Corridor”; and Rafael Ferrer, who exhibited ice blocks outside the museum. Musicians Philip Glass and Steve Reich and filmmaker Michael Snow also participated, with attention focused on procedures and temporality in music and film.

Also that year, “Live in Your Head: When Attitudes Become Form. Works–Concepts–Processes–Situations–Information,” curated by Harald Szeemann to include the new expressive currents of the time such as Land Art, Conceptual Art, and Arte Povera, toured Europe beginning at Kunsthalle Bern in Switzerland. The project, demonstrating Szeemann’s incisive curating, was recognized for its major influence on subsequent developments in contemporary art and was recreated in 2013 as “When Attitudes Become Form: Bern 1969/Venice 2013.”

In Britain, there are also painter Bernard Cohen, who depicts the painting process by drawing figures made of straight and curved lines on a canvas until they fill the picture; Michael Craig-Martin, who used ordinary stationery to depict relationships among them that are difficult to recognize; and John Hilliard, who recorded the process of a camera reflected in a mirror repeatedly photographing itself while changing the aperture and shutter speed.
Robert Morris is one representative artist of process art.
Robert Morris’s 1968 essay “Anti Form” conveys the essence of process art.
Anti-form dismantles the geometric forms seen in Minimalism and prioritizes contingency caused by gravity and natural forces. It is therefore sometimes considered part of Post-Minimalism.
Robert Morris advocated and expressed the concept of perceiving indeterminate forms, including wood and metal scattered around a room, felt hanging from walls, and steam erupting from the ground.
Anti-form tendencies can also be seen in artists including Richard Serra, a contemporary of Robert Morris.

body.t: Tenchusatsu is a period considered in Sanmeigaku and the Four Pillars of Destiny to be “a time when heaven does not favor you,” during which fortune becomes unstable. It comes equally to everyone at intervals such as 2 years every 12 years, 2 months every 12 months, and 2 days every 12 days; annual Tenchusatsu is considered particularly influential. Rather than thinking “bad things will happen,” this period can be seen as a “recharging/hibernation period” for avoiding new starts and reflecting on yourself, offering an opportunity to reconsider how you live.

body.t: The Eleusinian Mysteries were the greatest mystery religion, worshipping the agricultural goddess Demeter and her daughter Persephone, practiced for approximately 2000 years at Eleusis in ancient Greece. With themes of death and rebirth, these rites promised initiates a happy afterlife. Their precise content remains mysterious because secrecy was strictly maintained, but they were revered as the holiest rites in classical antiquity.

body.t: Hexis is a Greek concept meaning “possession,” “state,” or “quality.” In Aristotle's ethics, it is an important term referring to virtues (dispositions, habits) acquired through repetition. It represents an “established state of mind and body” underlying actions, rather than a merely temporary condition.
Established virtue and disposition: In Aristotelian ethics, a state in which good actions (virtue) are established as a person's character rather than temporary.
“Having” or “state”: derives from Greek “echein” (to have) and means the state of possessing a certain quality.
Habit: also the etymological source of “habitus,” a disposition acquired through repeated action.
Phronesis (prudence): hexis (the disposition of desire) agrees with standards of appropriate action based on logos (reason).
Habitus: Bodily tendencies socially internalized, a term used in sociology (Bourdieu).

body.t: “Contemplative” means a state of deep, quiet, serious thought or introspection. It often refers to a calm, reflective mood, or to activities aimed at understanding or observation rather than action, such as meditation, prayer, and time spent in nature. Key aspects of contemplation: Deep thought: It means concentrating one's thoughts on a subject and thinking deeply, often over long periods. Quietness and stillness: Often associated with silence, stillness, and a calm, thoughtful attitude. Spirituality and religion: Historically, it referred to a life devoted to spiritual contemplation, as seen in religious orders. Presence: It means being fully present in the current moment and accepting it without immediate judgment or analysis.

body.t: “Niche picking” and “sxarr 1983” refer to a theoretical model in developmental psychology concerning heredity–environment interaction (gene–environment correlation), published in 1983 by psychologists Sandra Scarr and Kathleen McCartney.
*Your “sxarr” is presumed to be a typo for psychologist “Scarr.”
Explains “niche selection,” a central concept in this theory.
Scarr and McCartney proposed a Gene-Environment Correlation model in human development in which “genes direct the environment an individual experiences.”
Children are said not merely to passively accept given environments, but to select and construct environments (niches) suited to their own genetic traits (phenotype).
This 1983 model explains that children's engagement with their environment changes through the following 3 stages as they grow.

• Characteristics: parents transmit genes to children and also provide an environment based on their own genetic tendencies. For example, musically talented parents fill their home with instruments, and children naturally grow up in that environment.
• Period: Childhood and similar periods (decreases somewhat with age).

• Characteristics: Children's genetic characteristics and behavior (phenotypes) elicit specific responses from others. For example, an always-smiling, active child induces favorable engagement from adults, resulting in a more stimulating, social environment.
• Period: Adolescence and adulthood onward (becomes most dominant with growth).

• Characteristics: As people become more independent and their range of activity expands, they actively select and create specific environments (niches) that most comfortably fit their genetic temperament and abilities (genotype). For example, someone with a genetic tendency toward introversion and a love of reading will, as they grow, choose environments such as libraries, quiet clubs, or research careers.
The conclusions suggested by this theory

Scarr & McCartney's (1983) theory rejected extreme environmental determinism claiming “environment shapes humans completely.” It presents an important developmental-psychology perspective: as humans grow, they actively select “niches” in which they can realize their genetic potential to the fullest.
